(Madaniyya [except the last two verses, which are Makkan], and its verses are 130, though it is said 129. [It was revealed after al-Ma'ida].) It purges (tuqashqishu) from hypocrisy, meaning it clears (tubri'u) one of it, and it scatters (tuba'thiru) the secrets of the hypocrites, searching (tabhathu) for them, stirring them up, digging them out, exposing them, chastising them, expelling them, disgracing them and destroying them (tudamdimu) upon them. [The phrase "tabhath" (searches) — perhaps it is actually "tabhath" ("it searches"). (ʿ)]

If you say: why was it not introduced with the basmala (بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم), as in the other surahs? I say: Abdullah ibn Abbas asked Uthman, may Allah be pleased with them both, about that, and he said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) received a surah or a verse, he would say: 'Place it in the position where such and such is mentioned.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died without explaining to us where to place it. Its story was similar to the story of al-Anfal (The Spoils), so I combined them." [The phrase "its story was similar" refers to al-Anfal, as shown by the comparison, even though no mention of it has preceded here. The wording of al-Khazin is: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died without explaining to us where to place it. Al-Anfal was among the first things revealed at Madina, and al-Tawba was among the last things revealed of the Qur'an, and its story ..." etc. (ʿ)] Therefore they were joined together, and the two were called "the two companions" (al-qarinatayn). [Related by the compilers of the Sunan, Ibn Hibban, Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Ya'la and al-Bazzar, through Yusuf ibn Mihran and Yazid al-Farisi, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "I asked Uthman ibn Affan: what led you to put al-Anfal, which is of the mathani (oft-repeated), and al-Bara'a, which is of the ma'in (hundred-verse surahs), together, so you combined them?" He then related the hadith at length, except his words "and the two were called the two companions," which only Ishaq mentions.]

It is related from Abu Ka'b: "They only imagined that, because al-Anfal mentions the covenants, while al-Bara'a announces the abrogation of covenants."

Ibn Uyayna, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked and said: "The name of Allah is peace and security (salam wa aman), so it is not written in a repudiation or a state of war." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not say to one who offers you peace, "You are not a believer."﴾ It was said to him: "But the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to the people of war: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.'" He said: "That was only an opening, calling them, and he had not repudiated them. Do you not see that He says: ﴿And peace upon those who follow guidance﴾? So whoever is called to Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and responds, and is called to pay the jizya and responds, has followed guidance. As for the repudiation (nabdh), it is only disavowal (bara'a) and curse, and the people of war are not greeted with peace, nor is it said to them: 'Do not fear, and do not be afraid.'" [The word "mutaris" (ومترس), with a fatha on the mim and ta' and a sukun on the ra', is Persian and means "security/safe-conduct." (ʿ)] "And there is no harm": this is all security. [The hadith of Ibn Abbas (the long one) concerning Abu Sufyan, which is agreed upon (muttafaq ʿalayh). In it: he read the letter, and in it was: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. From Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, to Heraclius, the great one of the Romans: Peace upon those who follow guidance." The hadith continues.]

It was also said: al-Anfal and al-Tawba are one surah, both revealed concerning fighting, and they are counted as the seventh of the long surahs (al-tuwal). [The word "min al-tuwal" — al-tuwal, with a kasra then fatha, means "the long ones," as stated in al-Sihah. Another author's wording: al-tiwal.] After that come the ma'in. This is an apparent opinion, because together they are two hundred and six verses, so they are equal to one of the long surahs.

Others said: they are two surahs, so a gap was left between them for the view of those who say they are two surahs, and the basmala was omitted for the view of those who say they are one surah.

﴿Bara'a﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "This is a repudiation." And "min" (from) is for the starting point (ibtida' al-ghaya), attached to an omitted element, and is not a complement, as in your saying: "I am free of the religion" (bari'tu min al-din). The meaning is: "This is a repudiation coming from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made covenant," just as one says: "A letter from so-and-so to so-and-so." It is permissible that ﴿Bara'a﴾ be the subject, specified by its description, with the predicate being ﴿to those with whom you made covenant﴾, just as you say: "A man from the Banu Tamim is in the house."

It was read as "Bara'atun" in the accusative (nasb), meaning: "Hear a repudiation." The people of Najran read "min Allah" with a kasra on the nun, but the correct reading is the fatha with the definite article, because it is more common. The meaning is that Allah and His Messenger are free of the covenant you made with the polytheists, and that it is to be announced to them (manbudh ilayhim).

[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "Its meaning is: 'Allah and His Messenger have been freed from the covenant you made with the polytheists ...' etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "He related what he mentioned, but there is another secret, which is the one to be considered, and Allah knows best. That is because attributing the covenant to Allah and His Messenger, in a context where repudiation is attributed to the polytheists, is not fitting in the Law. Do you not see the instruction of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the commanders of the expeditions, where he says to them: 'When you alight at a fortress and they ask to descend under the judgment of Allah, then bring them down under your judgment, for you do not know whether you have hit upon the judgment of Allah concerning them or not. Therefore the covenant was attributed to the Muslims, without disowning it toward Allah. And Allah knows best."]

If you say: why did you attach the repudiation to Allah and His Messenger, and the covenant to the Muslims? I say: Allah had first permitted the covenant with the polytheists, so the Muslims agreed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and made covenant with them. Then, when they broke the covenant, Allah, exalted is He, made it obligatory to announce the repudiation to them. So the Muslims were addressed with what was renewed of that, and it was said to them: "Know that Allah and His Messenger have been freed from what you covenanted with the polytheists."

It is related that they made covenant with the polytheists of Makka and other Arabs, and they broke it, except for some people among them, namely the Banu Damra and the Banu Kinana. So the covenant was repudiated to those who broke it, and they were ordered to travel freely in the land for four months, secure wherever they wished, and no one would attack them. These are the sacred months (al-ashhur al-hurum) in His saying: ﴿So when the sacred months have passed﴾. That was to protect the sacred months from killing and fighting in them.

Its revelation was in the ninth year after the Hijra, and the conquest of Makka was in the eighth year. The commander there was ʿAttab ibn Asid. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) appointed Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, over the pilgrimage of the ninth year. Then he sent Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, riding al-ʿAdba (his she-camel), to recite it to the people of the pilgrimage. It was said to him: "Would it not be better to send it with Abu Bakr?" He said: "Only a man from me can convey it on my behalf." When Ali drew near, Abu Bakr heard the sound of the camel and stopped, and said: "This is the groaning of the camel of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." When he reached him, he said: "Are you a commander or one under command?" He said: "One under command."

It is related that when Abu Bakr was on part of the road, Jibril, peace be upon him, descended and said: "O Muhammad, none may convey your message except a man from you." So he sent Ali. Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, has something been revealed from heaven?" He said: "Yes. Go, and you remain over the pilgrimage, while Ali proclaims the verses."

When it was the day before the Tarwiya, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, gave a sermon and informed them about their rites. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, stood on the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) near the Jamrat al-ʿAqaba and said: "O people, I am the messenger of the Messenger of Allah to you." They said: "With what?" So he recited to them thirty or forty verses. [The statement "I said" here is compiled from several places. Its beginning is mentioned in the Maghazi of Ibn Ishaq. The phrase "they are the Banu Damra and the Banu Kinana" means those who broke the covenant, except those excepted from them, as is understood from its outward meaning, and its explanation will come shortly after some hadiths. That is because the covenant was in the sixth year, and the breaking and the revelation and the conquest were in the eighth year, as will come shortly: the period without breaking was eighteen months. Based on this, the first breaking was in Rabi' al-Akhir of the eighth year; this is the verified reporting. As for his words "and the commander there, that is, in the eighth year, over Makka and over the Hajj," this was mentioned by al-Waqidi in the Maghazi. As for his words "Abu Bakr was appointed over the pilgrimage of the ninth year, etc.," it is in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayra with the same meaning. As for his words "and he sent Ali after him," it was related by Ahmad and Abu Ya'la from the narration of Abu Ishaq, from Yazid ibn Mani', from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) sent him with al-Bara'a to the people of Makka," and he related the hadith, in which: "He travelled for three days, then said to Ali: 'Catch up with him, take back Abu Bakr and deliver it yourself.' He did so. When Abu Bakr arrived he wept and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, has something happened concerning me?' He said: 'Nothing has happened concerning you except good. But I was ordered that none should convey it except myself or a man from me.'" And in the Mustadrak, through Jumay' ibn Umayr: "I came to Ibn Umar and asked him about Ali, and he rebuked me, then said: 'Shall I not tell you about Ali? The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Abu Bakr and Umar with al-Bara'a to the people of Makka. They set out, and suddenly they encountered a rider and said: "Who is this?" He said: "I am Ali ibn Abi Talib." He said: "O Abu Bakr, bring the letter," etc.' And it was related ... [There is a blank space of several lines in one of the two manuscripts; the other manuscript omits the speech without leaving a blank. Its corrector (muṣaḥḥiḥ) said so.]

It is related from Mujahid, may Allah be pleased with him, that it was thirteen verses. Then he said: "He was ordered with four: that no polytheist should approach the House after this year, that no one should circumambulate the House naked, that none enters Paradise except a believing soul, and that every person with a covenant should be given his covenant in full." Then they said at that: "O Ali, tell your cousin: we have thrown the covenant behind our backs, and there is no covenant between us and him except piercing with spears and striking with swords."

It was also said: he was only ordered that none should convey it on his behalf except a man from him, because the custom of the Arabs in breaking their covenants is that a man from the tribe takes charge of it. So if Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, had taken charge of it, they could have said: "This is contrary to what is known among us regarding breaking covenants." Thus their objection was removed by appointing Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, to that.

If you say: what are the four months? I say: It is related from al-Zuhri, may Allah be pleased with him, that al-Bara'a was revealed in Shawwal, so the four months are: Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'da, Dhu al-Hijja, and Muharram. It was also said: they are twenty days of Dhu al-Hijja, Muharram, Safar, the month of Rabi' al-Awwal, and ten days of Rabi' al-Akhir. They were sacred (hurum), because they were granted security during them, and killing and fighting them were forbidden. Or it is by way of predominance (taghlib), because Dhu al-Hijja and Muharram are among them. It was also said: they are from the tenth of Dhu al-Qa'da to the tenth of Rabi' al-Awwal, because the Hajj in that year was at that time, due to the nasi' (intercalation) that was practised among them, and then it became in the second year in Dhu al-Hijja.

If you say: what is the reason for the agreement of most scholars on the permissibility of fighting the polytheists in the sacred months, when Allah has protected them from that? I say: They said that the obligation of protecting them was abrogated (nusikha wujub al-siyana), and fighting the polytheists in them was permitted, by His saying: ﴿not incapacitating Allah﴾, meaning you cannot escape Him even if He gives you respite, and ﴿He will disgrace you﴾, meaning He will humiliate you in this world by killing and in the Hereafter by punishment.

It was also said: they are from the tenth of Dhu al-Qa'da to the tenth of Rabi' al-Awwal, because the Hajj in that year was at that time, due to the nasi' (intercalation) that was practised among them, and then it became in the second year in Dhu al-Hijja.

If you say: what is the reason for the agreement of most scholars on the permissibility of fighting the polytheists in the sacred months, when Allah has protected them from that? I say: They said that the obligation of protecting them was abrogated (nusikha wujub al-siyana), and fighting the polytheists in them was permitted, by His saying: ﴿not incapacitating Allah﴾, meaning you cannot escape Him even if He gives you respite, and ﴿He will disgrace you﴾, meaning He will humiliate you in this world by killing and in the Hereafter by punishment.

Its raising is like the raising of Bara'a (the first clause), in both readings. Then the sentence is conjoined to a similar one. There is no basis for the view of those who say that it is conjoined to Bara'a, just as one would not say "'Amr is conjoined to Zayd" in your saying "Zayd is standing, and 'Amr is sitting."

Al-adhan (the proclamation) means al-iydhan (the notification), which is informing, just as al-aman (security) and al-ata' (giving) mean al-iman (granting security) and al-i'ta' (giving).

If you ask: what is the difference between the meaning of the first sentence and the second? I answer: the first is a report of the establishment of the disavowal (bara'a), and the second is a report of the obligation to notify what has been established.

If you ask: why was the disavowal linked to those among the polytheists with whom a covenant had been made, while the proclamation was linked to "the people"? I answer: because the disavowal is specific to those bound by covenant and those among them who broke it, whereas the proclamation is general to all people, whether covenanted or not, and whether among the covenanted those who broke it or those who did not.

﴿On the day of the greatest pilgrimage﴾: the day of 'Arafa. It is said: the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr), because in it the pilgrimage is completed and most of its rites take place: the circumambulation (tawaf), the sacrifice (nahr), the shaving (halq), and the stoning (ramy).

From 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: a man took hold of the bridle of his mount and said: "What is the greatest pilgrimage?" He said: "Your day this." "Release my mount."
[[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Tabari, from the transmission of Shu'ba, from al-Hakam, from Yahya ibn al-Jazzar, from 'Ali: "He went out on the day of sacrifice on a white mule, intending the cemetery, when a man came, took hold of the bridle of his mount, and asked him about the greatest pilgrimage. He said: 'It is your day this; release its way.'"]]

From Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood on the day of sacrifice at the Jamarat during the Farewell Pilgrimage and said: "This is the day of the greatest pilgrimage."
[[Narrated by al-Bukhari in suspended form (ta'liq), and by Abu Dawud and al-Hakim, from the transmission of Hisham ibn al-Ghaz, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, in a lengthy form. It was also related by al-Tabarani, al-Tabari, Abu Nu'aym in al-Hil?????abba, and Ibn Abi Hatim in abridged form, by way of Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both: "that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) threw the pebble at the Jamra on the day of sacrifice, and said: 'This is the day of the greatest pilgrimage.'" On this topic there is also a report from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, related by al-Tirmidhi, both as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) and as a mawquf (traced to a companion). There is also one from Ibn Abi Awfa in al-Tabarani. And from Ibn Mas'ud in Tarikh Isbahan by Abu Nu'aym, in the biography of 'Umar ibn Harun.]]

The pilgrimage is described as "the greatest" because the 'umra is called "the lesser pilgrimage." Alternatively, the standing at 'Arafa is made the greatest pilgrimage because it is the principal of its obligations, since if it is missed, the pilgrimage is missed. Likewise, if the day of sacrifice is intended, it is the greatest pilgrimage, because most of the rites of the pilgrimage are performed on it.

From al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him: the day was called the greatest pilgrimage because Muslims and polytheists gathered on it, and because it coincided with the festivals of the People of the Book, and this did not happen before it or after it, so it became great in the heart of every believer and unbeliever.

The preposition "bi" (which governs adhan) is omitted for lightness. It is read "inna Allaha" with a kasra, because the adhan has the sense of speech. "Wa rasuluhu" is conjoined to the pronoun implied in bari' (in the predicate), or to the position (mahall) of the kasra-marked "inna" with its noun. It is also read with a fatha, conjoined to the noun of "inna," or because the waw has the sense of ma'a ("with"): meaning "he is disavowed of them together with him." And it is read with a jarr (kasra) by way of al-jiwar (grammatical attraction). It is also said that it is by way of an oath, as in His saying: "la-'amruka" ("by your life").

It is related that a Bedouin heard a man reciting it and said: "If Allah is disavowed of His Messenger, then I am disavowed of him." The man seized him and brought him to 'Umar, and the Bedouin recounted his recitation. Thereupon 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, ordered the learning of Arabic (al-'Arabiyya).
[[I have not found it with its chain, but al-Qurtubi mentioned it in al-Tadhkira from Ibn Abi Mulayka, who said: "A Bedouin came in the time of 'Umar," and he mentioned it more completely, and added at its end: "He ordered Abu al-Aswad, and he laid down grammar (nahw)." The well-known view, however, is that it was 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who ordered Abu al-Aswad to lay down grammar.]]

﴿If you repent﴾ from disbelief and treachery, ﴿it is better for you﴾. ﴿But if you turn away﴾ from repentance, or remain upon turning away and aversion from Islam and fidelity, then know that ﴿you will not outrun Allah﴾ the Exalted, nor escape His seizing and His punishment.

**Question: What does the exception in His words ﴿except those with whom you made a covenant among the polytheists﴾ [[Mahmud said: "If you ask, what is this exception made from? I say its aspect is that it is an exception from ... etc." Ahmad said: "It is also permissible that His words ﴿so travel freely﴾ be an address from God Most High to the polytheists, without a speech-verb implied before it. On this reading the exception is from His words ﴿to those with whom you made a covenant﴾, as if it were said: 'A disavowal from God and His Messenger to those covenanted, not to those who remain upon the covenant. So complete for them, O Muslims, their covenant.' There would then be a shift from addressing the Muslims in His words ﴿to those with whom you made a covenant﴾ to addressing the polytheists in His words ﴿so travel freely﴾, and then a shift from the first person to the third person in His words ﴿and know that you cannot escape God﴾ and that God ... [the original reads: 'and that God, and the original is: and know that you are not those who can escape'] and whether... In this second shift, after the first shift, there is a variety of stylistic eloquence, an exaltation of the matter and a magnification of the affair. Then after this shift comes a return to addressing the Muslims with His words ﴿except those with whom you made a covenant, and they have not diminished anything of you, so complete for them﴾. All of this is among the excellences of eloquence. Al-Zamakhshari was led to posit a speech-verb before ﴿so travel freely﴾ out of concern that it correspond to His words ﴿so complete﴾, since the addressees on this reading are the Muslims both first and second, and there is nothing in it of the shifts founded on the interpretation we mentioned. Both aspects are distinguished by a kind of eloquence and a measure of fine expression, and God knows best."]]? I say: its aspect is that it is an exception from His words ﴿so travel freely in the land﴾, because the speech is addressed to the Muslims. Its meaning: a disavowal from God and His Messenger to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant. So say to them, "Travel freely," except those among them with whom you made a covenant and who have not broken it; then complete for them their covenant. The exception here carries the sense of a corrective qualification (istidrak), as if it were said after they had been commanded regarding the covenant-breakers: "But as for those who did not break faith, complete for them their covenant, and do not treat them as those others, and do not make the faithful one like the treacherous one." ﴿Indeed God loves the God-fearing﴾: meaning that the requirement of piety is that the two groups not be equated, so fear God in this matter. ﴿They have not diminished anything of you﴾: they did not kill any one of you, and did not harm you at all. ﴿Nor have they supported against you﴾: nor have they aided an enemy against you, as Banu Bakr aggressed against Khuza'ah, the confidants of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and Quraysh backed them with weapons, until 'Amr ibn Salim al-Khuza'i came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and recited:

O God, I appeal to Muhammad
the oath of our fathers and yours, the ancient one.

Indeed Quraysh broke their promise to you
and violated your binding and firm pact.

They attacked us by night at al-Hatim, while sleeping,
and they killed us while bowing and prostrating.

[[Indeed Quraysh broke their promise to you ... and they violated your firm pledge.
They claimed that you would save no one,
while they are humbled and fewer in number.
They attacked us at al-Hatim while asleep,
and they killed us while bowing and prostrating.
So help, may God guide you, with a help that is prepared,
and call the servants of God, that they may come as reinforcement.
Among them is the Messenger of God, having stripped for battle,
in a host like the sea flowing in abundance,
white like the sun, rising high,
if he is seen, his face grows dark like ash.
(Of 'Amr ibn Salim al-Khuza'i.) When the Messenger of God ﷺ left Mecca, Quraysh aided Banu Bakr against Banu Khuza'ah, so 'Amr came to him in Medina and recited this. The Prophet ﷺ said: "You will not be helped if I do not help you." "Lahumma" is originally "Allahumma," shortened and made explicit in place of the pronoun, to indicate exaltation and to stir up what he intended. "Al-Hilf" means covenant. "Al-Atlad" means the most ancient. He turned to address them to evoke compassion, and made him like a father to them for his care of their interests. "Thumma" is used for sequence in the report, and "nazza'a ilayhi" is a metonymy for breaking the covenant. "Al-Dhimam" means covenant; it is also said that "dhimmah" with the same meaning. Another version reads "mithaqaka" (your pact). "Adhall" and "aqall" are in the sense of "adhillah" and "qalilun," so it does not indicate increase. It is also permissible that it is on its own pattern, according to their claim, meaning: humbler and fewer than they claimed concerning you and your people. "Al-Hatim" is well known; in the pre-Islamic period they used to swear oaths there, and the liar would be crushed. It is also reported as "al-Atir," and al-Atir is the road, and its singular is "wattirah." Here it is the name of a water-source of Khuza'ah below Mecca. "Al-Hajd" is the plural of "hajid," the one awake from sleep for worship. "Al-Ateed" is the present one; it is said: "indahu ta'tidan," and "a'tadahu i'tidadan": he prepared it and made it present, so it is "ateed" and "a'tad." In it the superlative is used in the sense of the passive participle, perhaps from "a'dda" when it is present. The original is "a'adahu i'dadan," then the dal was changed to ta'. "Hadaka Allah" is a parenthetical supplicatory clause. "Al-Madad" means increase: that they come as an additional aid for us to help us against our enemies. In the attribution to God there is an incitement for them. "Al-Failaq" is the crowded, compact army, like the sea in abundance and speed of march. "Al-Mazid" is that which throws up foam from the intensity of march and boiling. "Yasmu" means rises; "sa'adan" means ascending. "In shiyam" means "if seen." It is also reported with the unpointed letter, meaning "ahaqq" (more deserving). "Tarbad" means changes and becomes changed, like the colour of ash. Anger at the arrival of what is hateful is a sign of courage. This was the cause of the conquest of Mecca.]] So the Prophet ﷺ, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "You will not be helped if I do not help you." [[Ibn Ishaq related it in al-Maghazi and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il by his chain. He said: Al-Zuhri narrated to me from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, from Marwan ibn al-Hakam and al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, who said: "It was in the treaty of the Messenger of God ﷺ on the day of al-Hudaybiyah," and he mentioned the story at length, and in it the poetry. And in it: "They broke the truce about seven or eighteen months." Al-Tabarani related by way of 'Ali ibn al-Husayn: Maymunah bint al-Harith narrated to me, she said: "There was between the Prophet ﷺ and Quraysh..." and he mentioned the story and the poetry. Al-Waqidi related it in al-Maghazi at length by several routes, then said: Abd al-Hamid ibn Ja'far narrated to me from 'Imran ibn Abi Anas from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ stood, dragging the edge of his cloak, saying: "O 'Amr, you will not be helped if I do not help the Banu Ka'b with what I help myself with."]] It is also read ﴿they have not diminished (lam yanqudukum)﴾ with the dotted dad, meaning they did not break your covenant. The meaning of ﴿then complete to them﴾ is: render it to them whole and complete. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, said: Among the Kinanah tribe's people there remained nine months of their covenant, so he completed their covenant for them.

The months have passed, like your saying "the month has been stripped away" (*injarada al-shahr*) and "a barren year" (*sanah jarda'*). ﴿And the sacred months in which the covenant-breakers were allowed to travel freely﴾. ﴿Then kill the polytheists﴾, meaning those who broke their covenant with you and backed others against you, ﴿wherever you find them﴾, whether within the sacred area or outside it, ﴿and seize them﴾ and take them captive. *Al-akhidh* is the captive. ﴿And besiege them﴾, meaning bind them and prevent them from moving about the land. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that their besieging means they are to be barred from reaching al-Masjid al-Haram. ﴿At every ambush﴾, meaning every passage and route of passing through, ﴿lie in wait for them﴾. Its being in the accusative is as in His saying ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾.

[[Mahmud said: "al-Marsad is the passage and the route ..." etc. Ahmad said: Its being in the accusative rather than the genitive is by way of *ittisa'* (extended usage), since *al-marsad* is a restricted adverb of place, and the original rule is that the verb does not govern it directly. It is like his saying, in the extended usage:

*As the fox trots along the road.*

It may also be—and Allah knows best—that *marsad* is a verbal noun, since the form for the noun of time, the noun of place and the verbal noun come from the same root. On this view it is in the accusative as a primary object, since *uq'udu* carries the sense of *irsadu*, as if it were said: "and lie in wait for them at every ambush." However, the adverbial sense is strengthened by His saying ﴿wherever you find them﴾, which requires matching the two adverbs of place. And Allah knows best.]] You lie in wait for them there. Its being in the accusative is as an adverb of place, like His saying ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾.

﴿Then let them go their way﴾, meaning release them after capture and siege. Or: refrain from them and do not harass them, as in the line:

*Leave the way open for him who builds the minaret upon it,
and go forth wherever necessity drives you.
I have feared, O son of her who died a hypocrite,
because of the foulness of Barda, that the rain will not fall.*

This is by Jarir, satirizing 'Umar ibn Lajā' al-Tamimi. It is also transmitted as: "Leave the road open." *Manar al-tariq* means its boundaries. He is saying: leave the path of noble deeds to him who builds its banners in it, establishes its rites, and marks its boundaries. He likens praiseworthy qualities to the straight road, with the common factor being reaching the goal by every route and not deviating from any, in the form of a *tasrihiyyah* (explicit metaphor). Building the minaret is a *tarshih* (a supporting element of the metaphor), and what is meant is establishing fine rites and improving their standing so that people follow them, or setting up signs of generosity so that the needy may be guided to it. Barzah is his mother, and it was said that it means a vast land. On that reading its diptote form is a poetic necessity. But the second line supports what we have said: go forth with your ugly mother to the necessity that the eternal decree has driven you to, namely the base traits with which you were stamped. The imperative in both places is meant to state his actual condition, not a genuine command. It is possible that the first is a command to abandon boasting, so the form of the second imperative is by way of *mushakalah* (matching), or it means a request that he acknowledge his own condition. The grammarians classed it as a case of *tahdhir* (warning), and used it as an example for mentioning the verb of the thing one is warned against, since it goes beyond a mere command to leave alone, because there is aversion between him and that path, so that warning against it is valid. *Khifta* is with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'*, but with a *fatḥah* it is more forceful in satire. The repetition of the name Barzah is for indefiniteness and for reproach through it, meaning that she is a bad omen to people, from whom drought is feared.

And from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him): leave them, and their coming to al-Masjid al-Haram. ﴿Indeed Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾, forgiving them what preceded of disbelief and treachery.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 6:

"Ahad" (anyone) is in the nominative as the subject of the conditional verb, with an implied verb that the apparent one explains. Its sense: "And if anyone among the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection." It is not in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), because "in" (if) is one of the particles that govern the verb and does not precede anything else. The meaning: "And if anyone among the polytheists comes to you after the expiry of the months, with no treaty or covenant between you and him, and he seeks your protection in order to hear what you call to of monotheism and the Qur'an, and to make clear [[The phrase "wa-tubayyin" (and to make clear) is perhaps "wa-yatabayyan" (and to ascertain), coordinated with "yasma'" (to hear). (Editor's note.)]] what you were sent with, then grant him protection until he hears the word of God and reflects upon it and comes to know the reality of the matter. Then convey him afterwards to his place of safety, if he does not accept Islam. Then fight him if you wish, without treachery or betrayal. This ruling is established for every time." On the authority of al-Hasan, may God be pleased with him: "It is decisive (muhkamah) until the Day of Resurrection." On the authority of Sa'id ibn Jubayr: a man from the polytheists came to 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, and said: "If one of us wishes to come to Muhammad after the expiry of this term to hear the word of God, or comes to him for some need, will he be killed?" He said: "No, for God Most High says: ﴿And if anyone among the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection...﴾ [the verse]." On the authority of al-Suddi and al-Dahhak, may God be pleased with them both: "It is abrogated (mansukhah) by His saying Most High: ﴿Then kill the polytheists﴾." "Dhalika" (that) refers to that matter, meaning the command to grant protection in His saying ﴿grant him protection﴾. "Bi-annahum" (because) [it is because] they are a people of ignorance who do not know what Islam is or the reality of what you call to; so it is necessary to give them safety until they hear and understand the truth.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 7–8:**

"How" (kayfa) is an interrogative (istifham) carrying the sense of disapproval and improbability (istinkar wa-istib'ad). It asks how the polytheists could have a covenant with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), when they are his opponents and their hearts are full of rancor (ghurrat sudurihim). [Note: his words "ghurrat sudurihim" mean "blazing with rage."] That is, it is impossible for a covenant to be established with these people, so do not hope for it, do not entertain it in your souls, and do not think of fighting them.

Then he makes an exception to this with His words, ﴿except those with whom you made a covenant﴾, meaning: but those among them with whom you made a covenant ﴿at the Sacred Mosque﴾, and who did not show any breach, such as the Banu Kinana and the Banu Damra. So wait for their affair and do not fight them. ﴿As long as they remain true to you, remain true to them﴾, keeping to the covenant likewise. ﴿Surely God loves the godfearing﴾, meaning that waiting with them is among the deeds of the godfearing.

"How" is repeated to express improbability of the polytheists' steadfastness in the covenant. [Note: Ahmad said: "The secret, God knows best, in the repetition of 'how' is that when He first mentioned it to express the improbability of their covenant being upheld before God, He had not yet stated the reason for the great distance, by making an exception for those who remained faithful to the covenant, and the speech had grown long. So 'how' was repeated to refresh the mention and so that part of the speech would hold onto part of it. He did not intend mere repetition, but this secret which it contains. Similar examples have been mentioned before, and God is the Granter of success."]

The verb is omitted because it is understood, as in the verse:

*"They told me that death is in the villages, so how [did it come] when here are the highlands and the well?"*

[Note: *"By the life of my father, the far past
and what is coming tomorrow are near."*

*"They told me that death is in the villages,
so how [did it come] when here are the highlands and the well?"*

This is by Ka'b al-Ghanawi in an elegy for his brother. "Al-hadba" is a great rock. The address is in the dual, following the Arab custom, even though the two were not there. The word "innama" is read with a kasra as a quotation, or with a fatha as the object: meaning, "and they told me that death and plague are only in the villages, so how can you both claim that, when my brother died in this desert, or how did my brother die there?" "Al-qalib" is the well, because it turns (qalaba) its soil from the depth of the earth to its surface. "Hata" points to the desert. It may also refer to the highland, meaning "and this is a well."]

That is, "how did he die," meaning: how can they have a covenant, when their condition is that if they gain the upper hand over you, after the strengthening of oaths and pacts that preceded, they will not regard any oath or covenant, and will not spare you. ﴿They do not observe with you any bond of kinship (ill) or covenant (dhimma)﴾. "Ill" means oath (hilf), covenant (ahd) or kinship. It is said that it means kinship. Hassan (may God be pleased with him) recited:

*"By your life, your kinship with Quraysh
is like the foal of a she-camel to the chick of the ostrich."*

[Note: This is by Hassan ibn Thabit. "Al" (with a kasra) means oath, covenant, or kinship. "Al-saqb" is the young of a she-camel. "Al-ra'l" is the chick of the ostrich. He says: by your life, your kinship with Quraysh is distant or non-existent, like the kinship of a she-camel's young to the ostrich's chick. It is also transmitted as "kaal-saif" ("like the sheath of the sword"), but the correct reading is that this is a distortion.]

It is also said that "ill" means "god" (ilah). It is read as "iyla," with the same meaning. It is also said that it means Gabriel, and Jibril and Jibril derive from this. It is also said that "al" in the sense of kinship (al, "family") is derived from it, just as "rahim" (womb, kinship) is derived from "Rahman." The more correct view is that the derivation of "ill" in the sense of oath is because when they clasped hands and swore allegiance, they raised their voices and proclaimed it aloud. It derives from the root meaning "wailing" (al-ju'ar), and from it comes *"aleel,"* meaning a moan with which one raises one's voice. And *"da'at alliha"* means: when she wailed.

[Note: His words "da'at alliha idha wawalat" (when she wailed). In al-Sihah: As for the verse of al-Kumayt praising a man:

*"You are not, in a dark dusty land,
when the young women of fine character wail..."*

It may be that he means "al-alal," then made it dual as if he meant one cry after another. End of quote from al-Sihah.]

Then every covenant and pact was called "ill." Kinship was also named by it, because kinship binds two men in a way that a pact does not bind them.

﴿They please you with their mouths﴾: this is a new statement describing their condition, namely their contradiction between outward and inward, and it confirms the improbability of their steadfastness to the covenant. "Refusal of the hearts" means the opposite of what is in them of hatred, in contrast to the fine words on their tongues. ﴿And most of them are wicked﴾, rebellious and unrestrained, without any manliness to restrain them or any praiseworthy character to deter them, as is found among some unbelievers, who avoid lying and breaking faith and abstain from what damages honor and brings bad repute.

This is by Ka'b al-Ghanawi in an elegy for his brother. "Al-hadba" is a great rock. The address is in the dual, following the Arab custom, even though the two were not there. The word "innama" is read with a kasra as a quotation, or with a fatha as the object: meaning, "and they told me that death and plague are only in the villages, so how can you both claim that, when my brother died in this desert, or how did my brother die there?" "Al-qalib" is the well, because it turns (qalaba) its soil from the depth of the earth to its surface. "Hata" points to the desert. It may also refer to the highland, meaning "and this is a well."]

That is, "how did he die," meaning: how can they have a covenant, when their condition is that if they gain the upper hand over you, after the strengthening of oaths and pacts that preceded, they will not regard any oath or covenant, and will not spare you. ﴿They do not observe with you any bond of kinship (ill) or covenant (dhimma)﴾. "Ill" means oath (hilf), covenant (ahd) or kinship. It is said that it means kinship. Hassan (may God be pleased with him) recited:

*"By your life, your kinship with Quraysh
is like the foal of a she-camel to the chick of the ostrich."*

[Note: This is by Hassan ibn Thabit. "Al" (with a kasra) means oath, covenant, or kinship. "Al-saqb" is the young of a she-camel. "Al-ra'l" is the chick of the ostrich. He says: by your life, your kinship with Quraysh is distant or non-existent, like the kinship of a she-camel's young to the ostrich's chick. It is also transmitted as "kaal-saif" ("like the sheath of the sword"), but the correct reading is that this is a distortion.]

It is also said that "ill" means "god" (ilah). It is read as "iyla," with the same meaning. It is also said that it means Gabriel, and Jibril and Jibril derive from this. It is also said that "al" in the sense of kinship (al, "family") is derived from it, just as "rahim" (womb, kinship) is derived from "Rahman." The more correct view is that the derivation of "ill" in the sense of oath is because when they clasped hands and swore allegiance, they raised their voices and proclaimed it aloud. It derives from the root meaning "wailing" (al-ju'ar), and from it comes *"aleel,"* meaning a moan with which one raises one's voice. And *"da'at alliha"* means: when she wailed.

[Note: His words "da'at alliha idha wawalat" (when she wailed). In al-Sihah: As for the verse of al-Kumayt praising a man:

*"You are not, in a dark dusty land,
when the young women of fine character wail..."*

It may be that he means "al-alal," then made it dual as if he meant one cry after another. End of quote from al-Sihah.]

Then every covenant and pact was called "ill." Kinship was also named by it, because kinship binds two men in a way that a pact does not bind them.

﴿They please you with their mouths﴾: this is a new statement describing their condition, namely their contradiction between outward and inward, and it confirms the improbability of their steadfastness to the covenant. "Refusal of the hearts" means the opposite of what is in them of hatred, in contrast to the fine words on their tongues. ﴿And most of them are wicked﴾, rebellious and unrestrained, without any manliness to restrain them or any praiseworthy character to deter them, as is found among some unbelievers, who avoid lying and breaking faith and abstain from what damages honor and brings bad repute.

**اشْتَرَوْا** (*ishtarawa*): they exchanged, meaning they took in exchange: **istabdalu** (they substituted) **بِآياتِ اللَّهِ** (*bi-ayati Allah*), that is, with the Qur'an and Islam, **ثَمَناً قَلِيلًا** (*thaman qalilan*), a small price, which is following desires and appetites. **فَصَدُّوا عَنْ سَبِيلِهِ** (*fa-saddu 'an sabilihi*): they turned away from His path, meaning they deviated from it, or diverted others from it.

It was said: they were the Bedouin Arabs whom Abu Sufyan gathered and fed.

**هُمُ الْمُعْتَدُونَ** (*hum al-mu'tadun*): the transgressors, those who go beyond the limit in wrongdoing and evil.

**اشْتَرَوْا** (*ishtarawa*): they exchanged, meaning they took in exchange: **istabdalu** (they substituted) **بِآياتِ اللَّهِ** (*bi-ayati Allah*), that is, with the Qur'an and Islam, **ثَمَناً قَلِيلًا** (*thaman qalilan*), a small price, which is following desires and appetites. **فَصَدُّوا عَنْ سَبِيلِهِ** (*fa-saddu 'an sabilihi*): they turned away from His path, meaning they deviated from it, or diverted others from it.

It was said: they were the Bedouin Arabs whom Abu Sufyan gathered and fed.

**هُمُ الْمُعْتَدُونَ** (*hum al-mu'tadun*): the transgressors, those who go beyond the limit in wrongdoing and evil.

Then if they repent of disbelief and breach of covenant, then they are your brethren in religion. [They are] your brethren, with the subject elided, like His saying: ﴿But if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brethren﴾. "And We detail the verses and make them clear." This is a parenthetical clause, as if it were said: "Whoever reflects upon its details is one who knows," urging and exhorting reflection upon what has been detailed of the rulings concerning the covenanted polytheists, and upon observing them.

And if they break their oaths after their covenant and revile your religion, then fight the leaders of disbelief, for indeed they have no oaths, so that they may desist.

Wait, that is not the passage; here is the faithful translation of the passage as given:

And they reviled your religion, disparaged it and found fault with it. "So fight the leaders of disbelief, and fight them." The leaders of disbelief were placed in the position of their pronoun, to indicate that when they broke their oaths in a state of polytheism, out of rebellion and transgression and casting off the customs of the noble and faithful Arabs, then embraced faith, established the prayer, paid the zakat, and became brothers to the Muslims in religion, and then turned back, apostatized from Islam, broke what they had pledged of faith and fidelity to covenants, and sat down reviling the religion of God, saying, "The religion of Muhammad is nothing," they are then the leaders of disbelief and those of leadership and preeminence in it, such that no disbelieving dust-raiser can keep pace with them. It was said: when the dhimmi reviles the religion of Islam openly, it is permissible to kill him, because the covenant was concluded with him on the condition that he not revile; so if he reviles, he has broken his covenant and left the protection (dhimma). ﴿Indeed, they have no oaths﴾, plural of yamin (oath). And it was recited: "la iman lahum" (they have no faith), meaning they have no Islam. Or: they are not given security after apostasy and breaking (their oaths), and there is no path to it.

If you say: how did He affirm oaths for them in His saying ﴿and if they break their oaths﴾, then negate them from them?

I say: He meant the oaths they had displayed, then He said: they have no oaths in reality, and their oaths are not oaths. By this Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him) cited evidence that the oath of a disbeliever is not an oath. According to al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him), their oath is an oath. He said: its meaning is that they do not fulfil it, as evidenced by His describing it as breaking.

﴿So that they may desist﴾ is connected to His saying "fight the leaders of disbelief," meaning: let your aim in fighting them, after what has occurred from them of the great offences, be that the fighting becomes a cause of their desisting from what they are upon. This is from the utmost of His generosity, His grace, and His returning kindness to the wrongdoer whenever he returns.

If you say: how is the word "a'imma" pronounced? I say: a hamza followed by a hamza, pronounced "bayn bayn" (between the two), meaning: between the place of articulation of the hamza and the yā'. Realizing both hamzas is a well-known recitation, though it is not accepted by the Basrians. As for explicitly pronouncing the yā', it is not a recitation, and it cannot be a recitation. Whoever pronounces it that way is a mistaken, distorted reciter.

Are you not going to fight a people who broke their oaths, and who intended to expel the Messenger, and who began (the fighting) against you the first time? (Al-Zamakhshari's words are at the start: "أَلا تُقاتِلُونَ" — the hamza (interrogative particle) entered upon "lā tuqātilūna" to establish the negation of fighting as a fact: "Are you not fighting?" Its meaning is urging them to it, by way of emphasis.)

Their oaths (ayman): the oaths they swore in the treaty. "They intended to expel the Messenger" from Makkah, when they consulted together about his affair in the Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of the Quraysh), until God Most High permitted him to emigrate, and he went out by himself.

"And they began against you the first time": that is, it was they who initiated the fighting. For the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to them first with the luminous Book and challenged them with it, but they turned from opposing it, being unable to do so, to fighting. So they are the ones who began the fighting, and the aggressor is the wrongdoer. What then prevents you from fighting them in the same way, and from striking them with evil as they struck you?

He rebuked them for abandoning the fight against them and urged them to it, then described them with what necessitates urging against them. He affirms that whoever has attributes like theirs, of breaking the covenant, expelling the Messenger, and beginning the fighting without cause, deserves that their opposition not be abandoned, and that whoever neglected it be rebuked.

"Do you fear them?": an affirmation of fear of them and a rebuke for it. "God has more right that you fear Him," so that you fight His enemies, "if you are believers." That is: the requirement of true faith is that the believer fear none but his Lord, and not care for anyone else, as in His saying, "and they fear none but God" (Qur'an 33:39).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 14–15:

When Allah rebuked them for abandoning fighting, He made the command to fight plain for them, saying ﴿Fight them﴾, and He promised them, to strengthen their hearts and correct their intentions, that He would punish them at your hands by killing, humiliate them by taking them captive, and grant you victory and dominance over them, ﴿and heal the breasts of a people of the believers﴾ [[His saying "and heal the breasts of a people" is the wording of the recitation; the more fitting reading is "and heal" (wa-yashfi), as a conjunction with ﴿He will punish them at your hands﴾, since it is part of the promise. (ʿIdh.)]], namely Khuzaʿa. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: They are tribes of Yemen and Saba'. They came to Makkah and embraced Islam, and they suffered severe harm from its people, so they sent to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ complaining to him, and he said: "Rejoice, for relief is near." ﴿And remove the rage of your hearts﴾ [[His saying "and remove the rage of your hearts" is in the recitation ghayza qulubihim (the rage of their hearts), and perhaps some copyists understood it as part of the good news, so they changed it to the second-person form. The more apt reading is ghayza qulubihim, referring to what they encountered; then his saying "and He will remove" in the nominative is a conjunction with ﴿He will punish them at your hands﴾, since it is part of the promise, as he will indicate. (ʿIdh.)]] caused by the hardship you met from them. Allah fulfilled all these promises for them, and that was a proof of the truth of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the soundness of his prophethood. ﴿And Allah turns in forgiveness to whomever He wills﴾ is a new statement and an announcement that some of the people of Makkah would turn away from their disbelief, and that too came to pass, for some of them embraced Islam and their Islam was sound. It is also recited as "wa-yatuba" in the accusative, with "an" implied, so that repentance enters among what the command is answered with in meaning. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾, He knows what will be just as He knows what has been, ﴿All-Wise﴾, He does nothing except what wisdom requires.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 14–15:

When Allah rebuked them for abandoning fighting, He made the command to fight plain for them, saying ﴿Fight them﴾, and He promised them, to strengthen their hearts and correct their intentions, that He would punish them at your hands by killing, humiliate them by taking them captive, and grant you victory and dominance over them, ﴿and heal the breasts of a people of the believers﴾ [[His saying "and heal the breasts of a people" is the wording of the recitation; the more fitting reading is "and heal" (wa-yashfi), as a conjunction with ﴿He will punish them at your hands﴾, since it is part of the promise. (ʿIdh.)]] caused by the hardship you met from them. Am (ﷺ)... 

Let me restate carefully: "أَمْ" here is munqati‘ah (disjunctive, "am" in the sense of "or rather"/"or"), and the meaning of the interrogative hamzah in it is rebuke for the presence of the supposition (ḥusbān). The meaning: you will not be left as you are, until those sincere among you are distinguished, namely those who strove in the way of Allah purely for the sake of Allah, and did not take a waliyjah, i.e., an intimate confidant (biṭānah), from among those who oppose the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, may Allah be pleased with them. "Wa-lammā" means anticipation (tawaqqu‘), and it indicates that the distinguishing of that and its manifestation is an anticipated, certain event, and that those who did not make their religion sincerely for Allah will be distinguished from the sincere ones. His saying "wa-lam yattakhidhū" is conjoined (ma‘ṭūf) to "jāhadū" and falls within the scope of the relative clause (ḥayyiz al-ṣilah), as if it were said: "And Allah has not yet known the strivers among you and the sincere ones who did not take a waliyjah apart from Allah."

Al-waliyjah is on the pattern fa‘īlah from walija, like al-dakhīlah from dakhala. The negation of knowledge is intended as the negation of what is known, like the saying of the speaker: "Allah does not know from me what was said about me," meaning: that was not found in me.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 17:

﴿It is not for the polytheists﴾ (ما كانَ لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ): it is not proper for them, nor fitting, ﴿to maintain the mosques of Allah﴾ (أَنْ يَعْمُرُوا مَساجِدَ اللَّهِ), meaning the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), in accordance with His words ﴿and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque﴾ (وَعِمارَةَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرامِ). As for the reading with the plural, it has two interpretations. The first is that it refers to the Sacred Mosque. It is called "mosques" (مساجد) because it is the qibla of all mosques and their leader (imam), so maintaining it is like maintaining all the mosques, and because every part of it is a mosque. The second is that it refers to the category of mosques. When they are not fit to maintain the category as a whole, it follows that they must not maintain the Sacred Mosque, which is the head and foremost of the category and is more emphatic, because its method is the method of allusion (kinaya). It is as if you said: "So-and-so does not read the Books of Allah," which negates his recitation of the Qur'an more strongly than your stating it explicitly.

﴿Testifying against themselves﴾ (وشاهِدِينَ) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the waw (الواو) in يَعْمُرُوا (ya'muruu). The meaning is: it is not fitting for them to combine two contradictory matters, the maintenance of the places of worship of Allah together with disbelief in Allah and in worshipping Him. The meaning of their testifying against themselves to disbelief is the manifestation of their unbelief: they set up their idols around the House (the Ka'ba), and they used to circumambulate it naked, saying:

"We do not circumambulate it in garments in which we have committed sins."

Whenever they completed a circuit around it, they would prostrate to them. It is also said that it was their saying: "Here I am, O Allah, there is no partner for You, except a partner that You own, and what he owns." It is also said that when the Muhajirun and the Ansar came upon the captives of Badr, they reproached them for their polytheism. Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) began to rebuke al-Abbas for fighting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and for severing the ties of kinship, and he spoke harshly to him. Al-Abbas said:

"You mention our evils and conceal our good qualities."

He said: "Do you have good qualities?" They said: "Yes, and we are better than you in reward: we maintain the Sacred Mosque, we guard the Ka'ba, we give drink to the pilgrims, and we ransom the captives." So this was revealed: ﴿Their deeds have become void﴾ (حَبِطَتْ أَعْمالُهُمْ), which are the maintenance, the guardianship, the provision of water, and the ransoming of captives.

Note by Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir): [Mahmud said: "When disbelief or a great sin destroys the deeds..." etc.] Ahmad said: this is a sound statement, except his saying "a great sin destroys deeds," for that is a derivation from the principle of the Mu'tazilites (Mu'tazila), and the truth is contrary to it.

When disbelief or a major sin destroys sound, established deeds if it follows them, then what is your opinion of what is concurrent with them? He indicated this in His saying ﴿testifying against themselves﴾ (شاهِدِينَ), where He made it a circumstantial clause regarding them, and it shows that they combined the maintenance and the testimony against themselves to disbelief at one and the same time, and that is impossible and not fitting.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 18:

﴿Only he maintains the mosques of Allah﴾ (inna-ma ya'muru masajida Allah). It is also read in the singular, *masjid* (tawhid, i.e., the singular reading). That is, the maintenance of these people is only sound and counted as valid when it is carried out properly. Maintenance (*'imarah*) includes repairing what has fallen into disrepair, sweeping and cleaning it, lighting it with lamps, honouring it, and making it a place habitually used for worship and remembrance of Allah. Among remembrance is the study of knowledge, indeed it is its most noble and greatest form. It also includes protecting the mosques from what they were not built for, such as worldly talk, let alone idle chatter.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "There will come in the last age people from my community who come to the mosques and sit in them in circles [[The phrase "sit in them in circles" (fa-yuqa'iduna fiha halqan) appears in one copy as "fa-ya'idun" and in another as "fa-yaghdun." Verify. (Ghayn)]], their talk is of this world and their love is for this world. Do not sit with them, for Allah has no need of them." [[Al-Tabarani transmitted it from the narration of Abu Wa'il, from Ibn Mas'ud, raised to the Prophet: "There will come in the last age people who sit in the mosques in circles, circle upon circle, their concern is the world. Do not sit with them, for Allah has no need of them." In its chain is Badi' Abu al-Khalil, who narrates from al-A'mash from him. He is abandoned (matruk). Al-Daraqutni said: he alone transmitted it, and there is scrutiny of it. Ibn Hibban transmitted it in his Sahih by way of Isa ibn Yunus from al-A'mash with the wording: "There will come in the last age people whose talk in their mosques is such that Allah has no need of them." On this theme there is also a report from Anas, raised: "A time will come upon people when they gather in circles in their mosques, and their only aspiration is this world. Do not sit with them, for Allah has no need of them." Al-Hakim transmitted it by way of al-Thawri from Awf from al-Hasan from him.]]

And in a hadith: "Talk in the mosque devours good deeds as the beast devours grass." [[It will come in Luqman.]]

The Prophet, peace be upon him, also said: "Allah the Exalted said: Indeed My houses on My earth are the mosques, and indeed those who visit them are their inhabitants. Blessed is the servant who purifies himself in his house and then visits Me in My house; it is a right upon the one visited to honour his visitor." [[I have not found it in this form. In al-Tabarani, from Salman, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever performs ablution in his house and does it well, then comes to the mosque, is a visitor of Allah, and it is a right upon the one visited to honour his visitor." Abd al-Razzaq narrated, and from his route al-Tabari, from Ma'mar, from Ibn Ishaq, from Amr ibn Maymun, who said: "The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: Indeed the houses of Allah on earth are the mosques, and indeed it is a right upon Allah to honour whoever visits them." And by this route Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak transmitted it in al-Zuhd.]]

And from him (ﷺ): "Whoever attaches himself to the mosque, Allah attaches Himself to him." [[Transmitted by Ibn Adi and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, from the narration of Ibn Lahi'a, from Daraj ibn al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id, with this wording.]]

He (ﷺ) also said: "When you see a man who frequents the mosques, bear witness to him of faith." [[Transmitted by al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim, from the narration of Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id.]]

And from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whoever lights a lamp in a mosque, the angels and the bearers of the Throne will keep asking forgiveness for him as long as its light remains in that mosque." [[Narrated by al-Harith ibn Usama from the narration of al-Hakam ibn Sifla al-Abdi, from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whoever lights a lamp in a mosque, it remains raised." By the route of al-Harith, Sulaym al-Razi transmitted it in the Kitab al-Targhib. In al-Tabarani's Musnad al-Shamiyyin, from the hadith of Ali ibn Abi Talib, raised: "Whoever hangs a lamp in a mosque, seventy thousand angels bless him," the hadith with a similar meaning.]]

If it is said: Why was faith in the Messenger (ﷺ) not mentioned? I say: Because it is known and well established that faith in Allah the Exalted is accompanied by faith in the Messenger, peace be upon him, since the testimony of faith (*shahadah*), the call to prayer (*adhan*), the iqamah and others contain both of them together, paired, as if they were one thing, neither separated from the other. Therefore faith in the Messenger, peace be upon him, is included under the mention of faith in Allah the Exalted. It has also been said: it is indicated by the mention of establishing prayer and giving zakat.

If it is said: How is it said ﴿and fears none but Allah﴾, when the believer fears dangers and cannot help but fear them? I say: This refers to fear and God-consciousness (*taqwa*) in matters of religion, and to not preferring the pleasure of another over the pleasure of Allah out of anticipation of some threat. When two things confront him: one is the right of Allah, the other is the right of his own self, he should fear Allah, and so prefer the right of Allah over the right of himself.

It has also been said: they used to fear and hope in the idols, so the intent is to negate that fear from them. ﴿It is hoped that those will be among the guided﴾ is a distancing of the polytheists from the positions of guidance, [[Mahmud said: "In this verse is a distancing of the polytheists... etc." Ahmad said: Most of them say that "'asa" (it is hoped) from Allah is binding, on the basis that its usage is not diverted to the addressees. The truth is what al-Zamakhshari said, but the address is directed to them, i.e., the state of these believers is a hoped-for state, and the outcome is known to Allah, and to Allah belongs the outcome of affairs.]] and a cutting off of their hopes of benefit from their deeds, which they regarded as great, took pride in, and hoped would bring them reward. The meaning is: those who believed and joined to their faith the practice of the laws, together with the awareness of fear and God-consciousness, their guidance lies between "'asa" and "la'alla" (perhaps and maybe). So why do the polytheists claim with certainty that they are guided and that they will attain the best reward with Allah? In this discourse and its like there is a gentle kindness to the believers, to prefer fear over hope and to reject complacency regarding Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 19:

Al-siqaya (the giving of drink) and al-'imara (the maintenance) are verbal nouns from saqa and 'amara, like al-siyana (the preservation) and al-wiqaya (the protection). A omitted modifier (mudaf mahdhuf) must be understood, its sense being: "Do you consider the people who give drink to the pilgrims and maintain the Sacred Mosque (equal to) one who believes in God and strives in His cause?" This is the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr and Abu Wajza al-Sa'di [[His words "Abu Wajza al-Sa'di": in al-Sihah, he is described as a poet and a transmitter of hadith. (Ibn 'Atiyya?)]], who was among the reciters: saqat al-hajj wa 'amarat al-masjid al-haram (the drink-givers of the pilgrims and the maintainers of the Sacred Mosque). The meaning is a denial that the polytheists should be likened to the believers, that their deeds which are nullified should be likened to deeds which are established, or that they should be equated with them. Their equating themselves with the believers is described as a wrong added to their earlier wrong of disbelief.

It is related that the polytheists said to the Jews: "We are the givers of drink to the pilgrims and the maintainers of the Sacred Mosque; are we better, or Muhammad and his companions?" The Jews replied to them: "You are better." It is also said that 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) said to al-'Abbas: "O uncle, will you not emigrate? Will you not join the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" He said: "Do I not hold a position better than emigration: I give drink to the pilgrims of the House of Allah and maintain the Sacred Mosque?" When it was revealed, al-'Abbas said: "I think I am only abandoning our drink-giving." So the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Continue in your drink-giving, for there is good for you in it." [[Al-Tha'labi mentions it from al-Hasan without an isnad, but its isnad to him at the beginning of the book, in the tafsir of 'Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar from 'Umar, namely Ibn 'Ubayd from al-Hasan, who said: "It was revealed concerning 'Ali and al-'Abbas, and 'Uthman and Shayba discussed that. Al-'Abbas said: 'I think I am only abandoning our drink-giving.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said..." and he mentioned it.]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 20–22:

They are greater in rank with Allah than the people of the watering of the pilgrims (al-siqayah) and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque (al-'imarah) in your estimation. ﴿And those are the successful﴾, not you; and it is they who are singled out for success, to the exclusion of you.

It has been read as ﴿yubashshiruhum﴾ with the light and the heavy (tashdid) forms. The indefiniteness of the good news (al-mubashshar bihi) is because it comes after the description of the one who describes (sifat al-wasif), and the definiteness of the one who is given the news (al-mu'arraf).

On the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: it refers specifically to the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun). [[Recorded by al-Tha'labi through the narration of Juwaybir from al-Dahhak from him.]]

Before the conquest of Makkah, whoever embraced Islam did not complete his faith except by emigrating (hijrah) and cutting off his disbelieving relatives, severing his ties of allegiance to them. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, if we withdraw from those who oppose us in religion, we will cut off our fathers, our sons and our clans, our trade will be ruined, our wealth will perish, and we will be driven from our homes, and we will be left lost." So it was revealed, and they emigrated. A man would have his son, his father, his brother or some of his relatives come to him, and he would not turn to them, nor would he host them or spend on them. Then they were granted a concession after that. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the nine who apostatized and joined Makkah. [Al-Tha'labi also mentioned this from Muqatil, and his chain to him is at the beginning of the book.] So Allah the Exalted forbade allying with them.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "None of you will taste the sweetness of faith until he loves for the sake of Allah and hates for the sake of Allah: he loves for the sake of Allah the most distant of people, and hates for the sake of Allah the nearest of people to him." [I have not found it with this wording. In al-Tabarani, from 'Amr ibn al-Hamiq, that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "A servant does not find the pure faith until he loves for the sake of Allah and hates for the sake of Allah." Its chain contains Rushd ibn Sa'd, who is weak. On this subject there is also a report from Abu Umamah narrated by Abu Dawud, and from Mu'adh ibn Anas narrated by Abu Ya'la and others.] Also read: "'ashiratakum" and "'ashiratukum."

Al-Hasan recited: "wa 'asha'irukum." ﴿So wait until Allah brings His command﴾ — a warning. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is the conquest of Makkah. From al-Hasan: it is an immediate or delayed punishment. This is a most severe verse, the severest one can see, as if it censures people for the slackness of the bond of religion and the instability of the cord of certainty. Let the most scrupulous and God-fearing of people be fair with himself: does he find within himself such firmness for the sake of Allah and steadfastness upon the religion of Allah that he prefers his religion over fathers, sons, brothers, clans, wealth, dwellings, and all the shares of this world, and strips himself of them for its sake? Or does Allah withhold from him the least of them for his benefit, so that he does not know which of his two sides is longer? And Satan misleads him away from the most noble share of the shares of religion, so that he is unconcerned, as if a fly had landed on his nose and he simply shooed it away?
