**The places of war: their stations and positions.** [Mahmud said: "Mawatin al-harb: maqamatuha wa mawqifuha..." etc.] Ahmad said: There is no objection, God knows best, to conjoining the two adverbials, the place and the time, one to the other, just as one of two objects is conjoined to the other when the verb is one. For you may say: "Zayd struck 'Amr in the mosque and on Friday," just as you say: "I struck Zayd and 'Amr." There is no need to posit a new verb other than the first. Moreover, the two verbs governing the two objects must in reality be different, for when you say: "I strike Zayd today and 'Amr tomorrow," no one doubts that the two strikings differ by the difference of the two times, yet the verb is one in grammatical terms (*al-sina'a*, the technical grammatical analysis). On this basis it is permissible in the verse, God knows best, for each of the two adverbials to remain as it is, without being interpreted as the other. However, al-Zamakhshari made it obligatory that the verb be plural and that a governor for the time-adverbial other than the first verb be posited, even though both are, in his view, times, on the ground that their multiplicity was not established in all the places.

He means: even if I were to hold to the unity of the governor, that would necessarily follow, but this is not necessary. Do you not see that if you said: "I strike Zayd when he stands and when he sits," the governor of the two adverbials would be one while they are different? The operation of one verb on two different times is prohibited only when there is no intervening conjunction between them, God knows best.

He said:

*How many a place of war, had it not been for me, you would have fallen, as one falls
with his body from the summit of a steep cliff, flung down.*

*You flatter me unwillingly, as if you were a sincere adviser,
while your eye reveals that your breast holds rancor toward me.*

*Your tongue is like honey, and your eye like colocynth,
your evil is spread out and your good is folded up.*

*Would that your whole good were a mere sufficiency,
and your evil kept from me as much as water is kept from the thirsty drinker.*

*How many a place of war, had it not been for me, you would have fallen as one falls
with his body from the summit of a steep cliff, flung down.*

*You have gathered backbiting, slander, and vile speech,
three traits from which you will not refrain.*

It is by Yazid ibn al-Hakam ibn Abi al-'As al-Thaqafi. *Al-mukashara* means to laugh with someone; he chose this word to indicate that it is not a true laughter agreeing with the heart, but merely the showing of teeth before him, to make him believe that he is a sincere adviser to the man, like a sick person whose heart has become corrupt. *Dawi* means pure affection. *Dawi* of the breast also means enmity; it is *dawi* with light stress like *ʿamī*, or with doubled consonant like *ghaniyy*, on the pattern *fa'il* or *fa'il*. If it is with the doubled consonant, then the lightening of it is for the metre.

*Al-madhi* is the honey of bees, because it flows (*yamdhi*) from them, and wine is also called *madhiyya* because of its ease of flow. *Al-ʿalqam* is colocynth, and every bitter tree and everything bitter. That is: your tongue is like honey in the sweetness of speech, and your eye is like colocynth in the aversion and repugnance of the soul, as you look at me with the gaze of a hostile, enraged envier. He likened evil and good to two expanses (*basatin*) by way of metaphor (*al-makniyya*, the metaphor in which only the comparand is mentioned and its attribute implied), and "spreading" and "folding" are imaginative representation (*takhyil*). The name of *layta* is the pronoun of the matter or the omitted second-person pronoun; *khayruka* is the subject of *kana*, and *kafafan* is its predicate. *Sharruka* is conjoined to *khayruka*. It is possible that it is an instance of *tanazuʿ* (competition, where two governors compete for one object), according to those who permit it with particles, since *layta* requires governing *khayruka* and *kana* also requires governing it; so the second governs it, and its pronoun is deleted from the first, because although it is a principal element, it resembles a secondary element in being in the accusative, just as the Kufans allowed its deletion in the chapter of *kana* and the chapter of *zanna*, the deleted element being known from its explainer. That is: "Would that the matter and situation were that your whole good and your evil..." *Kafafan*, with a fatha, means one who suffices and is adequate for you regarding me. If it were read with a kasra as *kifafan*, from the verbal noun of *kaffa* (to restrain), it would be permissible, and the verbal noun would have the sense of the active participle, as an intensive: "one who suffices you, or who withdraws from me as long as the thirsty one drinks water," that is, draws it: always.

*Kam* is an exclamatory noun of multiplicity, meaning "many a..." Many a place of war, had it not been for my presence, you would have been destroyed in it, as one falls. *Tuha* may be with a kasra or a damma on the *ta*', from the pattern of *ba'a*. He said: "As one falls," that is, a falling one fell from the summit of the steep cliff. It is also transmitted as *qinnat al-niq*, and the meaning is the same: from the top of the high mountain. Sibawayh's view is that *lawla* is a preposition when followed by an accusative pronoun. Al-Akhfash's view is that an accusative pronoun is placed in the position of a nominative pronoun in the nominal sentence. Al-Mubarrad denied that this occurs, and this view is refuted by the present line. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the verb and its intransitive counterpart may both be intransitive together, as *hawa* and *inhawa*, *ghawa* and *ingawa*, as shown by a line like this one. Most scholars took it as a poetic necessity (*darura*). The analogical forms would be *hawin* and *ghawin*. Some have held that they are intransitive counterparts of *ahdaytuhu* and *aghwaytuhu*, but the intransitive counterpart of these is the *infaʿala* form, not the *fa'ala* form, which is anomalous. If one were to say that *inhawa* is the intransitive counterpart of *hawwa bihi*, it would be permissible, but it is not analogical.

Then he said to him: "You have gathered backbiting, slander, and vile speech," placing the conjoined element first for the sake of metre. Ibn Jinni took it as an object of accompaniment (*maf'ul maʿah*), and permitted placing it before its companion, holding to that; it may also be a poetic necessity. In it there is an indication from the very start of the intention of multiplicity and abundance. *Thalath khisal* ("three traits") is an apposition to what precedes. *Lasta ʿanha*: that is, you are not one who refrains from them. The element was placed first for emphasis. The *ya'* in the rhyme is for the extension of the vowel.

Its being diptote is because it is a plural of a form that no singular has. The many places were: the battles of Badr, Qurayza, al-Nadir, al-Hudaybiyya, Khaybar, and the Conquest of Mecca. If you say: how is time and place conjoined with the day of Hunayn to the places? I say: the meaning is "and the place of the day of Hunayn," or "in days of many places and the day of Hunayn." It is also permissible to intend by "place" the time, as in "the killing of al-Husayn." But it is necessary that the day of Hunayn be in the accusative by a hidden verb, not by this apparent verb. The reason is that His saying ﴿when your multitude pleased you﴾ is a substitute for "the day of Hunayn." So if you made its governor this apparent verb, it would not be correct, because their multitude did not please them in all those places, and they were not numerous in all of them. So it remains that its governor must be a verb specific to it, unless *idh* is put in the accusative by a hidden "remember."

[Note: "His saying 'they were not pleased by their multitude in all those places'" — it only follows if their multitude had pleased them in all of them, even though this contradicts reality if ﴿when your multitude pleased you﴾ were made a substitute for the places as well, so reflect. (ʿ)]

Hunayn is a valley between Mecca and al-Ta'if, where the battle took place between the Muslims, who were twelve thousand, those who had attended the Conquest of Mecca, joined by two thousand of the Tulaqa' (those freed at the conquest), and between Hawazin and Thaqif, who were four thousand, together with those who joined them from the reinforcements of the rest of the Arabs, so they became a vast multitude. When they met, a man from the Muslims said: "We will not be defeated today through lack of numbers," and this displeased the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is said the one who said it was the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is said it was Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him).

[Note: I have not found this exact wording. As for the statement that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said it: it has been transmitted that he said "Twelve thousand will not be defeated through lack of numbers" in a hadith other than this one. As for this account, if the author relied on something of that, then his statement "the admiration for multitude overtook them and they slipped away from it" etc. would be appropriate. As for his saying "It is said Abu Bakr said it," I have not found it. His saying "and from Hawazin and Thaqif and in four thousand boys with shaved heads" — the correct view is that Hawazin and Thaqif were polytheists. What is in Muslim's Sahih from the hadith of al-ʿAbbas is: "I witnessed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of Hunayn," and then he recounts the story; in it there is alteration and a deficiency from what the author related, and there is no "clan by clan" in it, but rather: "al-ʿAbbas called out to the companions of the tree (the Pledge of al-Ridwan) and called out to the companions of the Samura (the tree), and they turned back like a cow to its calves." Yunus ibn Bukayr, in his Ziyadat al-Maghazi, related from Abu Jaʿfar al-Razi, from al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas, that "a man said on the day of Hunayn: 'We will not be defeated today through lack of numbers.' This displeased the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and God revealed—" and he mentioned the verse. Al-Rabiʿ said: they were twelve thousand, among them two thousand from the people of Mecca.]

That is His saying ﴿when your multitude pleased you, but it availed you nothing﴾... they fought a fierce battle, and the words of admiration for numbers overtook the Muslims, and they forgot that God is the Helper, not the multitude of soldiers, so they fled until they reached the lowlands of Mecca. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) remained alone, steadfast in his position, unshaken, with no one with him except his uncle al-ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him), holding the bridle of his mount, and Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, his cousin. Suffice it that this solitude is a testimony of truth to the utmost of his courage and steadfastness of heart (ﷺ), and it is nothing but one of the signs of prophethood.

[Note: "steadfastness of heart" — *al-jashsh* is the fright of the heart at alarm; *rabit al-jash* is one who binds himself against fleeing for the sake of his courage. (ʿ)]

He said: "My Lord, give me what You promised me." He (ﷺ) said to al-ʿAbbas, who had a loud voice: "Shout to the people." So he called to the Ansar clan by clan, then he called: "O companions of the tree! O companions of the cow!" and they turned back as one man, saying:

*Here we are, here we are!*

The angels descended upon them on white horses with spots. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) looked at the fighting of the Muslims and said: "Now the furnace has become hot," then he took a handful of dirt and threw it at them, and said:

*Defeated, by the Lord of the Ka'ba!*

So they were defeated. Al-ʿAbbas said: "It is as if I see the Messenger of God (ﷺ) spurring his mule after them."

﴿with what vastness it was﴾: *ma* here is verbal (the "what" is a verbal "ma"), and the *ba'* means "with," that is, "with its vastness," and its literal sense is "accompanied by its vastness," with the prepositional phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause, as when you say: "I entered upon him in travel clothes," that is, accompanied by them, not having removed them, meaning "with the travel clothes." The meaning is: you find no place to make ready for your flight to and your escape, because of the excessive terror, so it was as if it had grown narrow for you. ﴿Then you turned back in retreat﴾: then you fled. ﴿His tranquility﴾: his mercy, by which they were calmed and became secure. ﴿Upon the believers﴾: those who fled. It is said: they are those who stood firm with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when the flight occurred. ﴿And He sent down armies﴾: meaning the angels, who were eight thousand; it is said five thousand, and it is said sixteen thousand. ﴿And He punished those who disbelieved﴾: by killing and capture, and the taking of women and children as captives. ﴿Then God relents﴾: that is, some of them became Muslims after that. It is related that some of them came and pledged allegiance to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for Islam, and said: "O Messenger of God, you are the best of people and the most righteous of people. Our families and children have been taken captive, and our wealth has been seized." It is said that on that day six thousand souls were taken captive, and camels and sheep were taken in countless numbers. He said: "Indeed, what you see is with me. Indeed the best speech is the truest. Choose:

*either your offspring and your women, or your wealth.*"

They said: "We would not put anything on par with our lineages." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood and said: "These people have come as Muslims, and we have given them the choice between their offspring and their wealth, and they have not put anything on par with lineage. So whoever has anything in his hand and is content to return it, the matter is his. And whoever does not, let him give us, and it shall be a loan upon us until we obtain something and give him its equivalent." They said: "We are content and submit." He said: "I do not know, perhaps among you there are some who are not content. So let your chiefs (*ʿurafa'*) convey that to us." The chiefs conveyed to him that they were content.

[Note: al-Tha'labi mentioned it without a chain. This story was mentioned by Ibn Ishaq in al-Maghazi from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, at length. al-Bukhari mentioned it from the narration of al-Zuhri, from ʿUrwa, from al-Miswar and Marwan. al-Tabari and others related it from the narration of Zuhayr ibn Hirr, and in it is the poetry that Zuhayr recited.]

The reason is that His saying ﴿when your multitude pleased you﴾ is a substitute for "the day of Hunayn." So it remains that its governor must be a verb specific to it, unless *idh* is put in the accusative by a hidden "remember."

[Note: "His saying 'they were not pleased by their multitude in all those places'" — it only follows if their multitude had pleased them in all of them, even though this contradicts reality if ﴿when your multitude pleased you﴾ were made a substitute for the places as well, so reflect. (ʿ)]

When they met, a man from the Muslims said: "We will not be defeated today through lack of numbers," and this displeased the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is said the one who said it was the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is said it was Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him).

[Note: I have not found this exact wording. As for this account, if the author relied on something of that, then his statement "the admiration for multitude overtook them and they slipped away from it" etc. would be appropriate. As for his saying "It is said Abu Bakr said it," I have not found it. Suffice it that this solitude is a testimony of truth to the utmost of his courage and steadfastness of heart (ﷺ), and it is nothing but one of the signs of prophethood.

[Note: "steadfastness of heart" — *al-jashsh* is the fright of the heart at alarm; *rabit al-jash* is one who binds himself against fleeing for the sake of his courage. (ʿ)]

He said: "My Lord, give me what You promised me." He (ﷺ) said to al-ʿAbbas, who had a loud voice: "Shout to the people." So he called to the Ansar clan by clan, then he called: "O companions of the tree! O companions of the cow!" and they turned back as one man, saying:

*Here we are, here we are!*

The angels descended upon them on white horses with spots. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) looked at the fighting of the Muslims and said: "Now the furnace has become hot," then he took a handful of dirt and threw it at them, and said:

So they were defeated. Al-ʿAbbas said: "It is as if I see the Messenger of God (ﷺ) spurring his mule after them."

It is said: they are those who stood firm with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when the flight occurred. ﴿And He sent down armies﴾: meaning the angels, who were eight thousand; it is said five thousand, and it is said sixteen thousand. ﴿And He punished those who disbelieved﴾: by killing and capture, and the taking of women and children as captives. ﴿Then God relents﴾: that is, some of them became Muslims after that. It is related that some of them came and pledged allegiance to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for Islam, and said: "O Messenger of God, you are the best of people and the most righteous of people. Our families and children have been taken captive, and our wealth has been seized." It is said that on that day six thousand souls were taken captive, and camels and sheep were taken in countless numbers. He said: "Indeed, what you see is with me. Indeed the best speech is the truest. Choose:

*either your offspring and your women, or your wealth.*"

They said: "We would not put anything on par with our lineages." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood and said: "These people have come as Muslims, and we have given them the choice between their offspring and their wealth, and they have not put anything on par with lineage. So whoever has anything in his hand and is content to return it, the matter is his. And whoever does not, let him give us, and it shall be a loan upon us until we obtain something and give him its equivalent." They said: "We are content and submit." He said: "I do not know, perhaps among you there are some who are not content. So let your chiefs (*ʿurafa'*) convey that to us." The chiefs conveyed to him that they were content.

[Note: al-Tha'labi mentioned it without a chain. **The places of war: their stations and positions.** [Mahmud said: "Mawatin al-harb: maqamatuha wa mawqifuha..." etc.] Ahmad said: There is no objection, God knows best, to conjoining the two adverbials, the place and the time, one to the other, just as one of two objects is conjoined to the other when the verb is one. For you may say: "Zayd struck 'Amr in the mosque and on Friday," just as you say: "I struck Zayd and 'Amr." There is no need to posit a new verb other than the first. Moreover, the two verbs governing the two objects must in reality be different, for when you say: "I strike Zayd today and 'Amr tomorrow," no one doubts that the two strikings differ by the difference of the two times, yet the verb is one in grammatical terms (*al-sina'a*, the technical grammatical analysis). On this basis it is permissible in the verse, God knows best, for each of the two adverbials to remain as it is, without being interpreted as the other. However, al-Zamakhshari made it obligatory that the verb be plural and that a governor for the time-adverbial other than the first verb be posited, even though both are, in his view, times, on the ground that their multiplicity was not established in all the places.

He means: even if I were to hold to the unity of the governor, that would necessarily follow, but this is not necessary. Do you not see that if you said: "I strike Zayd when he stands and when he sits," the governor of the two adverbials would be one while they are different? The operation of one verb on two different times is prohibited only when there is no intervening conjunction between them, God knows best.

He said:

*How many a place of war, had it not been for me, you would have fallen, as one falls
with his body from the summit of a steep cliff, flung down.*

*You flatter me unwillingly, as if you were a sincere adviser,
while your eye reveals that your breast holds rancor toward me.*

*Your tongue is like honey, and your eye like colocynth,
your evil is spread out and your good is folded up.*

*Would that your whole good were a mere sufficiency,
and your evil kept from me as much as water is kept from the thirsty drinker.*

*How many a place of war, had it not been for me, you would have fallen as one falls
with his body from the summit of a steep cliff, flung down.*

*You have gathered backbiting, slander, and vile speech,
three traits from which you will not refrain.*

It is by Yazid ibn al-Hakam ibn Abi al-'As al-Thaqafi. *Al-mukashara* means to laugh with someone; he chose this word to indicate that it is not a true laughter agreeing with the heart, but merely the showing of teeth before him, to make him believe that he is a sincere adviser to the man, like a sick person whose heart has become corrupt. *Dawi* means pure affection. *Dawi* of the breast also means enmity; it is *dawi* with light stress like *ʿamī*, or with doubled consonant like *ghaniyy*, on the pattern *fa'il* or *fa'il*. If it is with the doubled consonant, then the lightening of it is for the metre.

*Al-madhi* is the honey of bees, because it flows (*yamdhi*) from them, and wine is also called *madhiyya* because of its ease of flow. *Al-ʿalqam* is colocynth, and every bitter tree and everything bitter. That is: your tongue is like honey in the sweetness of speech, and your eye is like colocynth in the aversion and repugnance of the soul, as you look at me with the gaze of a hostile, enraged envier. He likened evil and good to two expanses (*basatin*) by way of metaphor (*al-makniyya*, the metaphor in which only the comparand is mentioned and its attribute implied), and "spreading" and "folding" are imaginative representation (*takhyil*). The name of *layta* is the pronoun of the matter or the omitted second-person pronoun; *khayruka* is the subject of *kana*, and *kafafan* is its predicate. *Sharruka* is conjoined to *khayruka*. It is possible that it is an instance of *tanazuʿ* (competition, where two governors compete for one object), according to those who permit it with particles, since *layta* requires governing *khayruka* and *kana* also requires governing it; so the second governs it, and its pronoun is deleted from the first, because although it is a principal element, it resembles a secondary element in being in the accusative, just as the Kufans allowed its deletion in the chapter of *kana* and the chapter of *zanna*, the deleted element being known from its explainer. That is: "Would that the matter and situation were that your whole good and your evil..." *Kafafan*, with a fatha, means one who suffices and is adequate for you regarding me. If it were read with a kasra as *kifafan*, from the verbal noun of *kaffa* (to restrain), it would be permissible, and the verbal noun would have the sense of the active participle, as an intensive: "one who suffices you, or who withdraws from me as long as the thirsty one drinks water," that is, draws it: always.

*Kam* is an exclamatory noun of multiplicity, meaning "many a..." Many a place of war, had it not been for my presence, you would have been destroyed in it, as one falls. *Tuha* may be with a kasra or a damma on the *ta*', from the pattern of *ba'a*. He said: "As one falls," that is, a falling one fell from the summit of the steep cliff. It is also transmitted as *qinnat al-niq*, and the meaning is the same: from the top of the high mountain. Sibawayh's view is that *lawla* is a preposition when followed by an accusative pronoun. Al-Akhfash's view is that an accusative pronoun is placed in the position of a nominative pronoun in the nominal sentence. Al-Mubarrad denied that this occurs, and this view is refuted by the present line. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the verb and its intransitive counterpart may both be intransitive together, as *hawa* and *inhawa*, *ghawa* and *ingawa*, as shown by a line like this one. Most scholars took it as a poetic necessity (*darura*). The analogical forms would be *hawin* and *ghawin*. Some have held that they are intransitive counterparts of *ahdaytuhu* and *aghwaytuhu*, but the intransitive counterpart of these is the *infaʿala* form, not the *fa'ala* form, which is anomalous. If one were to say that *inhawa* is the intransitive counterpart of *hawwa bihi*, it would be permissible, but it is not analogical.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 28:

Najas (najas): it is a verbal noun (maṣdar); one says "najisa najasan" and "qadhira qadhaṣan," meaning "he was impure." Its meaning is "possessing impurity" (dhū najas), because shirk, which is like impurity, is with them, and because they do not purify themselves, do not perform ritual bathing, and do not avoid impurities, so impurity clings to them. Or they were made as if they were impurity itself, as an exaggeration in describing them with it. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that their very persons are impure, like dogs and swine. It is reported from al-Hasan: whoever shakes hands with a polytheist must perform ablution. The schools of law differ from these two opinions. It has also been read as "najas," with a kasra on the nun and a sukun on the jim, on the assumption that a noun being described has been omitted, as if it were said: "Indeed the polytheists are an impure kind (jins najas), or an impure sort (ḍarb najas)." Most often it comes as a follower of rijs, which is a lightened form of najs, as in: kabd for kabid. "So let them not approach the Sacred Mosque" means they shall not perform the hajj or the ʿumrah as they used to do in the Jahiliyyah. "After this year of theirs" means after the hajj of this year of theirs, which is the ninth year after the Hijrah, when Abu Bakr was appointed over the pilgrimage season. This is the position of Abu Hanifa and his companions, and it is supported by the words of ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, when he proclaimed the Bara'ah: "Let no polytheist perform the hajj after this year of ours." They are not prevented from entering the Haram, the Sacred Mosque, and all the other mosques according to him. According to al-Shafiʿi, they are prevented only from the Sacred Mosque in particular. According to Malik, they are prevented from it and from other mosques. It is reported from ʿAta', may Allah be pleased with him, that the intended meaning of "the Sacred Mosque" is the Haram, and that it is incumbent upon the Muslims not to enable them to enter it; the prohibition on the polytheists from approaching it returns to the prohibition on the Muslims from enabling them to enter it [[Mahmud said: "This prohibition returns to the prohibition on the Muslims from enabling them to enter it." Ahmad said: Those who hold that disbelievers are addressed by the branches of the Shariah, especially its prohibitions, may cite this, since the apparent wording of the verse directs the prohibition at the polytheists. However, this is far-fetched, because it is known of the polytheists that they do not desist from this prohibition, and the aim is to purify the Sacred Mosque by keeping them away from it, which is achieved only by prohibiting the Muslims from enabling them to approach it. What points to the fact that the one addressed in reality is the Muslims is the opening of the statement with their address in "O you who have believed," and the explicit inclusion of their address in His words "and if you fear poverty." It is common for a prohibition to be directed at one whose opposite is intended, and at what is meant as its opposite when there is a necessary connection, as in His words: "Let me not see you here," and "do not die except as Muslims." And Allah knows best.]] It is also said that the intended meaning is that they should be prevented from taking charge of the Sacred Mosque and attending to its affairs, and be removed from that. "And if you fear poverty" means fear of destitution caused by the prevention of the polytheists from the hajj, and what you used to gain from their coming to you of profits and earnings. "Then Allah will enrich you from His bounty" means from His gift, or from His grace in another way. So He sent down the sky upon them in abundant rain, and He made their good abundant and their provisions plentiful. The people of Tabalah and Jurash embraced Islam, and they brought food and what sustains life to Makkah, so that this was more beneficial to them than the poverty they feared from its loss. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him: Satan cast fear into their hearts and said, "From where will you eat?" So Allah commanded them to fight the People of the Book and enriched them through the jizyah. It is also said: through the conquest of lands and spoils of war. It has been read as "ʿaylah" as a verbal noun like "ʿafiyah," or as a circumstantial state, "ʿa'ilah." The meaning of His words "if Allah wills" is: if wisdom requires your enrichment, and it is a benefit for you in your religion. "Indeed Allah is All-Knowing" of your conditions, "All-Wise," who gives and withholds only with wisdom and rightness.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 29:

"From those who have been given the Book" (min alladhina utu al-kitab) is an explanation (bayan) of "those" (alladhina) together with what is in its scope (hayyiz). He negated faith in God from them, because the Jews are dualists (mathnTya) and the Christians are trinitarians (muthallatha). And [he negated] their faith in the Last Day, because they hold views about it contrary to what is required, and [they do not forbid] what God and His Messenger have forbidden, because they do not forbid what was forbidden in the Book and the Sunnah.

It is narrated from Abu Rawq: they do not act upon what is in the Torah and the Gospel; and [the meaning of] "nor do they adopt the religion of truth" is that they do not believe in the religion of Islam, which is the truth, and that everything else is falsehood. It was also said: "the religion of God." It is said: "So-and-so follows (yadin) such-and-such" when he takes it as his religion and belief.

It is called jizya (poll-tax), because it is a portion of what is due from the protected people (ahl al-dhimma), that they should pay it (yajuzzahu), i.e., discharge it; or because they pay it in return for the one who has granted them exemption from being killed. "From a hand" (an yad): either the hand of the giver or the hand of the taker is meant. [Mahmud said: "either the hand of the giver or the hand of the taker... etc." Ahmad said: this is like the hand in his (peace be upon him) saying "Do not sell gold... except hand to hand" (yadan bi-yad).]

So, on the interpretation that the giver's hand is meant, the sense is "until they give it from a hand", i.e., from a compliant hand, not a refusing one [Qawluhu "ay 'an yad mu'atiyya ghayr mumtani'a" — in al-Sihah: "I came to him upon that matter with mu'atah (accord), when I agreed with him and obeyed him." The common people say "wa'atahu" (ʿ).] because whoever refuses and resists does not give his hand, unlike the obedient, submissive one. For this reason they say "a'ta bi-yadihi" (he gave with his hand) when he submits and becomes easy after difficulty. Do you not see their saying "nazaʿa yadahu ʿan al-ta'ah" (he withdrew his hand from obedience), just as one says "khala'a rabqata al-ta'ah 'an ʿunqihi" (he removed the noose of obedience from his neck)? Or [the sense is] "until they give it from a hand to a hand", cash, not deferred, not sent through the hand of anyone else; rather from the hand of the giver to the hand of the taker. As for interpreting it as the taker's hand, the sense is "until they give it from a hand that is dominant and subduing them, or from a favour bestowed upon them", because accepting the jizya from them and leaving them their lives is a great favour upon them.

"And they are humbled" (wa hum saghirun): i.e., it is taken from them with humiliation and abasement. This is that one comes with it himself, on foot and not riding, and hands it over while standing, while the receiver sits; and that he is shaken violently (yatalatal talatala), and seized by the collar of his garment, and it is said to him: "Pay the jizya." Even if he is paying it, he is pushed on the back of his neck (yuzakh fi qafahi).

It is dropped by Islam according to Abu Hanifa, but the land tax (kharaj) is not dropped by it. There is disagreement about who is subject to it. According to Abu Hanifa, it is imposed on every unbeliever: a dhimmi, a Magian, a Sabian, and a harbi (combatant), except the polytheists of the Arabs alone. Al-Zuhri narrated that the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) made a treaty with the idol-worshippers for the jizya, except those who were Arabs, and he said to the people of Makkah: "Would you agree to a word which, if you say it, the Arabs will submit to you by it and the non-Arabs will pay you the jizya?" [Narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzaq in his Tafsir: Ma'mar reported to us from al-Zuhri with this, and he added: "It was also said that the jizya was from Bahrain, and they were Magians."]

According to al-Shafi'i, it is not taken from the polytheists of non-Arabs. What is taken according to Abu Hanifa at the beginning of each year: from the poor man who has earnings, twelve dirhams; from the middle-income man, double that; and from the wealthy, double that again, forty-eight; and it is not taken from a poor man with no earnings. According to al-Shafi'i: one dinar is taken at the end of the year from each person, whether poor or wealthy, whether he has earnings or not.

Al-Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 9, verse 30:

"ʿUzayrun ibnu Allah" (﴿ʿUzayr is the son of Allah﴾) is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate), like His saying ﴿the Messiah is the son of Allah﴾. ʿUzayr is a non-Arabic proper noun, like Ka'zar, ʿAyzar and ʿAzrāʾīl. Because it is non-Arabic and definite, it is prohibited from ṣarf (declension, i.e. it takes no tanwin). Whoever pronounces it with tanwin has made it Arabic.

As for the view of those who said that the omission of tanwin is due to the meeting of two unvocalised letters (iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn), like the reading of those who read "aḥadu Allah" (﴿Aḥad Allah﴾), or that "ibn" is a description (ṣifa) and the predicate is omitted, meaning "our god", there is no need for such contrivance (tamahhul). This is the view of some Jews who were in Medina, but it was not the view of all of them. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that Salam ibn Mishkam, Nuʿmān ibn Awfā, Shāsh ibn Qays and Mālik ibn al-Ṣayf came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said that. It was also said that Finḥāṣ said it.

The reason for this view is that the Jews killed the prophets after Moses, peace be upon him, so Allah lifted the Torah from them and erased it from their hearts. ʿUzayr, while still a youth, went out wandering in the earth, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to him and said: "Where are you going?" He said: "I seek knowledge." So he memorised the Torah, and he dictated it to them from memory without omitting a letter. They said: "Allah has only placed the Torah in his breast while he was a youth because he is His son." [[I say: the takhrīj (source-tracing) has been combined with what precedes it, and the one who transmitted it is not mentioned. The correct view is that it is a different hadith which he transmitted.]]

The evidence that this statement was made among them is that the verse was recited to them, and they neither denied it nor called it a lie, despite their eagerness to deny.

If you say: every saying is uttered by the mouth, so what is the meaning of His saying ﴿That is their saying by their mouths﴾? I reply: there are two interpretations. The first is that it means it is a saying unsupported by any proof; it is merely a word they utter, empty of any meaning beneath it, like meaningless words which are only jingles and tunes, indicating no meanings. A saying that indicates a meaning is uttered by the mouth, and its meaning affects the heart; but what has no meaning is uttered by the mouth alone. The second is that "saying" means doctrine, as in the phrase "the saying of Abu Hanifa", meaning his school of thought and what he holds. It is as if it were said: that is their doctrine and their religion, on their mouths, not in their hearts, because there is no argument or doubt with it that would affect the hearts. For when they acknowledge that He has no consort, there remains no doubt about the negation of offspring.

﴿Yuḍāhiʾūna﴾ (they imitate) necessarily involves an omitted noun (muḍāf). Its implied sense is "resembling the saying of", so that "their saying" (qawlahum) is repeated; then the muḍāf is omitted and the pronoun which was its muḍāf ilayhi takes its place, and it becomes marfūʿ (nominative).

The meaning is: those among the Jews and Christians who were in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), their saying resembles the saying of their forefathers, meaning that this disbelief was ancient among them and not newly invented. Or it resembles the saying of the polytheists: "The angels are the daughters of Allah", exalted is He far above that. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the Christians, meaning: their saying "the Messiah is the son of Allah" resembles the saying of the Jews "ʿUzayr is the son of Allah", because they were earlier than them.

It was read as yuḍāhiʾūna with a hamza, from the expression "imraʾa ḍahyaʾ" (a woman of the form faʿīl), which is the woman who resembles men in that she does not menstruate. Its hamza is added. [[His saying "its hamza is added" does not fit with his saying "on the pattern of faʿīl". Perhaps the intended phrase is "or the hamza is added...". (ʿ)]]

﴿Qātalahumu Allah﴾ (may Allah destroy them): they deserve to be told this, expressing amazement at the monstrousness of their saying, just as one says to people who have committed something monstrous: "May Allah destroy them, how astonishing is their action!" ﴿How are they turned away?﴾ meaning: how are they diverted from the truth?

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 31:

"Taking them as lords" (ittikhadhahum arbaban): they obeyed them in commanding acts of disobedience, and in declaring lawful what God had made unlawful and declaring unlawful what He had made lawful, just as lords are obeyed in their commands. Similar to this is the naming of the followers of Satan, in what he whispers to them, as "his worshippers" (ʿibādahu). Indeed, [some] worshipped the jinn. [Abraham said:] ﴿O my father, do not worship Satan﴾.

And from ʿAdiyy ibn Hatim (may God be pleased with him): "I came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while there was a golden cross around my neck, and he said: 'Do they not declare unlawful what God has made lawful, and you then declare it unlawful, and declare lawful what He has made unlawful, and you then declare it lawful?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'That is their worship.'"[[Al-Waqidi, through the route of ʿAmir ibn Saʿd from ʿAdiyy ibn Hatim, with this wording. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through another route from ʿAta ibn Yasar from ʿAdiyy ibn Hatim. Al-Tirmidhi narrated it through the route of Musʿab ibn Saʿd from ʿAdiyy ibn Hatim with this wording and more complete than it, except his words "That is their worship," and said: "Hasan gharib; we do not know it except from the hadith of ʿAbd al-Salam ibn Harb from ʿAtiyf ibn Aʿyan, and ʿAtiyf is not well known." Ibn Abi Shayba, al-Tabarani, al-Tabari and Abu Yaʿla narrated it through this route. Al-Bayhaqi narrated it likewise in al-Madkhal and added "That is their worship."]]

And from Fudayl (may God be pleased with him): "I do not care whether I obey a created being in disobedience to the Creator, or pray facing other than the qibla."

As for the Messiah, when they made him a son of God, they made him worthy of worship. Do you not see His words: ﴿Say: If the Most Merciful had a son, I would be the first of the worshippers﴾? And ﴿They were commanded only to worship one God﴾: the proofs of reason and the texts in the Gospel commanded them to this, and the Messiah, upon him be peace, said: "Whoever associates others with God, God has forbidden him Paradise." ﴿Glory be to Him﴾: exalted above their associating others with Him, and far removed from it.

It is also permissible that the pronoun in ﴿They were commanded﴾ refers to those who were taken as lords, meaning: those whom they regard as lords were commanded only to worship God and to make Him one; so how could they be lords when they are commanded and enslaved like them?

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 32–33:

The likeness of their state, in seeking to nullify the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) through denial, is that of one who wants to blow out a great light spread across the horizons, while God wants to increase it and bring it to its furthest extent of brightness and illumination, so that He may extinguish it by their blowing and obliterate it. ﴿And He will make it prevail﴾, so that the Messenger, peace be upon him, may prevail ﴿over all religion﴾, over the people of all religions. Or it means: that the religion of truth may prevail over every religion.

If you say: how is it permissible to say "abā Allāh illā kadhā" (God refused except this), when one does not say "karihtu aw abghadtu illā Zaydan" (I disliked or hated, except Zayd)?

[[Mahmud said: "If you say, how is it permissible, 'abā Allāh illā kadhā' (God refused except this), and one does not say, 'karihtu...' etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: It may not be said, on this basis, that ibā' (refusal) means the absence of will. For just as the affirmative (construction) is valid after the negation of will, it should be valid after what has the same meaning absolutely. We say: the presence of the negative particle has an effect in validating the coming of the affirmative particle after it, so this does not follow. And God knows best.]]

I say: He has treated "abā" as equivalent to "lam yurid" (did not will). Do you not see how ﴿they desire to extinguish﴾ was set against His saying ﴿but God refuses except to perfect His light﴾, and how He placed it in the position of ﴿and God wills not except to perfect His light﴾?

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 9, verses 34–35:**

The phrase *akl al-amwal* ("consuming wealth") can be understood in two ways. Either *akl* (eating) is used metaphorically for *akhdh* (taking), as in the expressions "he took the food" (*akhadha al-ta'am*) and "he received the food" (*tanawalahu*). Or wealth is the means by which one eats, that is, wealth is the cause of eating. From this second sense comes the line of the poet:

*"Indeed we have lean donkeys*
*that eat a saddle-pad every night."*

[[The explanation of this line of evidence is in volume one, page 216; consult it if you wish. Its corrector's note.]]

He means: fodder bought with the price of a saddle-pad. The meaning of their "eating falsely" (*akl bil-batil*) is that they used to take bribes (*al-rishā*) in legal rulings, and to make lenient and accommodating concessions in the religious laws.

As for ﴿وَالَّذِينَ يَكْنِزُونَ﴾ ("those who hoard"), it may refer to the many rabbis and monks, to show that two blameworthy traits were combined in them: taking bribes (*al-barātīl*), and hoarding wealth while withholding it from spending on good causes. It may also be that the reference is to the Muslims who hoard, other than the hypocrites, and they are paired with the Jewish and Christian bribe-takers, as a severe warning and to indicate that whoever among them takes unlawful gain (*al-suḥt*), and whoever among you withholds the good of his wealth, are equal in deserving the announcement of painful punishment.

It has been said: the verse on hoarding was abrogated (*nasakha*, meaning abrogated by a later ruling) by zakat (obligatory almsgiving). It has also been said: the ruling stands, and by not spending in the way of Allah is meant withholding zakat. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whatever has had its zakat paid is not a treasure, even if it is hidden; and whatever has reached the point where zakat is due but zakat has not been paid on it, that is a treasure, even if it is visible."

[[Al-Bayhaqi narrated it through Muhammad ibn Jubayr, from Sufyan, from Abdullah ibn Dinar, from Ibn Umar, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), with the wording: "Everything whose zakat has been paid is not a treasure, even if it is buried, and everything whose zakat is not paid is a treasure, even if it is visible." Al-Bayhaqi said: this is not preserved; the well-known report from Sufyan ibn Ubayd Allah, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, is his own statement (not raised). Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Adi, narrated it through Suwayd ibn Abd al-Aziz, from Ubayd Allah, with the same chain, raised, with the wording: "Every wealth, even if it is under seven earths, whose zakat is paid is not a treasure, and every wealth whose zakat is not paid, even if it is visible, is a treasure." Ibn Adi said: Suwayd and others narrate it as a statement of Ibn Umar (not raised). The statement form was narrated by Abd al-Razzaq from Ubayd Allah al-Umari, and al-Shafi'i from Ibn Uyaynah, from Ibn Ajlan, from Nafi', similarly. On this topic there is also a report from Umm Salamah, who said: "I came wearing gold anklets, and I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, is this a treasure?' He said: 'Whatever reaches the amount whose zakat is paid is not a treasure.'" Narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Hakim.]]

And from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): a man asked him about land he had sold, and he said: "Secure your wealth that you received; dig a hole for it under your wife's bed." The man said: "Is that not a treasure?" He said: "Whatever has had its zakat paid is not a treasure."

[[Abd al-Razzaq narrated it through Bishr ibn Sa'id, that a man sold another man an orchard or property for a great sum, and Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said to him: "Put this wealth in the best place"—the hadith. Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it through another chain, from Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id, that Umar asked a man, and so on.]]

And from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "Whatever has had its zakat paid is not a treasure, even if it is under seven earths, and whatever has not had its zakat paid is what Allah the Exalted mentioned, even if it is on the surface of the earth."

[[This has already been discussed.]]

If you say: what do you make of what Salim ibn al-Ja'd (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated, that when this verse was revealed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ruin to gold, ruin to silver," saying it three times? They asked him: "What wealth should we acquire?" He said: "A remembering tongue, a humble heart, and a wife who helps one of you in his religion."

[[He narrated it in this way as a mursal report (one whose chain omits a companion), but it is well known from the narration of Salim ibn Thawban. Al-Tabari and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated it through Mawthil ibn Isma'il, from al-Thawri, from al-A'mash, Mansur, and Amr ibn Murrah, from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, from Thawban with this wording. Al-Tirmidhi and Ahmad in al-Zuhd narrated it from the report of Isra'il, from Mansur, and extended it. In that version there is no "Ruin to gold, ruin to silver"; rather it says: some of his companions said, "If we knew which wealth is best, we would acquire it." Al-Bukhari and others said: Salim did not hear from Thawban. Ibn Majah, Ahmad, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah narrated it from the report of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Murrah, from his father, from Salim, from Thawban, and Ibn Majah, Ahmad, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah narrated it through Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Murrah, from his father, from Salim, from Thawban, who said: "When it was revealed, they said: 'Which wealth should we acquire?' Umar said: 'I will find out this for you,' so he mounted his camel and caught up with the Prophet (ﷺ) while I was behind him, and he said: 'O Messenger of Allah, which wealth should we acquire?'"—the hadith. On this topic there is also a report from Ali, narrated by Abd al-Razzaq through al-Thawri, from Abu Husayn, from Abu al-Duha, from Ju'dah ibn Sabrah, from him. And from Buraydah, narrated by Ibn Mardawayh through al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr, from Alqamah ibn Murthid, from Sulayman ibn Buraydah, from his father. And from one of the Companions, narrated by Ahmad through Sa'id, from Salim ibn Atiyyah, from Abdullah ibn Atiyyah, from Abdullah ibn Abi al-Hudhayl: "My companion told me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'Ruin to gold, ruin to silver,' and my companion told me that he went with Umar, and he said: 'O Messenger of Allah'"—and he mentioned something similar.]]

and by his saying (peace be upon him): "Whoever leaves gold or silver, it will be branded with it."

[[Al-Bukhari in al-Tarikh, al-Tabari, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through Abdullah ibn Abd al-Wahid al-Thaqafi, from Abu al-Najib al-Shami: "The sword-sheath of Abu Hurayrah was of silver, and Abu Dharr forbade him from it, and said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: whoever leaves gold or silver, it will be branded with it.'" On this topic there is also a report from Abu Umamah, narrated by al-Tabarani with the wording: "No servant dies and leaves gold or silver except that it will be branded with it." And from Thawban, narrated by Ibn Mardawayh and al-Tabarani in Musnad al-Shamiyyin through Artat ibn al-Mundhir, from Ibn Amir, from him, with the wording: "No one leaves gold or silver, gold or silver, except that it is made into plates and then they are branded with it."]]

A man died and a dinar was found in his loincloth, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A brand." Another died and two dinars were found in his loincloth, and he said: "Two brands."

[[Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabarani, and al-Tabari narrated it through Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Abu Umamah, with a wording that is transmitted in both places. Ibn Hibban in his Sahih narrated the second part from a hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]]

I say: this was before zakat was made obligatory. As for after zakat became obligatory, Allah is more just and more generous than to gather wealth for His servant from what He permitted to him, and have zakat paid on his behalf for what He obligated upon him in it, and then punish him. Many of the Companions, such as Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Talhah ibn Ubayd Allah, and Ubayd Allah (may Allah be pleased with them all), possessed wealth and managed it, and no one among those who abstained from possession criticized them, because abstention is a choice of the better course; otherwise it would fall under scrupulousness (*wara'*) and asceticism in this world. Possession is permitted with a wide latitude, and its owner is not blamed, but everything has a limit.

As for what is narrated from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "Four thousand or less is spending money, and what exceeds it is a treasure"—

[[Abd al-Razzaq and al-Tabari narrated it with the chain mentioned earlier, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), two hadiths before this.]]

—that is a statement about what is better.

If you say: why was it said ﴿وَلَا يُنْفِقُونَهَا﴾ ("nor spend them") when two things have been mentioned? I say: this is taking the pronoun in reference to the meaning rather than the wording, because each of the two is a complete unit, a great amount, and [comprises] dinars and dirhams. It is like His saying ﴿وَإِنْ طَائِفَتَانِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا﴾ ("if two groups of the believers fight," 49:9). It has also been said: he took the pronoun back to the treasures. It has been said: to the wealth. And it has been said: the meaning is "nor spend them," and the gold [is understood] similarly, just as the meaning of the poet's line:

*"Indeed I and Qayyar here are strangers,"*

[[The explanation of this line was given in volume one, page 629; consult it if you wish. Its corrector's note.]]

and Qayyar is similarly [understood].

If you say: why were these two singled out from among the rest of the wealth? I say: because they are the standard of value and the prices of things, and only someone who has more than he needs, and whose holdings of them are large, would hoard them; and whoever has them in abundance, so that he hoards them, does not lack the other kinds of wealth. Therefore mentioning the hoarding of these two is an indication of what is other than them.

If you say: what is the meaning of ﴿يُحْمَىٰ عَلَيْهَا﴾ ("heated upon them")? Why was it not said ﴿تُحْمَىٰ﴾ ("they will be heated"), from your saying: "he heated the branding iron" (*hamā al-mīsam*) and "I heated it" (*ahmaytuhu*)? And you do not say "I heated upon the iron"? I say: its meaning is that the fire is heated upon them, that is, is kindled into a state of heat and intense burning, from His saying ﴿نَارٌ حَامِيَةٌ﴾ ("a blazing fire," 101:11). If it had been said "a day when they will be heated," this meaning would not have been conveyed. [Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "If you say: why was it not said 'heated' as one says 'he heated the branding iron' and 'I heated it'…" Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: in this section there are subtleties of grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) whose beauty is marred by obscurity, and Allah is the granter of success.]]

If you say: when the heating is done by the fire, why was the verb mentioned? I say: because it is attributed to the prepositional phrase (the preposition with its object). The original is: "the day the fire is heated upon them." When "the fire" was omitted, it became "heated upon them," because the attribution shifted from the fire to "upon them," just as you say: "the case was raised to the emir"; if you do not mention the case, you say: "it was raised to the emir."

It is narrated from Ibn Amir that he read ﴿تُحْمَىٰ﴾ with a *ta'* (feminine form). Abu Haywah read ﴿فَيُكْوَىٰ﴾ with a *ya'*.

If you say: why were these body parts singled out? I say: because in not spending their wealth in the way of Allah, they sought only worldly aims: standing and prestige among people, advancement, keeping their honor preserved in their eyes; they are greeted with praise, welcomed with honor, revered and shown deference; and [they seek] to eat good things until they are filled and puff up their sides, and to wear soft garments that they throw over their backs. As you see the wealthy of your time, these are their aims and demands from their wealth; they never think of the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The people of wealth have gone off with the rewards."

[[Muslim narrated it through Abu al-Aswad, from Abu Dharr: "Some people among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the people of wealth have gone off with the rewards; they pray as we pray'"—the hadith.]]

It has also been said: because when they saw a poor man they frowned, and when they sat in a gathering with him they turned away from him, turned their sides to him, and turned their backs on him. It has been said: the meaning is that on the four sides, their fronts, their backs, and their sides, [the fire] will be upon them.

﴿هَٰذَا مَا كَنَزْتُمْ﴾ ("This is what you hoarded") is with the implied verb "it will be said" (*'alā irādat al-qawl*).

His saying ﴿لِأَنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ ("for yourselves") means: you hoarded it so that your souls might benefit from it, find pleasure in it, and attain the aims that they hovered around. And you did not know that you hoarded it so that your souls would be harmed by it and tormented, and this is a rebuke to them. ﴿فَذُوقُوا مَا كُنْتُمْ تَكْنِزُونَ﴾ ("So taste what you used to hoard"). It has been read as *taknizūna* with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn*, meaning: the consequence of the wealth you used to hoard, or the consequence of your being hoarders.
