[[The explanation of this line of evidence is in volume one, page 216; consult it if you wish. Its corrector's note.]]

He means: fodder bought with the price of a saddle-pad. The meaning of their "eating falsely" (*akl bil-batil*) is that they used to take bribes (*al-rishā*) in legal rulings, and to make lenient and accommodating concessions in the religious laws.

As for ﴿وَالَّذِينَ يَكْنِزُونَ﴾ ("those who hoard"), it may refer to the many rabbis and monks, to show that two blameworthy traits were combined in them: taking bribes (*al-barātīl*), and hoarding wealth while withholding it from spending on good causes. It may also be that the reference is to the Muslims who hoard, other than the hypocrites, and they are paired with the Jewish and Christian bribe-takers, as a severe warning and to indicate that whoever among them takes unlawful gain (*al-suḥt*), and whoever among you withholds the good of his wealth, are equal in deserving the announcement of painful punishment.

It has been said: the verse on hoarding was abrogated (*nasakha*, meaning abrogated by a later ruling) by zakat (obligatory almsgiving). It has also been said: the ruling stands, and by not spending in the way of Allah is meant withholding zakat. From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whatever has had its zakat paid is not a treasure, even if it is hidden; and whatever has reached the point where zakat is due but zakat has not been paid on it, that is a treasure, even if it is visible."

[[Al-Bayhaqi narrated it through Muhammad ibn Jubayr, from Sufyan, from Abdullah ibn Dinar, from Ibn Umar, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ), with the wording: "Everything whose zakat has been paid is not a treasure, even if it is buried, and everything whose zakat is not paid is a treasure, even if it is visible." Al-Bayhaqi said: this is not preserved; the well-known report from Sufyan ibn Ubayd Allah, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, is his own statement (not raised). Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Adi, narrated it through Suwayd ibn Abd al-Aziz, from Ubayd Allah, with the same chain, raised, with the wording: "Every wealth, even if it is under seven earths, whose zakat is paid is not a treasure, and every wealth whose zakat is not paid, even if it is visible, is a treasure." Ibn Adi said: Suwayd and others narrate it as a statement of Ibn Umar (not raised). The statement form was narrated by Abd al-Razzaq from Ubayd Allah al-Umari, and al-Shafi'i from Ibn Uyaynah, from Ibn Ajlan, from Nafi', similarly. On this topic there is also a report from Umm Salamah, who said: "I came wearing gold anklets, and I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, is this a treasure?' He said: 'Whatever reaches the amount whose zakat is paid is not a treasure.'" Narrated by Abu Dawud and al-Hakim.]]

And from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): a man asked him about land he had sold, and he said: "Secure your wealth that you received; dig a hole for it under your wife's bed." The man said: "Is that not a treasure?" He said: "Whatever has had its zakat paid is not a treasure."

[[Abd al-Razzaq narrated it through Bishr ibn Sa'id, that a man sold another man an orchard or property for a great sum, and Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said to him: "Put this wealth in the best place"—the hadith. Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it through another chain, from Sa'id ibn Abi Sa'id, that Umar asked a man, and so on.]]

And from Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "Whatever has had its zakat paid is not a treasure, even if it is under seven earths, and whatever has not had its zakat paid is what Allah the Exalted mentioned, even if it is on the surface of the earth."

[[This has already been discussed.]]

If you say: what do you make of what Salim ibn al-Ja'd (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated, that when this verse was revealed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Ruin to gold, ruin to silver," saying it three times? They asked him: "What wealth should we acquire?" He said: "A remembering tongue, a humble heart, and a wife who helps one of you in his religion."

[[He narrated it in this way as a mursal report (one whose chain omits a companion), but it is well known from the narration of Salim ibn Thawban. Al-Tabari and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat narrated it through Mawthil ibn Isma'il, from al-Thawri, from al-A'mash, Mansur, and Amr ibn Murrah, from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, from Thawban with this wording. Al-Tirmidhi and Ahmad in al-Zuhd narrated it from the report of Isra'il, from Mansur, and extended it. In that version there is no "Ruin to gold, ruin to silver"; rather it says: some of his companions said, "If we knew which wealth is best, we would acquire it." Al-Bukhari and others said: Salim did not hear from Thawban. Ibn Majah, Ahmad, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah narrated it from the report of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Murrah, from his father, from Salim, from Thawban, and Ibn Majah, Ahmad, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah narrated it through Abdullah ibn Amr ibn Murrah, from his father, from Salim, from Thawban, who said: "When it was revealed, they said: 'Which wealth should we acquire?' Umar said: 'I will find out this for you,' so he mounted his camel and caught up with the Prophet (ﷺ) while I was behind him, and he said: 'O Messenger of Allah, which wealth should we acquire?'"—the hadith. On this topic there is also a report from Ali, narrated by Abd al-Razzaq through al-Thawri, from Abu Husayn, from Abu al-Duha, from Ju'dah ibn Sabrah, from him. And from Buraydah, narrated by Ibn Mardawayh through al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr, from Alqamah ibn Murthid, from Sulayman ibn Buraydah, from his father. And from one of the Companions, narrated by Ahmad through Sa'id, from Salim ibn Atiyyah, from Abdullah ibn Atiyyah, from Abdullah ibn Abi al-Hudhayl: "My companion told me that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'Ruin to gold, ruin to silver,' and my companion told me that he went with Umar, and he said: 'O Messenger of Allah'"—and he mentioned something similar.]]

and by his saying (peace be upon him): "Whoever leaves gold or silver, it will be branded with it."

[[Al-Bukhari in al-Tarikh, al-Tabari, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through Abdullah ibn Abd al-Wahid al-Thaqafi, from Abu al-Najib al-Shami: "The sword-sheath of Abu Hurayrah was of silver, and Abu Dharr forbade him from it, and said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: whoever leaves gold or silver, it will be branded with it.'" On this topic there is also a report from Abu Umamah, narrated by al-Tabarani with the wording: "No servant dies and leaves gold or silver except that it will be branded with it." And from Thawban, narrated by Ibn Mardawayh and al-Tabarani in Musnad al-Shamiyyin through Artat ibn al-Mundhir, from Ibn Amir, from him, with the wording: "No one leaves gold or silver, gold or silver, except that it is made into plates and then they are branded with it."]]

A man died and a dinar was found in his loincloth, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A brand." Another died and two dinars were found in his loincloth, and he said: "Two brands."

[[Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabarani, and al-Tabari narrated it through Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Abu Umamah, with a wording that is transmitted in both places. Ibn Hibban in his Sahih narrated the second part from a hadith of Ibn Mas'ud.]]

I say: this was before zakat was made obligatory. As for after zakat became obligatory, Allah is more just and more generous than to gather wealth for His servant from what He permitted to him, and have zakat paid on his behalf for what He obligated upon him in it, and then punish him. Many of the Companions, such as Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, Talhah ibn Ubayd Allah, and Ubayd Allah (may Allah be pleased with them all), possessed wealth and managed it, and no one among those who abstained from possession criticized them, because abstention is a choice of the better course; otherwise it would fall under scrupulousness (*wara'*) and asceticism in this world. Possession is permitted with a wide latitude, and its owner is not blamed, but everything has a limit.

As for what is narrated from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "Four thousand or less is spending money, and what exceeds it is a treasure"—

[[Abd al-Razzaq and al-Tabari narrated it with the chain mentioned earlier, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), two hadiths before this.]]

—that is a statement about what is better.

If you say: why was it said ﴿وَلَا يُنْفِقُونَهَا﴾ ("nor spend them") when two things have been mentioned? I say: this is taking the pronoun in reference to the meaning rather than the wording, because each of the two is a complete unit, a great amount, and [comprises] dinars and dirhams. It is like His saying ﴿وَإِنْ طَائِفَتَانِ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ اقْتَتَلُوا﴾ ("if two groups of the believers fight," 49:9). It has also been said: he took the pronoun back to the treasures. It has been said: to the wealth. And it has been said: the meaning is "nor spend them," and the gold [is understood] similarly, just as the meaning of the poet's line:

*"Indeed I and Qayyar here are strangers,"*

[[The explanation of this line was given in volume one, page 629; consult it if you wish. Its corrector's note.]]

and Qayyar is similarly [understood].

If you say: why were these two singled out from among the rest of the wealth? I say: because they are the standard of value and the prices of things, and only someone who has more than he needs, and whose holdings of them are large, would hoard them; and whoever has them in abundance, so that he hoards them, does not lack the other kinds of wealth. Therefore mentioning the hoarding of these two is an indication of what is other than them.

If you say: what is the meaning of ﴿يُحْمَىٰ عَلَيْهَا﴾ ("heated upon them")? Why was it not said ﴿تُحْمَىٰ﴾ ("they will be heated"), from your saying: "he heated the branding iron" (*hamā al-mīsam*) and "I heated it" (*ahmaytuhu*)? And you do not say "I heated upon the iron"? I say: its meaning is that the fire is heated upon them, that is, is kindled into a state of heat and intense burning, from His saying ﴿نَارٌ حَامِيَةٌ﴾ ("a blazing fire," 101:11). If it had been said "a day when they will be heated," this meaning would not have been conveyed. [Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "If you say: why was it not said 'heated' as one says 'he heated the branding iron' and 'I heated it'…" Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: in this section there are subtleties of grammatical analysis (*i'rab*) whose beauty is marred by obscurity, and Allah is the granter of success.]]

If you say: when the heating is done by the fire, why was the verb mentioned? I say: because it is attributed to the prepositional phrase (the preposition with its object). The original is: "the day the fire is heated upon them." When "the fire" was omitted, it became "heated upon them," because the attribution shifted from the fire to "upon them," just as you say: "the case was raised to the emir"; if you do not mention the case, you say: "it was raised to the emir."

It is narrated from Ibn Amir that he read ﴿تُحْمَىٰ﴾ with a *ta'* (feminine form). Abu Haywah read ﴿فَيُكْوَىٰ﴾ with a *ya'*.

If you say: why were these body parts singled out? I say: because in not spending their wealth in the way of Allah, they sought only worldly aims: standing and prestige among people, advancement, keeping their honor preserved in their eyes; they are greeted with praise, welcomed with honor, revered and shown deference; and [they seek] to eat good things until they are filled and puff up their sides, and to wear soft garments that they throw over their backs. As you see the wealthy of your time, these are their aims and demands from their wealth; they never think of the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The people of wealth have gone off with the rewards."

[[Muslim narrated it through Abu al-Aswad, from Abu Dharr: "Some people among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the people of wealth have gone off with the rewards; they pray as we pray'"—the hadith.]]

It has also been said: because when they saw a poor man they frowned, and when they sat in a gathering with him they turned away from him, turned their sides to him, and turned their backs on him. It has been said: the meaning is that on the four sides, their fronts, their backs, and their sides, [the fire] will be upon them.

﴿هَٰذَا مَا كَنَزْتُمْ﴾ ("This is what you hoarded") is with the implied verb "it will be said" (*'alā irādat al-qawl*).

His saying ﴿لِأَنْفُسِكُمْ﴾ ("for yourselves") means: you hoarded it so that your souls might benefit from it, find pleasure in it, and attain the aims that they hovered around. And you did not know that you hoarded it so that your souls would be harmed by it and tormented, and this is a rebuke to them. ﴿فَذُوقُوا مَا كُنْتُمْ تَكْنِزُونَ﴾ ("So taste what you used to hoard"). It has been read as *taknizūna* with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn*, meaning: the consequence of the wealth you used to hoard, or the consequence of your being hoarders.

In the Book of Allah, in what He has established and made obligatory of His rulings, and deemed wise and right. It is also said: in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh). "Four of them are sacred": three in succession, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and al-Muharram, and one standing alone, which is Rajab. From this is his (ﷺ) saying in his sermon at the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Verily, time has turned back to the form it had on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth." [Agreed upon (muttafaq 'alayh) from the hadith of Abu Bakrah. On this matter there is also a report from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), related by al-Tabari through the narration of Musa ibn 'Ubaydah from Sadaqah ibn Yasar from him, with the wording of the author. It is weak. And from Ibn 'Abbas, related by Ibn Mardawayh.] The year is twelve months, of which four are sacred: three in succession, Dhu al-Qa'dah and Dhu al-Hijjah, and al-Muharram. And Rajab of Mudar, which lies between Jumada and Sha'ban. The meaning: the months returned to what they had been, the Hajj returned to Dhu al-Hijjah, and the intercalation (al-nasi') that was practised in the Jahiliyyah was annulled. The Farewell Pilgrimage coincided with Dhu al-Hijjah, whereas the pilgrimage of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) before it had been in Dhu al-Qa'dah.

﴿That is the upright religion﴾: meaning that the sanctity of the four months is the straight religion, the religion of Ibrahim and Isma'il. The Arabs had held fast to it as an inheritance from them, and they used to venerate the sacred months and forbid fighting in them, to the extent that if a man met the killer of his father or brother, he would not attack him. They called Rajab "al-Asamm" and "Munassil al-Asinnah" (the one that strips the spear-points). Then they introduced the intercalation and altered it.

﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein﴾: that is, within the sacred months, do not make their sanctity lawful. From 'Ata': "By Allah, it is not lawful for people to raid in the Sacred Precinct or in the sacred months unless they are fighting." And it was not abrogated. And from 'Ata' al-Khurasani (may Allah be pleased with him): fighting in the sacred months was made lawful by a declaration of immunity (bara'ah) from Allah and His Messenger. It is also said: the meaning is "do not sin therein," indicating the great sanctity of these months, just as He magnified the months of Hajj by His saying: ﴿Whoever undertakes the obligation of Hajj therein, there is no sexual relations, no transgression, and no quarrelling...﴾ (2:197), though that is forbidden in all the other months.

﴿All together﴾: a circumstantial phrase (hal) referring either to the subject or the object. ﴿With the God-fearing﴾: He is their helper, urging them to piety by guaranteeing victory to its people.

Al-Nasi' (postponement): it is the postponement of the sanctity of a month to another month. That is because they were people of wars and raids. When a sacred month came and they were engaged in fighting, abandoning fighting weighed heavily on them, so they would make it lawful and render another month sacred in its place, until they rejected restricting the sacred months to prohibition, and they would declare sacred from the months of the year four months, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That they may make up the number of what Allah has made sacred﴾. That is, that they might agree with the number which is four and not contradict it. They contradicted the specification, which is one of the two obligations. Sometimes they would increase the number of months, making them thirteen or fourteen, so that the time would be ample for them. For this reason, Exalted and Mighty is He said: ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months﴾, meaning without the addition they had added. The pronoun in "yuhillunahu" and "yuharrimunahu" refers to al-nasi'. That is, if they made lawful a sacred month for one year, they would return and make it sacred in the following year. It is narrated that this occurred among Kinanah, because they were poor and in need of raiding. Junadah ibn 'Awf al-Kinani was obeyed in the pre-Islamic era, and he would stand on a camel during the season and say at the top of his voice: "Indeed your gods have made the Muharram lawful for you, so make it lawful." Then the following year he would stand and say: "Indeed your gods have made the Muharram forbidden to you, so forbid it." He made al-nasi' an increase in disbelief, because the disbeliever, whenever he commits a sin, increases in disbelief, so it added to them filth upon their filth, just as the believer, when he performs an act of obedience, increases in faith: ﴿And it increases them in faith, while they rejoice﴾. It is read "yudall" in the passive voice, and "yadill" with a fatha on the ya' and the dad, and "yudallu" on the basis that the verb belongs to Allah, Exalted and Mighty. Al-Zuhri read: "liyuwti'u" with shaddah. Al-nasi' is a verbal noun of "nasa'ahu" when he postponed it. It is said: nasa'ahu, nasa'an, and nasa'an and nasiy'an, like your saying: massahu massan and misasan and masisan. It is also read with all of these. It is read "al-nasa" on the pattern of "al-nada," and "al-nasa" on the pattern of "al-nuha," and these are the lightened forms of al-nasi' and al-nasi'. If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿so that they make lawful what Allah has made unlawful﴾? I say: its meaning is that they make lawful by agreeing on the number alone, without specifying what Allah has made forbidden of fighting, or by abandoning the specification of the months by themselves. ﴿Their evil deeds were made attractive to them﴾: Allah forsook them, so they regarded their ugly deeds as good. ﴿And Allah does not guide﴾, that is, He does not show them kindness, but rather forsakes them. It is also read: "zuyyina lahum sū'u a'mālihim" with the verb in the active voice, the agent being Allah, Exalted and Mighty.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 38–41:

*Ithaqqaltum* (ﺍﺛَّﺎﻗَﻠْﺘُﻢ) is read *tathaqaltum* (تثاقلتم, "you were heavy/sluggish"), and al-A'mash (a Qur'an reciter) also read it this way. It means you were slow and remiss. It carries the sense of inclining and settling, which is why it takes *ila* (إلى, "to"). The meaning is: you inclined to this world and its desires, and disliked the hardships and troubles of travel. Similar is the verse "he clung to the earth and followed his desire." It was also said: you inclined to remain in your land and your homes.

It is also read *a-thaqaltum?* (with the interrogative *alif*), which carries the sense of denial and rebuke. If you ask: what governs *idha* (إذا, "when"), given that the interrogative particle prevents it from governing? I answer: it is what is indicated by *ithaqaltum*, or the verbal sense within *ma lakum* (ما لكم, "what is the matter with you"), as if it were said: "What will you do when it is said to you..." just as you would say "*malak qa'iman*" (what is the matter with you standing).

This occurred at the Battle of Tabuk in the ninth/tenth year (of the Hijra), after their return from al-Ta'if. They were called to march in a time of hardship, drought and intense summer heat, with the distance great and the enemy numerous, so it was difficult for them. It was also said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not set out on any expedition without concealing its destination by mentioning another, except for the expedition of Tabuk. (Agreed upon, from the hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik.) This was so that the people might prepare the full provisions.

*Min al-akhirah* (مِنَ الْآخِرَةِ) means "instead of the Hereafter," as in His saying: "We would have made among you angels" (i.e., in exchange for you). *Fi al-akhirah* (فِي الْآخِرَةِ) means "in comparison with the Hereafter."

*Illa tanfiru* (إِلَّا تَنْفِرُوا, "unless you march forth") contains a great wrath against those who were sluggish. (Al-Zamakhshari said: "In this verse there is great wrath against the sluggish, for He threatened them with a painful punishment..." Ahmad (ibn al-Munir) said: It is close to returning the pronoun to the Messenger, since the pronoun in His saying "unless you help him" that follows is agreed to refer to him, and Allah knows best.) He threatened them with a painful punishment, unrestricted, encompassing the punishment of both abodes. He would destroy them and replace them with another people better than them and more obedient. He is independent of them in supporting His religion, and their sluggishness does not harm it in any way.

It was also said that the pronoun refers to the Messenger, meaning: they will not harm him, because Allah promised to protect him from the people and to give him victory, and the promise of Allah is certain to occur. It was said that by "a people other than you" He means the people of Yemen. It was also said: the sons of Persia. The apparent meaning is free of the need for specification.

If you ask: how can His saying "then Allah has indeed helped him" (*faqad nasarahu Allah*) be the answer to the condition? I answer: there are two aspects. First: "If you do not help him, then the one who helped him will help him (again)," since he had no companion but one man, and no fewer than one. By His saying "Allah has indeed helped him," it indicates that He will help him in the future, as He helped him at that time. Second: He made victory obligatory for him and made him one who is helped at that time, so he will not be forsaken after that.

The expulsion is attributed to the disbelievers, as it is attributed to them in His saying "from your town which expelled you," because when they resolved to expel him, Allah permitted him to leave, so it is as if they expelled him.

*Thani ithnayn* (ثانِيَ اثْنَيْنِ, "the second of two") means "one of two," like His saying "the third of three." The two were the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him). It is related that when Jibril (peace be upon him) commanded him to leave, he said: "Who will leave with me?" He said: Abu Bakr. Its position is accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*). It is also read *thani* (with a sukun) in *thani ithnayn*.

*Idh humaa* (إِذْ هُما, "when they two") is a substitute for *idh akhrajahu* (when he expelled him). The cave (*al-ghar*) is a hole at the top of Thawr, a mountain on the right of Makkah at a distance of one hour's walk. They stayed in it for three days.

*Idh yaqulu* (إِذْ يَقُولُ, "when he said") is a second substitute. It was said: when the polytheists reached above the cave, Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) became fearful for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he said: "If one of them looks down today, the religion of Allah will be lost." [I have not found it in this form. In the two Sahihs, from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), he said: "I looked at the feet of the polytheists above our heads while we were in the cave, and I said: O Messenger of Allah, if one of them looked at the place of his feet he would see us. He said: O Abu Bakr, what do you think of two whose third is Allah?"] Then he (peace be upon him) said: "What do you think of two whose third is Allah?"

It was also said: when the two entered the cave, Allah sent two doves which laid eggs at its base, and a spider which spun a web over it. [Al-Bazzar related it through 'Awf ibn 'Amr from Abu Mus'ab al-Makki, who heard Anas ibn Malik and others say: "On the night of the cave, Allah commanded a rock which stood in front of the Prophet (ﷺ) and concealed him, and He commanded the spider which spun a web across his face and concealed him, and He commanded two wild doves which stood at the mouth of the cave..." (the hadith).]

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, blind their eyes." [I have not found it.] So they kept circling around the cave without noticing. Allah had indeed blinded their eyes from him. They also said: whoever denies the companionship of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) has disbelieved, because he denies the speech of Allah, and this is not the case for the rest of the Companions.

*Sakinatahu* (سَكِينَتَهُ, "his tranquility") is what was cast into his heart of security, in which he found calm, knowing that they would not reach him.

*Al-junud* (the hosts) are the angels on the day of Badr, and at al-Ahzab and Hunayn.

*Kalimat alladhina kafaru* (the word of those who disbelieved) is their call to disbelief, and *kalimat Allah* (the word of Allah) is His call to Islam. It is also read *kalimatu Allah* in the accusative, but the nominative is more eloquent. *Hiya* (هِيَ) is either a separating pronoun (*fasl*) or a subject (*mubtada'*), and it contains an emphasis on the elevation of the word of Allah, and that it is specific to Him over all other words.

*Khifafan wa thiqalan* (خِفافاً وَثِقالًا, "light and heavy") means: light in marching forth because of your eagerness for it, and heavy from it because of its hardship for you. Or light because of the few of your dependents and burdens, and heavy because of their many. Or light from weapons and heavy with them. Or riders and foot-soldiers. Or young and old. Or lean and fat. Or healthy and sick.

It is related from Ibn Umm Maktum that he said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Is it obligatory for me to march forth?" He said: "Yes," until the verse "There is no blame upon the blind" was revealed.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: it was abrogated by His saying "There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick..."

It is related from Safwan ibn 'Amr: "I was governor of Homs, and I met an old man, from the people of Damascus, whose eyebrows had fallen over his eyes, on his riding-beast, intending to go on the raid. I said: 'O uncle, Allah has already excused you.' He raised his eyebrows and said: 'O son of my brother, Allah has called us to march forth, light and heavy, except that whomever Allah loves, He tests.'"

It is related from al-Zuhri: "Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab went out to the raid after one of his eyes had been lost. It was said to him: 'You are ill and have a harmful condition.' He said: 'Allah has called us to march forth, the light and the heavy. If I cannot fight, I will increase the numbers and guard the baggage.'"

*Wa jahidu bi amwalikum wa anfusikum* (وَجاهِدُوا بِأَمْوالِكُمْ وَأَنْفُسِكُمْ, "and strive with your wealth and your selves") is an obligation to strive with both, if possible, or with one of them according to the circumstance and the need.

*They say, "Do not be lost (tabʿad)," while they are burying him,*
*And there is no being lost except what the slabs conceal.*

It is said *baʿida* (to be far), in the pattern of *karuma* and *taʿiba*, and its verbal noun is *al-buʿd* with a fatha and a fatha, or with a damma and then a sukun. The pattern *taʿiba* has become known in the sense of perishing. *Lā tabʿad* with a fatha is a phrase that runs on their tongues at a calamity, indicating the extreme of grief. *Wa-lā buʿd* means: there is no distance except what the slabs conceal. Or: *wa-lā dhū buʿd* (no one who is distant) except what the slabs conceal. Or: *lā baʿīd* (no one far) except what the slabs conceal, with the verbal noun used in the sense of an adjective.

*Mā* is used for a rational being, because what is meant by it is the attribute. Or what is meant is bodies and forms, stripped of perceptions and spirits. *Al-ṣafāʾiḥ* (the slabs) are broad stones with which the grave is roofed. The "distance" (*al-buʿd*) in its reality is what the grave covers, a **kināya** (euphemism) for his death.

*Bi-llāh* is connected to *sa-yaḥlifūna* (they will swear), or it is part of their speech. The saying is intended in both readings. That is: they will swear, meaning the ones who stayed behind, offering excuses when you return from the expedition of Tabūk, saying, by God, **"If we had been able, we would have gone out with you"** ﴿لَوِ اسْتَطَعْنا لَخَرَجْنا مَعَكُمْ﴾. Or: they will swear by God, saying, "If we had been able." His words *la-kharajnā* ("we would have gone out") take the place of the answers both to the oath and to *law* (if). The report of what will happen after the return, of their oath and excuse, is among the miracles.

The meaning of *al-istiṭāʿa* (ability) is the ability of equipment and provisions, or the ability of bodies, as if they were feigning sickness. It is recited *law istaṭaʿnā* with a damma on the waw, assimilating it to the waw of plurality in His words **﴿فَتَمَنَّوُا الْمَوْتَ﴾** ("then wish for death"). **﴿يُهْلِكُونَ أَنْفُسَهُمْ﴾** ("they destroy themselves") may be a substitute for *sa-yaḥlifūna*, or a circumstantial clause in the sense of "destroying." The meaning is that they put themselves into ruin by their false oath and by what they swear to of staying behind. It may also be a circumstantial clause from *la-kharajnā*, meaning: we would have gone out with you, even though we would have destroyed ourselves and cast ourselves into ruin by bearing the journey over that distance. He brought it in the third-person form because it is a report about them. Do you not see that if it were said, "They will swear by God, 'If they had been able, they would have gone out,'" it would be correct? One says: "He swore by God that he will certainly do it" (*la-yafʿalanna*) and "I will certainly do it" (*la-afʿalanna*). So the third person follows the rule of reporting, and the first person follows the rule of direct quotation.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 43:**

﴿Allah has pardoned you﴾ is a kinaya (a figure of speech in which a thing is referred to by an implied meaning, here metonymy) for the offence, because pardon (al-'afw) is a synonym for it [[Mahmud said: "This is a kinaya for the offence, because pardon is a synonym for it..." etc. Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It is not permissible for him to interpret this verse in this way, for it is one of two things: either it is not what is meant, or it is what is meant, but Allah has exalted His noble Prophet above being addressed with explicit rebuke, especially regarding the Chosen One, peace and blessings be upon him. So al-Zamakhshari, in either case, has overlooked what is owed to him, peace and blessings be upon him. Well has someone said regarding this verse:

Among the kindness of Allah the Exalted toward His Prophet is that He began with pardon before reproach. Had He said to him at the outset, "Why did you grant them permission?", his heart, peace and blessings be upon him, would have been broken. Such courtesy must be emulated in regard to the master of mankind, may the best of prayers and peace be upon him.]]. Its meaning is: you erred, and what you did was evil [[His statement "Its meaning is: you erred, and what you did was evil" addresses the Prophet with the language of gentleness and tenderness, but the author (al-Zamakhshari) explained it with the language of harshness and severity, and how far apart the two are. (ʿ)]]. ﴿Why did you grant them permission?﴾ is an explanation of what was alluded to by the pardon. Its meaning: What was the matter with you that you permitted them to stay behind from the campaign when they asked your leave and offered you their excuses? Why did you not wait before granting permission until it became clear to you who was truthful in his excuse from among those who lied in it? It was said that there were two things which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did without being commanded to do them: his granting permission to the hypocrites, and his taking ransom from the captives, so Allah the Exalted rebuked him for them.

﴿They do not ask your permission﴾ (lā yastaʾdhinuka): not the custom of the believers.

The commentator (al-Zamakhshari) resumed: "His words, ﴿Those who believe in God, [and the Last Day, do not ask your permission]﴾, up to his words, ﴿Only those who do not believe in God [ask your permission]﴾ ... the verse." He said: its meaning is that it is not the custom of the believers to ask your permission to strive. ... Etc."

Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This courtesy should be followed in every case. It is not fitting for a person to ask his brother's permission to do him a kindness, nor for a host to ask his guest's permission to serve him food, for asking permission in such situations is a sign of formality and reluctance. May God's blessings and peace be upon His friend (Abraham). His generosity and his courtesy toward his guests were such that he would not undertake any of the preparations for hospitality in their sight. For this reason God, the Exalted, praised him through the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ) for this beautiful trait and noble manners. He said, ﴿So he turned quietly to his household and brought a fatted calf﴾ (Qur'an 51:26), that is, he went away secretly so that they would not notice. One who attends to his guest's needs in front of him may be regarded as having asked his permission to host him. This is among the courtesies that people of manliness and chivalry should adhere to. Even more serious than asking permission to leave for jihad and to support the religion is being slow to respond to it after it has been urged and called for. The worst state of one who is slow, when people have been called to the battle, is that he holds to a branch of hypocrisy. We seek refuge in God from incurring His wrath.

...that they strive. The sincere ones among the Emigrants (muhajirun) and the Helpers (ansar) used to say: "We will never ask the Prophet's permission, and we will certainly strive with him, always, with our wealth and our lives."

The meaning of ﴿anyuʾjihadu﴾ (that they strive) is "that they strive," or "out of aversion to striving." ﴿God is Knowing of the God-fearing﴾ is a testimony to them that they are included among the company of the God-fearing (al-muttaqun), and a promise to them of the greatest reward.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 45–48:

"Only those seek your permission" — meaning the hypocrites, who were thirty-nine men, "who waver" (yataraddadun), an expression for being bewildered, because wavering is the habit of the bewildered, just as steadiness and firmness are the habit of the one who has clear insight. It was read as "ʿaddahu," meaning "ʿuddatahu" (his equipment/preparation), so that the equipment was treated as the equipment was treated, from the words of the poet:

"And they failed you in the matter they had promised" [[See the explanation of this witness in volume one, page 323; refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

This is by dropping the feminine tā' and substituting the genitive pronoun in its place. It was also read as "ʿiddatun" with a kasra on the ʿayn without an annexed noun, and "ʿaddihi" with an annexed noun. If you ask: what is the position of the particle of exception (lākin, "but")? I say: since His saying "and if they had wished to go out" (wa law arādū al-khurūja) gives the meaning of denying their departure and their readiness for the campaign, it was said "but God disliked their being sent forth" (wa lākin kariha Allāhu inbiʿāthahum), as if it had been said: they did not go out, but they held back from going out because God disliked their being sent forth, just as you say: "Zayd did not treat me well, but he wronged me." "God held them back" (fa-thabbaṭahum): He made them sluggish, forsook them, and weakened their desire to set out. "It was said: sit back" (wa qīla uqʿudū): God's placing in their hearts the dislike of going out is regarded as a command to remain seated. It was also said that it is the whisper of Satan through temptation; it was also said that it is their own words to themselves; and it was also said that it is the permission of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for them to stay behind.

If you ask: how is it permissible for God Most High to place in their souls the dislike of going out to the campaign, when that is ugly, and God is exalted above inspiring what is ugly? I say: their going out would have been corrupting, because of His saying "If they had gone out among you, they would have added to you nothing but corruption" (law kharajū fīkum mā zādūkum illā khabālan), so placing dislike of that going out in their souls was good and beneficial. If you ask: then why did the Messenger of God (ﷺ) err in giving them permission in a matter that was beneficial? I say: the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) permission to them was not for considering this benefit, nor did he know it except after the return, by God's informing him; rather, it was because they asked his permission for that and offered excuses to him, so it was incumbent upon him to examine the reality of their excuses and not to be lenient in accepting them, and therefore the rebuke came to him. It is also possible that in the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) not granting them permission, along with God's holding them back, there was another benefit, and by his granting them permission that benefit was lost, for when God held them back and they did not set out, and their sitting back was without permission from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the proof would have been established against them and they would have had no excuse left.

God indeed made up for that when He exposed their secrets, uncovered their hidden affairs, and bore witness against them of hypocrisy, and that they do not believe in God and the Last Day. If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying "with those who sit back" (maʿa al-qāʿidīn)? I say: it is a censure of them and a declaration of their incapacity, and an attaching of them to the women, children and the disabled, whose habit is sitting and crouching in the houses; they are the "qāʿidūn" (those who sit), the "khālifūn" (those who stay behind), and the "khawālif" (the left-behinds). This is clarified by His saying, Exalted is He, "They are content to be with the left-behinds" (raḍū bi-an yakūnū maʿa al-khawālif). "Except for corruption" (illā khabālan) is not at all a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ) as they say, because a disjunctive exception is when the excepted item is not of the same genus as the item excepted from, as in your saying: "They added to you nothing good except corruption." The item excepted from in this statement is not mentioned, and when it is not mentioned the exception falls from the most general of the general, which is "thing," so it is a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil), since corruption is a part of the most general of the general; it is as if it had been said: "They added to you nothing but corruption." Khabāl means corruption and evil.

"And they would have hurried about among you" (wa la-awḍaʿū khilālakum): they would have spread through your midst by incitement (bi-al-tadrīb) and tale-bearing and the sowing of discord. It is said: "wada'a al-baʿīr waḍʿan" when it hastened, and "awḍaʿtuhu" I made it hasten. The meaning: they would have driven their mounts among you, and what is intended is hastening with tale-bearing, because the rider is swifter than the walker. Ibn al-Zubayr, may God be pleased with him, read "wa la-arqaṣū" (and they would have danced about), from "raqisat al-nāqatu raqṣan" when the she-camel hastened, and "arqaṣtuhā" I made her hasten. He said:

"And the dancing ones toward Mina and al-Ghabghab"

It was also read "wa la-awfaḍū." If you ask: how was "wa lā awḍaʿū" written in the codex with an added alif? I say: the fatha used to be written as an alif before the Arabic script, and the Arabic script was invented close to the revelation of the Qur'an, and a trace of that alif remained in the habits of writers, so they wrote the form of the hamza as an alif and its fatha as another alif, and similarly "awa lā adhbahannahu" (or I shall surely slaughter him).

"They seek to cause you trouble" (yabghūnakumu al-fitnata): they try to tempt you, by causing dissension among you and corrupting your intentions in your campaign. "And among you are listeners to them" (wa fīkum sammāʿūna lahum): that is, tale-bearers who listen to your speech and then convey it to them; or there are among you people who listen to the hypocrites and obey them.

"They had already sought trouble" (laqad ibtaghawu al-fitnata): that is, distress, the setting of traps, and the effort to scatter your company and separate your companions from you, as Abdullah ibn Ubayy did on the day of Uhud when he withdrew with those who were with him. From Ibn Jurayj, may God be pleased with him: they lay in wait for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at the mountain pass on the night of ʿAqabah, twelve men in number, intending to assassinate him. "Before" (min qablu): before the expedition to Tabuk. "And they turned matters over for you" (wa qallabū laka al-umūra): they devised schemes and plots for you, and considered opinions for the purpose of nullifying your affair. It was also read "wa qallabū" with the lighter form. "Until the truth came" (ḥattā jāʾa al-ḥaqqu): that is, your support and victory, "and the command of God became manifest" (wa ẓahara amru Allāh): His religion prevailed and His law became supreme.

"Until the truth came" (ḥattā jāʾa al-ḥaqqu): that is, your support and victory, "and the command of God became manifest" (wa ẓahara amru Allāh): His religion prevailed and His law became supreme.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 45–48:

"Only those seek your permission" — meaning the hypocrites, who were thirty-nine men, "who waver" (yataraddadun), an expression for being bewildered, because wavering is the habit of the bewildered, just as steadiness and firmness are the habit of the one who has clear insight. It was read as "ʿaddahu," meaning "ʿuddatahu" (his equipment/preparation), so that the equipment was treated as the equipment was treated, from the words of the poet:

"And they failed you in the matter they had promised" [[See the explanation of this witness in volume one, page 323; refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

This is by dropping the feminine tā' and substituting the genitive pronoun in its place. It was also read as "ʿiddatun" with a kasra on the ʿayn without an annexed noun, and "ʿaddihi" with an annexed noun. If you ask: what is the position of the particle of exception (lākin, "but")? I say: since His saying "and if they had wished to go out" (wa law arādū al-khurūja) gives the meaning of denying their departure and their readiness for the campaign, it was said "but God disliked their being sent forth" (wa lākin kariha Allāhu inbiʿāthahum), as if it had been said: they did not go out, but they held back from going out because God disliked their being sent forth, just as you say: "Zayd did not treat me well, but he wronged me." "God held them back" (fa-thabbaṭahum): He made them sluggish, forsook them, and weakened their desire to set out. "It was said: sit back" (wa qīla uqʿudū): God's placing in their hearts the dislike of going out is regarded as a command to remain seated. It was also said that it is the whisper of Satan through temptation; it was also said that it is their own words to themselves; and it was also said that it is the permission of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for them to stay behind.

If you ask: how is it permissible for God Most High to place in their souls the dislike of going out to the campaign, when that is ugly, and God is exalted above inspiring what is ugly? I say: their going out would have been corrupting, because of His saying "If they had gone out among you, they would have added to you nothing but corruption" (law kharajū fīkum mā zādūkum illā khabālan), so placing dislike of that going out in their souls was good and beneficial. If you ask: then why did the Messenger of God (ﷺ) err in giving them permission in a matter that was beneficial? I say: the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) permission to them was not for considering this benefit, nor did he know it except after the return, by God's informing him; rather, it was because they asked his permission for that and offered excuses to him, so it was incumbent upon him to examine the reality of their excuses and not to be lenient in accepting them, and therefore the rebuke came to him. It is also possible that in the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) not granting them permission, along with God's holding them back, there was another benefit, and by his granting them permission that benefit was lost, for when God held them back and they did not set out, and their sitting back was without permission from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), the proof would have been established against them and they would have had no excuse left.

God indeed made up for that when He exposed their secrets, uncovered their hidden affairs, and bore witness against them of hypocrisy, and that they do not believe in God and the Last Day. If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying "with those who sit back" (maʿa al-qāʿidīn)? I say: it is a censure of them and a declaration of their incapacity, and an attaching of them to the women, children and the disabled, whose habit is sitting and crouching in the houses; they are the "qāʿidūn" (those who sit), the "khālifūn" (those who stay behind), and the "khawālif" (the left-behinds). This is clarified by His saying, Exalted is He, "They are content to be with the left-behinds" (raḍū bi-an yakūnū maʿa al-khawālif). "Except for corruption" (illā khabālan) is not at all a disjunctive exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ) as they say, because a disjunctive exception is when the excepted item is not of the same genus as the item excepted from, as in your saying: "They added to you nothing good except corruption." The item excepted from in this statement is not mentioned, and when it is not mentioned the exception falls from the most general of the general, which is "thing," so it is a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil), since corruption is a part of the most general of the general; it is as if it had been said: "They added to you nothing but corruption." Khabāl means corruption and evil.

"And they would have hurried about among you" (wa la-awḍaʿū khilālakum): they would have spread through your midst by incitement (bi-al-tadrīb) and tale-bearing and the sowing of discord. It is said: "wada'a al-baʿīr waḍʿan" when it hastened, and "awḍaʿtuhu" I made it hasten. The meaning: they would have driven their mounts among you, and what is intended is hastening with tale-bearing, because the rider is swifter than the walker. Ibn al-Zubayr, may God be pleased with him, read "wa la-arqaṣū" (and they would have danced about), from "raqisat al-nāqatu raqṣan" when the she-camel hastened, and "arqaṣtuhā" I made her hasten. He said:

"And the dancing ones toward Mina and al-Ghabghab"

It was also read "wa la-awfaḍū." If you ask: how was "wa lā awḍaʿū" written in the codex with an added alif? I say: the fatha used to be written as an alif before the Arabic script, and the Arabic script was invented close to the revelation of the Qur'an, and a trace of that alif remained in the habits of writers, so they wrote the form of the hamza as an alif and its fatha as another alif, and similarly "awa lā adhbahannahu" (or I shall surely slaughter him).

"They seek to cause you trouble" (yabghūnakumu al-fitnata): they try to tempt you, by causing dissension among you and corrupting your intentions in your campaign. "And among you are listeners to them" (wa fīkum sammāʿūna lahum): that is, tale-bearers who listen to your speech and then convey it to them; or there are among you people who listen to the hypocrites and obey them.

"They had already sought trouble" (laqad ibtaghawu al-fitnata): that is, distress, the setting of traps, and the effort to scatter your company and separate your companions from you, as Abdullah ibn Ubayy did on the day of Uhud when he withdrew with those who were with him. From Ibn Jurayj, may God be pleased with him: they lay in wait for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at the mountain pass on the night of ʿAqabah, twelve men in number, intending to assassinate him. "Before" (min qablu): before the expedition to Tabuk. "And they turned matters over for you" (wa qallabū laka al-umūra): they devised schemes and plots for you, and considered opinions for the purpose of nullifying your affair. It was also read "wa qallabū" with the lighter form. "Until the truth came" (ḥattā jāʾa al-ḥaqqu): that is, your support and victory, "and the command of God became manifest" (wa ẓahara amru Allāh): His religion prevailed and His law became supreme.

Permit me to stay behind and do not put me to trial (lit. do not expose me to fitna), meaning do not put me into fitna, which is sin, by not granting me permission, for if I stay behind without your leave I will have sinned. It was also said: "and do not throw me into ruin," for if I go out with you my wealth and my dependents will be destroyed. It was also said: al-Jadd ibn Qays said, "The Ansar know that I am addicted to women" [[His words "I am addicted" (innī mustahtir) mean: devoted to it, not caring what is said about me. End of quote. (Gh.)]], "so do not tempt me with the daughters of al-Asfar," meaning the women of Rome, "but I will help you with wealth, so leave me be."

It was recited as "wa-lā tuftinnī" (from aftana), and "Alā fī al-fitnati saqaṭū" (Surely in fitna they have fallen), meaning that fitna is precisely what they fell into, namely the fitna of staying behind. In the codex of Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads "saqaṭa" (singular), because "man" is singular in wording but plural in meaning.

﴿And indeed, Hell encompasses the disbelievers.﴾ Meaning: it will encompass them on the Day of Resurrection. Or: it encompasses them now, since the causes of encompassing are with them, so it is as though they are in its midst.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 50:

If good befalls you in some of the military campaigns, a victory and booty, it grieves them (﴿إِنْ تُصِبْكَ في بعض الغزوات حَسَنَةٌ ظفر وغنيمة تَسُؤْهُمْ﴾). And if a misfortune befalls you, a setback and hardship in some of them, such as what happened on the Day of Uhud (﴿وَإِنْ تُصِبْكَ مُصِيبَةٌ﴾ nakbah wa shiddah fi ba'diha, nahw ma jara fi yawm Uhud), they rejoice in their own situation in turning away from you (﴿يفرحوا بحالهم في الانحراف عنك﴾), and they say (﴿وَيَقُولُوا﴾) "We had already taken our affair" (﴿قَدْ أَخَذْنا أَمْرَنا﴾), that is, our affair with which we are characterized (﴿أى أمرنا الذي نحن متسمون به﴾), namely caution, vigilance, and acting with resolve (﴿مِنَ الحذر والتيقظ والعمل بالحزم﴾), "from before" (﴿مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾), that is, from before what occurred (﴿من قبل ما وقع﴾). And they turn away (﴿وَتولوا﴾) from the place of speaking about that and gathering for it, to their families (﴿عن مقام التحدّث بذلك والاجتماع له إلى أهاليهم﴾), while they are rejoicing (﴿وَهُمْ فَرِحُونَ﴾), delighted. It is said: "They turned away" means they turned away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (﴿تولوا: أعرضوا عن رسول الله ﷺ﴾).

Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) read: "Qul hal yusibuna" (Say: "Will there befall us..."). Talha (may Allah be pleased with him) read: "Hal yusibuna," with the yā' doubled (shaddah).

The reasoning behind this reading is that the form is "yufayil" and not "yafil," because it derives from the weak root with waw, as in their saying: al-sawab (the correct course), and "ṣāba al-sahm yaṣūbu" (the arrow hit its target), and "mṣāwib" in the plural of muṣība (calamity). Thus the form of "yafil" from it should be "yuṣawwib," do you not see their saying: "ṣawwaba ra'yahu" (he deemed his opinion correct)? Except if it is from the dialect of those who say "ṣāba al-sahm yuṣību" (the arrow hit). And from his saying: "asmā al-ṣā'ibāt wa al-ṣayb" [[Note: the text "ومن قوله" is likely "ومنه" or "ومنها"; in al-Sihah: ṣāba al-sahm al-qirṭās yuṣībuhu ṣaybān, a dialectal form of aṣāba.]].

The lām in His saying, "illā mā kataba Allāhu lanā" (except what Allah has prescribed for us), conveys the sense of exclusivity, as if it were said: "He will not befall us except what Allah has singled us out for by decreeing and making obligatory for us, namely victory over you or martyrdom." Do you not see His saying, "Huwa mawlānā" (He is our Protector), meaning the One who protects us and whom we protect? "That is because Allah is the Protector of those who believe, and the disbelievers have no protector" (Qur'an 47:11). "And upon Allah let the believers rely" (Qur'an 9:51). It is incumbent upon the believers not to rely on other than Allah, so let them do what is their duty.

Except for one of the two best outcomes, the two outcomes each of which is a good end: victory or martyrdom. "And we await for you" one of the two worst outcomes from among the consequences: either that God afflicts you with a punishment from Him, such as a calamity from the sky as came upon 'Ad and Thamud, or with a punishment at our hands, which is killing for disbelief. "So await" what we have mentioned of our consequences. "Indeed we are with you awaiting" what your consequence will be. So each of us will certainly meet what he awaits, and it will not go beyond it.

[Note: the editor's remark on "إحدى السوأتين" – that it is perhaps "السوأيين" – is a marginal note in the original and has been left out as a comment of my own.]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 53:

"Spend" (anfiqu), i.e., in the way of God and in the channels of righteousness, "willingly or unwillingly" (taw'an aw karhan): a accusative of circumstance (hal), meaning willingly or under compulsion. If you say: how did He command them to spend and then say "it will not be accepted from you"? I say: it is a command in the sense of a statement, like His words, blessed and exalted, ﴿Say: whoever is in error, the Most Merciful will extend for him an extension﴾ [Maryam 19:75], and its meaning is: "It will not be accepted from you, whether you spend willingly or unwillingly." Similar to it is His words, exalted, ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:80], and the verse of the poet:

"Treat us ill or treat us well, without blame (la malumah)
with us, nor will she be hateful if she turns against us."

This is said by Kuthayyir, companion of 'Azzah. He says: test me in love, and deal with me by harm and kindness, and see whether my state changes, and do what your husband compels you to do of abusing me, as it comes in his speech, and do not hesitate about it, for it is like your kindness; and therefore he mentioned kindness. The meaning: there is no blame nor hatred, whether you harm or benefit. So the command is in the sense of a statement. Then he turned and said: 'Azzah is not blameworthy in our eyes, nor hateful if she hates, i.e., if she burdens herself with hatred toward us and displays it. It is also permissible that the meaning is: you are neither blameworthy nor hated, so the shift (iltifat) in his words "if she hates" is only [a shift].

That is: God will not forgive them, whether you ask forgiveness for them or not. And we will not blame you, whether you have harmed us or done good to us.

If you say: when is such a thing permissible? I say: when the speech indicates it, just as its reverse is permissible in your saying "May God have mercy on Zayd and forgive him." If you say: why did he do that? I say: for a point in it, which is that Kuthayyir is as if saying to 'Azzah: test the sincerity of my position with you and the strength of my love for you, and deal with me by harm and kindness, and see whether my state with you varies, whether you act harmfully or kindly. In its meaning is the saying of the speaker:

"Your brother who, if you rise with the sword intending
to strike him, does not hold back from you in affection,

And if you come seeking his protection to spend the night [with him],
he hastens out of concern for you from refusal."

He sees that he is in affection and that he falls short, while in fact he has exceeded the limit in it and burdened himself beyond his capacity.

Likewise the meaning is: spend, and see whether it is accepted from you; ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them, and look whether you see any difference between the state of asking forgiveness and abandoning it. If you say: what is the purpose in denying acceptance? Is it that the Messenger of God ﷺ leaves accepting from them and returning to them what they offer? Or is it that it is not accepted by God, Exalted, going to waste as vanity with no reward? I say: it admits both matters together. His words "willingly or unwillingly" mean: willingly without compulsion from God and His Messenger, or under compulsion. He called the compulsion "coercion," because they were hypocrites, so their being obligated to spend was burdensome for them, like coercion. Or: willingly without coercion from your leaders, for the leaders of the hypocrites used to urge them to spend for the benefit they saw in it; or under compulsion on their part. It is related that it was revealed concerning al-Jadd ibn Qays when he stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk and said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "This is my wealth, with which I will help you, so leave me." ﴿Indeed, you were a people of defiance﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:53, lit. "you are" in the verse]: a causal explanation for the rejection of their spending. What is meant by "defiance" (al-fisq) is: rebellion and obstinacy.

The phrase "أَنَّهُمْ" is the subject (fa'il) of "منع" (prevented). "وهم" and "أن تقبل" are its two objects.

"أن تقبل" is also read with the verb in the feminine form, with a ta' and with a ya' (read as passive, "to be accepted"), and "نفقاتهم" and "نفقتهم" are read as plural and singular respectively. Al-Sulami read "أن يقبل منهم نفقاتهم", treating the verb as attributed to God, the Mighty and Majestic.

"كُسالى" with a damma and with a fatha is the plural of "كسلان" (lazy), like "سكارى" and "غيارى" are plurals of "سكران" and "غيران". Their laziness is because they do not hope for reward through their prayer, nor fear punishment for abandoning it, so it is burdensome to them, as in God's words, ﴿وَإِنَّها لَكَبِيرَةٌ إِلَّا عَلَى الْخاشِعِينَ﴾ (And indeed it is burdensome, except for the humble). It has been reported in some traditions that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) disliked for a believer to say, "I am lazy (kasilt)," as if he had this verse in mind, since laziness is one of the attributes of the hypocrites, and so a believer should not ascribe it to himself.

If you say: reluctance is the opposite of willingness, yet God described them as willing in His words, ﴿طَوْعاً﴾ (willingly), and then described them as not spending except while they are reluctant. I say:

What is meant by their willingness is that they give it without compulsion from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) or from their leaders. Their giving was only out of reluctance and necessity, not out of desire and choice.

Admiration for something means being delighted with it, pleased by it, and amazed at its beauty. The meaning is: do not find their adornments of worldly life admirable, and do not be seduced by what they have been given, as in His words ﴿And do not extend your eyes toward what We have given pairs of them to enjoy﴾. Indeed, Allah the Exalted gave them what He gave them as a punishment, by exposing it to plunder and captivity, and by afflicting them with calamities and misfortunes through it. He obliged them to spend from it on the paths of good, while they disliked it despite themselves, and He made them suffer every kind of burden and hardship in gathering and earning it and in raising their children.

If you say: if it is valid to link the punishment to the will of Allah the Exalted, then what about their souls departing while they are unwilling? I say: what is meant is gradual seduction through blessings, as in His words ﴿We only give them respite so that they increase in sin﴾. It is as if it were said: He wills to keep His blessing upon them continually until they die while they are disbelievers, occupied with enjoyment and distracted from considering the outcome.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 56–57:**

﴿Indeed, they are of you﴾: that is, among the body of the Muslims. ﴿But they are people who are fearful﴾: they fear being killed and what will be done to them by the polytheists, so they feign Islam out of caution (taqiyya). ﴿A refuge﴾ (malja'): a place to which they resort, seeking protection by it, such as the top of a mountain, a fortress, an island, ﴿or caves﴾ (magharat) ﴿or hiding places (ghayran)﴾.

It is recited with a ḍammah on the mim (mughārāt? no, the reading is "maghārāt" with ḍammah: "mughārāt"), from aghāra al-rajul and ghāra, when a man enters a ghawr (a hollow or depression). It has been said: it is a transitive form of ghāra al-shay' and aghartuhu, meaning places where they change their persons (i.e., hide themselves). It is also permissible that it derives from aghāra al-tha'lab, when he hastens, in the sense of places of flight and escape. ﴿Or a place of entry (mudkhalan)﴾, or a tunnel (naffaqan) into which they burrow and hide, and it is a form of muftaʿal from entering (al-dukhūl). It is also read mudkhalan from dakhala, and mudkhalan from adkhala: a place into which they cause themselves to enter. Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, read mutadakhalan. It is also read: ﴿If they found a refuge therein, they would certainly turn to it﴾ (la-watllaw ilayhi la-lataju'a ilayhi), ﴿rushing headlong﴾ (yajmahūna): they hasten with a speed that nothing can turn back, from the jamūḥ horse, which is one that, when it charges, is not turned back by the bridle. Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, read yajmazūn. When he was asked about it, he said: yajmahūna, yajmazūna and yashtaddūna all mean the same.
