Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 58:

﴿Among them are those who find fault with you concerning the distribution of the alms.﴾ [yalmizuka] means: he criticizes you regarding the distribution of the alms (sadaqat) and reproaches you. It was said: they are the al-Mu'allafa qulubuhum (those whose hearts are to be reconciled). And it was said: it is the son of Dhu al-Khuwaisira, the head of the Khawarij (the seceders). He was the one who, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was dividing the spoils of Hunayn, said: "Be just, O Messenger of Allah!" Whereupon the Prophet (ﷺ), peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, said: "Woe to you! If I am not just, who then will be just?" [Agreed upon from the hadith of Abu Sa'id, and the wording is that of al-Bukhari. In both (collections) is: "When Dhu al-Khuwaisira came," and this is the preserved version.] And it was said: he is Abu al-Jawwas, one of the hypocrites. He said: "Do you not see your companion! He distributes your alms among the shepherds of sheep, yet he claims that he is just!" So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May you have no father! Was Musa not a shepherd? Was Dawud not a shepherd?" Then, when he had gone, the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Beware of this man and his companions, for they are hypocrites."

It was recited as yalmuzuka with a damma (yalmizuka with the vowel u on the first letter), and as yallamizuka and yalamizuka. The doubling (tashdid) and the form on the pattern of mufa'ala (yalamizuka) are for emphasis in the act of reproach (lamz).

Then He described them: their approval and their anger are for themselves, not for the religion and what would bring about the welfare of its people. This is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that day sought to win over the hearts of the people of Makkah by lavishing spoils upon them, so the hypocrites were displeased with him. And [in the words ﴿idha﴾, "then/if"] the particle idha denotes sudden occurrence: that is, when they are not given anything from it, they suddenly become angry.

The answer to "law" (if) is omitted; its implied sense is: "And if only they had been content, it would have been better for them." The meaning is: "And if only they had been content with what the Messenger gave them from the spoils, and their souls had been pleased with it even though their share was small, and had said: 'Allah's grace and His provision are sufficient for us; what He has apportioned to us is enough. Allah will soon give us another spoil, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) will give us more than he has given us today. Indeed, we turn to Allah, hoping that He will grant us spoils and bestow His bounty upon us.'"

This passage is in the commentary's Arabic. The task: translate faithfully. Let me produce the English translation.

Indeed, the alms (al-sadaqat) are for the poor (li-l-fuqara'): a restriction (qasr) of the category of alms to the enumerated classes, and that they are exclusively for them [Mahmud said: "This is a restriction of the category of alms to the enumerated classes, and that they are exclusively for them, etc." Ahmad said: This is the position of Malik, may Allah be pleased with him. The view that it is obligatory to distribute them among all the classes, such that it is not permissible to omit any one of them, deriving from the indication of the lam (li-) of ownership, as al-Shafi'i held, is not supported by the context, for the verse opens with the particle of restriction (kalimat al-hasr), which indicates that others have no share in it. This is the purpose for which the verse was revealed, so there is no implication in it regarding anything other than that. And Allah knows best.] It does not go beyond them to others. As if it were said: "They are for them, not for others." Similar to your saying: "The caliphate is for Quraysh," meaning it does not extend beyond them and is not for anyone else. It therefore admits of being distributed among all the classes, and of being distributed among some of them. On this is the position of Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him. It is related from Hudhayfa, Ibn Abbas and others among the Companions and the Successors, may Allah be pleased with them, that they said: "Whichever class you place it in, it suffices you." And it is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with him: "If I were to look at a household of Muslims who are poor and modest, and I gave them enough to make them independent with it, that would be dearer to me." According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, it must be distributed among the eight classes. And it is related from Ikrimah, may Allah be pleased with him, that it is distributed among the eight classes. And it is related from al-Zuhri that he wrote to Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz that the alms should be distributed among the eight classes.

﴿And those employed to collect them﴾: the collectors who receive them. ﴿And those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾: nobles of the Arabs whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would win over so that they would embrace Islam, and he would give them a portion of it when the Muslims were few. ﴿And the slaves﴾: those who are contracted to buy their freedom, who strive to pay from it. It was also said: the captives. It was also said: the slaves are bought and then freed. ﴿And the debtors﴾: those whom debts have overwhelmed and who own, after them, nothing reaching the minimum threshold (nisab). It was also said: those who undertook guarantees (hamalat), borrowed on account of them, and incurred debts. ﴿And in the way of Allah﴾: the poor fighters and the pilgrims who have been cut off from their means. ﴿And the wayfarer﴾: the traveller cut off from his wealth; he is poor where he is, though rich where his wealth is.

﴿An obligation from Allah﴾: in the sense of an emphasizing infinitive (masdar), because His saying "The alms are only for the poor" means "Allah has made the alms obligatory for them." It was also read as "fariḍatun" in the nominative, meaning: "That is an obligation."

If you ask: why did it shift from the lam to "fi" (in) in the last four? [His speech resumes. He said: "If you ask, why did he shift from the lam to fi in the last four... etc." Ahmad said: There is another secret which is more evident and closer: that the first four classes are owners of what may be given to them, and they take it as owners, so the entry of the lam was fitting for them. As for the last four, they do not own what is spent on their behalf, nor is it spent directly into their hands; rather it is spent on interests connected with them. The money spent on slaves is taken by their masters, the contracting parties, so their share is not delivered into their hands, such that it would be expressed by the lam which implies their ownership of what is spent for them; rather they are the locus (mahall) for this expenditure and the interest connected with it. Likewise, the workers (al-'amilun), their share is spent on their creditors to clear their obligations, not for them. As for "in the way of Allah," this is clear in that respect. As for the wayfarer, it was as if he were included under "in the way of Allah," and he was singled out for mention to draw attention to his particularity, although he is free of both particles, and attaching him to the genitive governed by lam is possible, but attaching him to the nearer one is closer. And Allah knows best. My grandfather Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Faris, the jurist and vizier, derived from the difference between the two particles an argument in support of Malik that the purpose is to specify the destination of expenditure, and the lam in that case is the lam of ownership. He says: the complement of the prepositional phrase that occurs as the predicate of "the alms" is omitted, so its estimate must be determined. Either the estimate is: "the alms are spent on the poor," as Malik says, or "owned by the poor," as al-Shafi'i says. But the first is definite, because it is an estimate sufficient for both particles together: the lam is correctly attached to it and so is "fi," so one may say, "this thing is spent on such-and-such." Unlike the estimate "owned," which only fits with the lam, and when reaching "fi" requires an estimate of "spent" in order to fit. So the estimate "spent" is general in its attachment, comprehensive in its validity, and definite. And Allah is the Granter of success.]

The answer: to indicate that they are more deserving of being given alms than those mentioned before, because "fi" denotes a container, so this alerts that they are worthy of having alms placed in them and made the object of them and their target. This is because of what is involved in freeing slaves, whether contractual manumission, bondage or captivity, and in freeing debtors from the burden of debt through release and rescue, and because the poor fighter or the pilgrim cut off combines poverty with worship. Likewise the wayfarer combines poverty with estrangement from family and wealth. The repetition of "fi" in His saying "and in the way of Allah and the wayfarer" indicates the excellence of preference given to these two over the slaves and the debtors.

If you ask: how does this verse come amid the repeated mention of the hypocrites and their intrigues? The answer: by the fact that these classes are the exclusive recipients of alms, to the exclusion of others, it indicates that they are not among them, cutting off their greed and signalling that they deserve deprivation, that they are far from it and from its destinations. What have they to do with it? And what empowered them to speak about it or to slander its distributor, may Allah bless him and grant him peace?

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 61:

Al-udhun (الأذن): the man who believes everything he hears. [Mahmud said: "Al-udhun: the man who believes everything he hears... He named the man after the bodily organ which is the instrument of hearing..." etc.] Ahmad said: Nothing is more eloquent in refuting them than this mode, for at the beginning it raises their hopes of agreement, then it turns against their hopes with a decisive cut, and follows their disparagement of him with despair of him. Comparable to this among the jurists' usages is the "argument by its own premise" (al-qawl bil-mujib), because at its beginning it raises the opponent's hopes of acceptance, then cuts off that hope abruptly. Nothing is more decisive than raising hopes followed and succeeded by despair. And God is the Granter of success.

It is said of anyone whose speech is accepted, that he is named after the bodily organ which is the instrument of hearing, as if his whole being were a hearing ear. Its counterpart is their saying of a lookout (al-rabi'a [In al-Sihah: al-rabi'a is the vanguard scout. (A)]): "eye" (ʿayn). Their harming him is their saying about him, "he is an ear" (huwa udhun). "An ear of good" (udhun khayr) is like your saying "a man of truth" (rajul sidq), meaning excellence and righteousness. As if it were said: yes, he is an ear, but a fine ear. It is also permissible to mean: he is an ear for good and truth and for what must be heard and accepted, and he is not an ear for anything other than that. This is indicated by the reading of Hamzah, "and mercy" (wa-rahmatun) in the genitive, as a conjunction with it, meaning: he is an ear of good and mercy, hearing nothing else and accepting nothing else.

Then he explained his being "an ear of good" by saying that he believes in God, because of the proofs established for him, and accepts from the sincere believers among the Emigrants and the Helpers. "And mercy for those of you who believe" means: to those of you, hypocrites, who manifest faith, since he hears from you and accepts your outward faith, and does not expose your secrets or disgrace you, and does not do to you what he does to the polytheists, out of regard for the benefit God saw in sparing you. So he is an ear as you said, except that he is an ear of good for you, not an ear of evil. Thus he let their saying about him stand, not that he was interpreted as praise or commendation of him, even though they intended by it blame and a slight on his acuteness and generosity, and that he belongs to people of simple hearts and naivety.

It is said: a group of them blamed him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and this reached him, so their hearts were troubled, and some of them said: "Do not worry about it, for he is only an ear that hears the words of the one who conveys them, so he listens. We will go to him and apologize to him, and he will hear our excuse too and be pleased." So it was said: "He is an ear of good for you." It was also read: "an ear of good for you," with "ear" as the predicate of an omitted subject, and "good" likewise, meaning: he is an ear which is good for you, i.e., if he is as you say, then he is good for you, because he accepts your excuses and does not requite you for your evil inward state [Qawluhu "ʿala sooo dakhlatikum" means your blameworthiness. In al-Sihah, dakhlat al-rajul with a dammah is the inner side of his affair, and perhaps it has come to be used predominantly for blame. (A)]. Nafi' read with the lightening of the dhal.

If you ask: why was the verb of faith transitive with bi to God, and with li to the believers? I say: because he intended assent to God, which is the opposite of disbelief in Him, so it took bi; and he intended hearing from the believers, and that he should accept what they say and affirm it, because they are truthful in his sight, so it took li. Do you not see His saying: "You are not a believer to us, even if we were truthful" [What is meant by "ma anba'ahu 'an al-ba'" and similar is: how far it is from bi (A)]. And like it: "None believed in Moses except some offspring of his people" and "Shall we believe you, when the lowest follow you?" and "Do you believe in him before I have given you leave?"

If you ask: what is the reasoning behind Ibn Abi 'Ablah's reading "wa-rahmatan" in the accusative? I say: it is a cause whose causative element is omitted; its estimate is: "and as a mercy to you, he gives you leave," and it was omitted because His saying "an ear of good for you" indicates it.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 62:

"﴿...لَكُمْ لِيُرْضُوكُمْ﴾" (﴿...they swear to you in order to please you﴾). The address is to the Muslims. The hypocrites (al-munafiqun) used to speak with slander (al-matà'in, i.e. defamatory talk against the believers) or would lag behind from the jihad. Then they would come to them and make excuses to them, and would reinforce their pretexts with oaths, so that they would excuse them and be pleased with them. So it was said to them: "﴿If you are believers, as you claim, then God and His Messenger have more right that you please them, in obedience and accord﴾." The pronoun is singular because there is no difference between the pleasure of God and the pleasure of His Messenger (ﷺ). So the two are in the status of one object of pleasure, like your saying: "Zayd's kindness and his generosity have comforted me and mended me." Or it may be: "God has more right that they please Him, and likewise His Messenger."

Al-Muhaddah (opposition, defiance) is a verbal noun of the form mufa'alah derived from al-hadd (limit, boundary), just as al-mushaqqah (opposition) is derived from al-shaqq (split). Fa-inna lahu is with the predicate elided, meaning: so it is incumbent that for him is the Fire of Hell. It has also been said that the meaning is fa-lahu (so for him), and that inna is a repetition, because in His saying "annahu" there is emphasis. It is also permissible that fa-inna lahu be conjoined to annahu, with the answer to man (whoever) being elided, its estimate being: "Did they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger will perish, so that for him is the Fire of Hell?" It has also been read as "alam ta'lamu" with the ta' (you know).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 64:

They used to mock Islam and its people, and they were wary lest Allah expose them through the revelation concerning them, to the point that some of them said: "By Allah, we consider ourselves nothing but the worst of Allah's creation. I wish I had gone forward and been flogged a hundred lashes, and that nothing would be revealed about us that exposes us." The pronoun in ʿalayhim (against them) and tunabbiʾuhum (it informs them) refers to the believers. And in qulubihim (their hearts) refers to the hypocrites (munafiqun). This is correct because the meaning leads to it. It is also permissible that the pronouns refer to the hypocrites, since a surah revealed about their state is revealed against them. The meaning of "it informs them of what is in their hearts" is as if it says to them: "In your hearts is such-and-such," meaning that it broadcasts their secrets against them, so that they hear them spread widely, as though it were informing them of them. It has also been said that the meaning of yahdharu (be wary) is an imperative, i.e., let the hypocrites be wary. If you say: the wariness falls on the sending down of the surah in His words, "The hypocrites are wary lest a surah be sent down against them," then what is the meaning of His words, "Allah will bring out what you are wary of"? I say: its meaning is that Allah will bring to light and make manifest the sending down of the surah, or that Allah will manifest what you were wary of, i.e., of making known your hypocrisy.

While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was marching in the expedition of Tabuk, a group of the hypocrites were walking ahead of him. They said: "Look at this man! He wants to conquer the palaces and fortresses of Syria. Far-fetched, far-fetched!" Allah informed His Prophet, peace be upon him, of this. So he said: "Hold back the riders for me." He came to them and said: "You said such-and-such." They said:

"O Prophet of Allah, no, by Allah, we were not engaged in any matter concerning you or your Companions. We were only engaged in what riders engage in, to shorten the journey for one another."[[Al-Wahidi mentioned this from Qatadah without a chain. Al-Tabari connected it with a chain.]] ﴿Was it Allah, and His signs, and His Messenger, that you were mocking?﴾ He did not heed their excuse, because they were lying in it. They were treated as though they admitted their mockery and that it had occurred from them, until they were rebuked for their error, the place of mockery. Here the one mocked is placed after the interrogative particle of confirmation (ḥarf al-taqrīr), and that is only correct after the mockery has occurred and is established.

﴿Do not make excuses﴾: do not busy yourselves with your false excuses, for they will not benefit you after your hidden intent has been revealed. ﴿You have disbelieved﴾: your disbelief has become manifest through your mockery. ﴿After your belief﴾: after you had shown belief. ﴿If We pardon a group among you﴾: because of their repentance and their sincere belief after hypocrisy. ﴿We will punish a group, because they were criminals﴾: persisting in hypocrisy and not repenting from it.

Or, it means: ﴿If We pardon a group among you﴾, those who did not harm the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and did not mock him, ﴿We will not punish them in this world﴾; ﴿We will punish in this world a group, because they were criminals﴾, harming the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and mocking him.

Mujahid recited ﴿إن تعف عن طائفة﴾ with the passive form and the feminine marker (تعف, "if a group is pardoned"). The correct form is the masculine, because the subject of the verb is the adverbial phrase (al-ẓarf), as you say "سير بالدابة" (the animal was made to travel), and you do not say "سيرت بالدابة." However, he went by the meaning, as if it were said: "If a group is shown mercy," so he used the feminine for that reason, and it is a rare reading. The good reading, the one used by the common readers (al-ʿāmmah), is ﴿إن يعف عن طائفة﴾ with the masculine, and ﴿تعذب طائفة﴾ with the feminine. It is also read ﴿إن يعف عن طائفة يعذب طائفة﴾ with the active form, where the agent is Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was marching in the expedition of Tabuk, a group of the hypocrites were walking ahead of him. They said: "Look at this man! He wants to conquer the palaces and fortresses of Syria. Far-fetched, far-fetched!" Allah informed His Prophet, peace be upon him, of this. So he said: "Hold back the riders for me." He came to them and said: "You said such-and-such." They said:

"O Prophet of Allah, no, by Allah, we were not engaged in any matter concerning you or your Companions. We were only engaged in what riders engage in, to shorten the journey for one another."[[Al-Wahidi mentioned this from Qatadah without a chain. Al-Tabari connected it with a chain.]] ﴿Was it Allah, and His signs, and His Messenger, that you were mocking?﴾ He did not heed their excuse, because they were lying in it. The Hypocrites (Surah al-Tawbah 9:67–68)

Some of them are from others. He intends by this the negation that they are among the believers, and the refutation of their statement, "They swear by Allah that they are indeed of you" (9:56), and the affirmation of His saying, "they are not of you." Then He described them with what indicates the opposition of their condition to the condition of the believers: "They enjoin what is reprehensible" (al-munkar), meaning disbelief and acts of disobedience, "and forbid what is good" (al-ma'ruf), meaning faith and acts of obedience. "And they withhold their hands," meaning they are stingy with the giving of charity (sadaqat) and spending in the way of Allah. "They forgot Allah," meaning they neglected His remembrance, "so He forgot them," meaning He abandoned them from His mercy and His grace. "They are the defiant ones" (al-fasiqun), meaning they are the complete ones in transgression (fisq), which is rebellion in disbelief and stripping away from every good. It is enough of a deterrent for a Muslim to avoid whatever earns this foul name by which Allah described the hypocrites when He exaggerated in their censure. And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) disliked that a Muslim say "I have become lazy" (kasilt), because the hypocrites were described with laziness in His saying, "they stand up lazily" (kusala) (4:142).

"So what do you think of the transgression?" (9:68). "Abiding therein," meaning they are destined to abide forever. "It is sufficient for them," an indication of the magnitude of its punishment, and that there is nothing more severe than it, and that it cannot be increased upon. We seek refuge with Allah from His wrath and His punishment. "And Allah has cursed them," meaning He humiliated them with punishment and made them blameworthy, linking them with the accursed devils, just as He honored the people of Paradise and linked them with the honored angels. [The words "and linked them with the angels" are based on the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (a theological school), that the angel is superior to the human being. (ʿ)] "And for them is a lasting punishment," meaning they have a kind of punishment besides the burning in the Fire, lasting and permanent like the punishment of the Fire. It is also permissible that He intends: "and for them is a lasting punishment" with them in this world, from which they never separate, and that is what they suffer from the fatigue of hypocrisy and the outward showing that contradicts the inward, out of fear of the Muslims and their constant dread of exposure and of the descent of punishment should their secrets be discovered.

The kaf (ك) in "kamā" has a place in the grammar of i'rab that is either in the nominative, meaning "you are like those before you," or in the accusative, meaning "you did like what those before you did, namely that you enjoyed and plunged (into vain talk) as they enjoyed and plunged."

A similar usage is the verse of al-Namir:

"Until, when the dogs said to her, 'Like today, pursued and no pursuer…'"

This verse is attributed to Aws ibn Hajar, and it is also said to belong to al-Namir ibn Tawlab. In it there is an ellipsis without which the meaning does not hold, i.e., he said to her: "I have not seen [anything] like today, pursued," and the pronoun refers to the hunting bitch. "Al-Kilab" means the trainer of the dogs or the hunter with them, i.e., the pursued one and the pursuit on this day are not like them on any other day but greater. It may be that "al-talab" here means "the pursuer." Then it is possible that this is the content of the saying, and it is possible that it is the answer to "idha" (when), with the content of the saying omitted, indicating her swiftness: i.e., he said to her, "Go, as an example."

The phrase "I have not seen" is supplied before it. His saying, "They were stronger than you in might," is an explanation of their likeness to them and a representation of their action by their action.

Al-khalaq means the portion, which is what is created for a person, i.e., what is decreed of good, just as it is called "qism" (share) because it is apportioned.

And "naṣīb" (portion) because it is fixed, i.e., established. Al-khawd is entering into falsehood and frivolity. "Ka-alladhī khāḍū" means like the group who plunged, and like the plunging that they plunged. If you say: what is the benefit of His saying "fa-istamtaʿū bi-khalāqihim" (so they enjoyed their portion) and His saying "kamā istamtaʿa alladhīna min qablikum bi-khalāqihim" (as those before you enjoyed their portion), which would be sufficient without it, just as His saying "ka-alladhī khāḍū" suffices so that one need not say "wa-khāḍū, fa-khiḍtum ka-alladhī khāḍū"? I say: its benefit is to censure the earlier ones for enjoying what they were given of the worldly shares and being content with them, and for being distracted by their perishable desires from considering the outcome and seeking success in the Hereafter; and to abase the matter of enjoyment and disparage the matter of being content with it. Then He likens the state of those addressed to their state, just as you wish to alert some oppressor to the ugliness of his deed by saying: "You are like Pharaoh, who killed without cause, tortured and oppressed, and you do the like of his deed." As for "wa-khudtum ka-alladhī khāḍū" (and you plunged as they plunged), it is conjoined to what precedes it, attributed to it, and independent of that preliminary by its attribution to it: "Their deeds have become void in this world and the Hereafter," which is the opposite of His saying: "And We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed in the Hereafter he is among the righteous."

Companions of Madyan (Madyan) and the people of Madyan, who are the people of Shu'ayb; and al-Mu'tafikat (the overturned cities), the cities of the people of Lut. It was also said: they are the towns of the people of Lut, Hud and Salih. Its meaning (i'tifak) is the reversal of their conditions from good to evil.

﴿So Allah would not have wronged them﴾: it was not proper for Him to wrong them, for He is Wise, and what is ugly is not permissible for Him, nor is it (permissible) that He punish them without a crime. ﴿But they wronged themselves﴾ in that they disbelieved in Him, so they deserved His punishment.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 71–72:

"Some of them are allies of others" is in contrast to His saying about the hypocrites, "They are of one another" (9:67). "Allah will have mercy upon them" — the sin (sa) here indicates that the mercy will certainly exist, so it confirms the promise, just as it confirms the threat in your saying, "I will take revenge on you someday," meaning that you will not escape Me, even if it is delayed. Similar to this is His saying, "The Most Merciful will bestow love upon them" (19:96), and "Your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied" (93:5), and "He will surely give them their rewards" (4:152). "Indeed Allah is Mighty" — overpowering over everything, capable of everything, so He is able to give reward and punishment. "Wise" — placing each thing in its proper place according to what is deserved.

"And pleasant dwellings" — from al-Hasan: palaces of pearl, red ruby and chrysolite. "In Gardens of Eden" — Eden means "residence" (ʿadn), as evidenced by His saying, "Gardens of Eden, which the Most Merciful has promised to His servants" (19:61). This is supported by what Abu al-Darda, may Allah be pleased with him, related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Eden is the house of Allah which no eye has seen and which has not occurred to the heart of any human. Only three will dwell in it: the prophets, the truthful ones, and the martyrs. Allah the Exalted says: Blessed is the one who enters you." [Narrated by al-Bazzar through the route of Ziyadah ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi from Fadalah ibn Ubayd from him, and he said: "We do not know it except from this route, and Ziyadah is not known; only al-Layth related from him." It was also narrated by al-Tabarani, al-Daraqutni in al-Mu'talif, and Ibn Mardawayh by this route.]

It is also said: Eden is a city in Paradise. And it is said: it is a river whose gardens are on its banks.

"And the pleasure of Allah is greater" — and some of Allah's pleasure is greater than all of that, because His pleasure is the cause of every success and happiness, and because they attain through His pleasure with them His exaltation and honour, and honour is the greatest kind of reward. Also, when the servant knows that his Master is pleased with him, he becomes greater in his own eyes than the blessings beyond it, and it is only through His pleasure that they are pleasant for him, just as when he knows of His displeasure, they become bitter for him and he finds no delight in them, however great they are.

I heard from some of our shaykhs, people of lofty aspiration and strong, intense intellect [Note: "al-nafs al-marra" means the strong, intense-minded soul; al-mirrah, with a kasra, means strength and intensity of intellect, as in al-Sihah. (ʿIn)], that he would say: "My eye does not aspire, and my soul does not strive, toward anything that Allah has promised in the abode of honour, as it aspires and strives toward His pleasure with me, and that I be gathered in the company of those guided and pleasing to Him."

"That" refers to what Allah has promised, or to the pleasure: "That is the supreme triumph" — alone, apart from what people consider triumph.

And it is related that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says to the people of Paradise, "Are you pleased?" They say, "And why would we not be pleased, when You have given us what You have not given anyone of Your creation?" He says, "Shall I give you something better than that?" They say, "And what is better than that?" He says: "I shall cause My pleasure to descend upon you, so I will never be angry with you again." [Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id.]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 71–72:

"Some of them are allies of others" is in contrast to His saying about the hypocrites, "They are of one another" (9:67). "Allah will have mercy upon them" — the sin (sa) here indicates that the mercy will certainly exist, so it confirms the promise, just as it confirms the threat in your saying, "I will take revenge on you someday," meaning that you will not escape Me, even if it is delayed. Similar to this is His saying, "The Most Merciful will bestow love upon them" (19:96), and "Your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied" (93:5), and "He will surely give them their rewards" (4:152). "Indeed Allah is Mighty" — overpowering over everything, capable of everything, so He is able to give reward and punishment. "Wise" — placing each thing in its proper place according to what is deserved.

"And pleasant dwellings" — from al-Hasan: palaces of pearl, red ruby and chrysolite. "In Gardens of Eden" — Eden means "residence" (ʿadn), as evidenced by His saying, "Gardens of Eden, which the Most Merciful has promised to His servants" (19:61). This is supported by what Abu al-Darda, may Allah be pleased with him, related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Eden is the house of Allah which no eye has seen and which has not occurred to the heart of any human. Only three will dwell in it: the prophets, the truthful ones, and the martyrs. Allah the Exalted says: Blessed is the one who enters you." [Narrated by al-Bazzar through the route of Ziyadah ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi from Fadalah ibn Ubayd from him, and he said: "We do not know it except from this route, and Ziyadah is not known; only al-Layth related from him." It was also narrated by al-Tabarani, al-Daraqutni in al-Mu'talif, and Ibn Mardawayh by this route.]

It is also said: Eden is a city in Paradise. And it is said: it is a river whose gardens are on its banks.

(ʿIn)], that he would say: "My eye does not aspire, and my soul does not strive, toward anything that Allah has promised in the abode of honour, as it aspires and strives toward His pleasure with me, and that I be gathered in the company of those guided and pleasing to Him."

[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim), from the hadith of Abu Sa'id.]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 73:

﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers with the sword and against the hypocrites with argument﴾ [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is: strive against the disbelievers with the sword and against the hypocrites with argument... etc." Ahmad said: Praise be to God, who made him (al-Zamakhshari) speak with argument in our favour when we were harsh toward him at times, and God is the Granter of success.]] ﴿and be harsh with them in both kinds of struggle﴾, and do not show them affection. Whoever is found to be corrupt in belief, this ruling applies to him: he is to be struggled against with argument, and harshness is to be employed with him as far as possible. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud: "If he cannot do so with his hand, then with his tongue; if he cannot, then let him frown in his face [[His saying "fal-yakfahir fi wajhihi" (let him frown in his face): in al-Sihah, "iktafara al-rajul" means the man scowled when he frowned (A').]]; if he cannot, then with his heart"[[Recorded by al-Tabari and Ibn Mardawayh from the narration of Amr ibn Abi Jundab from him.]]. He means dislike, hatred, and disassociation from him. Al-Hasan understood the struggle against the hypocrites to mean enforcing the prescribed punishments upon them when they engage in their causes.

Al-Zamakhshari, al-Kashshaf, on Surah 9, verse 74:

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) remained during the expedition of Tabuk for two months, the Qur'an being revealed to him and he reproaching the hypocrites who had stayed behind, and those with him among them heard. Among them was al-Jallas ibn Suwayd. Al-Jallas said: "By God, if what Muhammad says is true concerning our brothers whom we left behind, who are our lords and nobles, then we are worse than donkeys." 'Amir ibn Qays al-Ansari said to al-Jallas: "Indeed, by God, Muhammad is truthful, and you are worse than a donkey." This reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he summoned him, and he swore by God that he had not said it. 'Amir raised his hands and said: "O God, send down upon Your servant and Your Prophet the confirmation of the liar and the denial of the truthful [[The phrase "confirmation of the liar and the denial of the truthful" is perhaps "confirmation of the truthful and denial of the liar." It is possible that he made himself the liar and al-Jallas the truthful, because that is what the apparent sense of the oath requires. (ʿA.)]]," and then the verse was revealed: ﴿They swear by God that they said nothing﴾. Al-Jallas then said:

"O Messenger of God, God has offered me repentance. By God, I did say it, and 'Amir spoke the truth." Al-Jallas repented and his repentance was good. ﴿And they disbelieved after their Islam﴾, that is, they showed their disbelief after displaying Islam. ﴿And they plotted what they could not attain﴾, which was the plot to assassinate the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and this was on his return from Tabuk: fifteen of them pledged together to push him from his mount into the valley when he ascended the pass at night. 'Ammar ibn Yasir took hold of the halter of his mount, leading it, and Hudhayfah was behind it, driving it. While they were so, Hudhayfah heard the sound of camels' hooves and the clatter of weapons, so he turned and saw a group of men with covered faces, and he said: "Away with you, away with you, enemies of God!" [[Ahmad transmitted it from the hadith of Abu al-Tufayl, who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) returned from the expedition of Tabuk, he ordered a caller to announce that no one should take the pass, for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was traveling alone. The Prophet (ﷺ) was traveling while Hudhayfah (may God be pleased with him) led him and 'Ammar (may God be pleased with him) drove him. Then a band of men with covered faces on their mounts came up until they surrounded the Prophet (ﷺ), so 'Ammar turned back and struck the faces of the mounts. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to Hudhayfah: 'Go on, go on.' Then 'Ammar caught up with him and said: 'Drive, drive,' until he made the camel kneel. The Prophet said to 'Ammar: 'Do you know the people?' He said: 'No, they were covered. But I recognized the saddles of the mounts.' He said: 'Do you know what they intended against the Messenger of God?' I said: 'God and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'They intended to scheme against the Messenger of God and throw him from the pass.' When that was over, something happened between 'Ammar (may God be pleased with him) and one of them, of the kind that occurs between people.

He said: 'I adjure you by God, how many are the companions of the pass who intended to scheme against the Messenger of God (ﷺ)?' He said: 'You think they were fourteen; if you were among them, then they were fifteen.'" It was also transmitted by al-Tabarani and al-Bazzar in this form, and al-Bazzar said: it was transmitted through a chain from Hudhayfah, and this is the best and soundest of its chains. Ibn Ishaq transmitted it in al-Maghazi, and through him al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, from al-A'mash, from 'Amr ibn Murrah, from Abu al-Bakhtari, from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, who said: "I was holding the halter of the she-camel of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), leading it, and 'Ammar (may God be pleased with him) was driving the she-camel, until when we were at the pass, there were twelve riders who confronted him there." He said: "So I reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and he shouted at them, and they turned back fleeing."]], and they fled. It was said: the hypocrites intended to kill 'Amir in return for his rebuttal of al-Jallas. It was also said: they intended to crown 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, even though the Messenger of God (may God's peace and blessings be upon him and his family) did not approve. ﴿And they found fault only because God had enriched them﴾. That is because when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to Medina they were in hardship of livelihood; they did not ride horses nor obtain booty, so they became wealthy through the spoils, and a client of al-Jallas was killed, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered his blood-money to be twelve thousand, and he became rich. ﴿But if they repent, it is better for them﴾: this is the verse at which al-Jallas repented. ﴿And if they turn away, God will punish them with a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter﴾, by killing and by the Fire.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 75–77:

It is related that Tha'laba ibn Hatib said: "O Messenger of Allah, supplicate Allah that He grant me wealth." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Tha'laba, a little of which you can render its thanks is better than much which you cannot bear" [Al-Tabarani, al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and al-Shu'ab, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabari and Ibn Mardawayh all related it, all through the route of 'Ali ibn Zayd from al-Qasim ibn 'Abd al-Rahman from Umama. This is a very weak chain. Al-Suhayli said, citing Ibn Ishaq: Tha'laba ibn Hatib is the moon of the Badr participants. And also from Ibn Ishaq, concerning the hypocrites, he mentioned this verse which was revealed concerning him. So perhaps they are two persons.] He pressed him again and said: "By Him who sent you with the truth, if Allah grants me wealth, I will surely give every person with a right his right." So he (ﷺ) prayed for him. He acquired sheep, and they multiplied as worms multiply, until the city became too small for them. So he moved to a valley and cut himself off from the congregation and the Friday prayer. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked about him, and it was said: "His wealth has increased so much that a valley cannot contain it." He said: "Woe to Tha'laba!" Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent two collectors of alms, and people met them with their charities. The two passed by Tha'laba and asked him for the charity and read to him the letter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) which contained the obligatory dues. He said: "This is nothing but a jizya, this is nothing but the sister of the jizya." He said: "Go back until I consider my opinion." When they returned, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), before they spoke to him, said: "Woe to Tha'laba!" twice. Then the verse was revealed. Tha'laba came with the charity and said: "Indeed Allah has forbidden me to accept it from you." So he put dust on his head, and the Prophet said: "This is your deed; I commanded you but you did not obey me." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away. He brought it to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), but he did not accept it; he brought it to 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) in his caliphate, but he did not accept it; and he died in the time of 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him).

It is also read "la-nassaddaqanna wa-la-nakununna" with the light nun in both.

﴿Among them are those who made a covenant with Allah: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and surely be among the righteous."﴾ Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: he means the Hajj.

﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts﴾ — according to al-Hasan and Qatada (may Allah be pleased with them), the pronoun refers to miserliness. That is: their miserliness caused them to inherit firmly rooted hypocrisy in their hearts, because it was the cause of it and its motive. The apparent view is that the pronoun refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The meaning: He forsook them until they became hypocrites.

[Note: his phrase "The meaning: He forsook them until they became hypocrites" is explained in this way according to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, that He, exalted is He, does not create evil.]

Their hypocrisy became firmly established in their hearts, so it does not leave them until they die, because of their breaking what they promised Allah of charity and righteousness, and because they were liars. From this comes the saying: "Breaking a promise is one third of hypocrisy." It is also read "yakdhibun" with shaddah.

And "a lam ta'lamu" with the ta' (taa), related from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him).

Their secret and their private counsel: what they concealed of hypocrisy and of resolve to break what they had promised, and what they confided to one another of slanders against the religion, and calling the charity (ṣadaqah) a tribute (jizyah), and planning to withhold it.

(Commentary of al-Zamakhshari, al-Kashshaf, on surah 9, verse 79)

Alladhina yalmizuna (﴿Those who find fault with﴾) may be in the accusative or the nominative case, by way of censure (dhamm). It may also be in the genitive case, as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in "sirrahum wa-najwahum" (their secret and their private counsel). It has also been read as "yalmuzuna" with a damma (yalmuzūna).

"Al-mutawwi'in" (﴿those who volunteer﴾) means al-mutatawwi'in, those who give voluntarily and generously.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) urged people to give charity, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf came with forty awqiyah of gold. It is also said: with four thousand dirhams, and he said: "I had eight thousand; I lent four thousand to my Lord and kept four thousand for my dependents." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "May Allah bless you in what you gave and in what you kept," so Allah blessed him, until his wife Tumadir was reconciled to a quarter of the price for eighty thousand.[[Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through 'Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding the words of Allah, ﴿Those who find fault with the volunteers among the believers﴾, that he said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with forty awqiyah of gold, and a man from the Ansar came with a sa' of dates. Some of the hypocrites said: "By Allah, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf has not brought what he brought except for show, and Allah and His Messenger are certainly above need of this sa'." And through the route of 'Atiyya al-'Awfi. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out one day to the people and called out to them: 'Gather your charities.' The people gathered their charities. A man came with a sa' of dates and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I spent my night drawing water with a rope...' – the hadith. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I have eight thousand; four thousand are for me, and four thousand I lend to my Lord' – and he mentioned it." 'Abd al-Razzaq said in his Tafsir: Ma'mar informed us from Qatada, who said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf gave in charity half of his wealth. He had eight thousand dinars, and he gave four thousand dinars. Some people among the hypocrites said: "'Abd al-Rahman is greatly showing off." So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed ﴿Those who find fault with the volunteers﴾. And a man from the Ansar had two sa's of dates; he brought one of them. Some of the hypocrites said: "Surely Allah is in no need of this sa'."

Then Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said ﴿except their effort﴾. Al-Bazzar narrated from the transmission of 'Umar ibn Abi Maslama from his father from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Give charity, for I intend to send out an army." 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf came and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I have four thousand dirhams: two thousand I lend to my Lord, and two thousand for my dependents" – the hadith. In it: "A man of the Ansar spent the night and obtained two sa's of dates." He narrated it from Talut ibn 'Ubada from Abu 'Awana from him, and he said: Talut alone transmitted it connected; then he narrated it from Abu Kamil from Abu 'Awana, and through his route Ibn Mardawayh. In al-Maghazi it says: "four thousand." 'Asim ibn 'Adi stood and gave a hundred wasq of dates in charity, and threw it into the charity; they mocked him and said: "Surely Allah is in no need of the sa' of Abu 'Aqil." End of quotation. The story of Abu 'Aqil was narrated by Ibrahim al-Harbi, al-Tabarani and al-Tabari from the transmission of Khalid ibn Yasar from Ibn Abi 'Aqil from his father, who said: "I spent the night drawing water with a rope on my back for two sa's of dates" – the hadith. In its chain is Musa ibn 'Abda, who is weak. I say: The story of Abu 'Aqil was narrated by al-Bukhari from the hadith of Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari in brief, and in it: "Another man came with more than that." In another narration: "with a great deal."]]

Abu 'Aqil al-Ansari, may Allah be pleased with him, came with a sa' of dates and said: "I spent my night drawing water with a rope on my back for two sa's; I left one sa for my dependents and brought one sa." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered him to scatter it over the charities. The hypocrites found fault with them and said: "'Abd al-Rahman and 'Asim gave only for show, and Allah and His Messenger are certainly above need of Abu 'Aqil's sa'; rather he loved to be mentioned himself so that he might be given from the charities." So it was revealed: ﴿except their effort﴾, meaning except their capacity. It has been read with fath and with damma (su'akhira / sakhira).

﴿Allah mocks them﴾, like His saying ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ (Q. 2:15), in that it is a statement and not a supplication. Do you not see His saying ﴿and for them there is a painful punishment﴾?

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 80:

Abdullah ibn Abdullah ibn Ubayy asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was a righteous man, to seek forgiveness for his father during his illness, and he did so. Then (the verse) was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has given me a concession, so I will add to the seventy." [[I have not found it with this wording; its origin is in the agreed-upon (hadith) from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "When Abdullah ibn Ubayy died, his son came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him to give him his shirt to shroud his father in. He gave it to him. Then he asked him to pray over him, and he stood to pray over him. Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, took hold of his garment and said: 'Will you pray over him when Allah has forbidden you to pray over him?' He said: 'I was only given a choice, for He said: "Seek forgiveness for them or do not seek forgiveness for them" (9:80), and I will add to the seventy.' So he prayed over him, and Allah the Exalted revealed: "And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever" (9:84), and so the prayer over them was abandoned." — the wording of Muslim.]] Then the verse was revealed: "It is the same for them whether you seek forgiveness for them or do not seek forgiveness for them." And we have mentioned that this imperative carries the meaning of a statement. [[Mahmud said: "We have mentioned that this imperative carries the meaning of a statement ..." etc. Ahmad said: What al-Zamakhshari claims in this and similar cases, that there is an omitted element which is the real intended meaning of the imperative, is correct, and this is used in its proper place, as in the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azza: "Treat us harshly or kindly, you will not be blamed."

It is as if he says to her: test your position with me and the strength of my love for you, and treat me with harshness and kindness, and see whether my state with you varies, whether harsh or kind? Likewise the meaning of the verse, "Seek forgiveness for them or do not seek forgiveness for them," and see whether they are forgiven in the two states of seeking forgiveness and abandoning it?

Do the two states differ or not? Ahmad said: It has also come in the form of a statement in the other verse, in the words of the Exalted: "It is the same for them whether you seek forgiveness for them or do not seek forgiveness for them; Allah will never forgive them." It is as if it were said: Allah will never forgive them, whether you seek forgiveness for them or do not seek forgiveness for them, and it contains the meaning of a condition. We have mentioned the point of its coming in the imperative form.

The seventy functions in their speech as a proverb for abundance. Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, said:

"I will surely make the rebel and the son of the rebel wake up
Seventy thousand, tying the forelocks,
Wearing coats of mail, shining,
Having brought their horses along with the mares,
Lions of a dry season when there is no escape."

These lines are by Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, about Amr ibn al-As. "Sabbahahu" means to greet him at morning time, the time of morning. Some transmit "la-usbihanna" from companionship, and it may be an error. He likened the infliction of hardship to the infliction of what is loved, by way of mockery, so it is a clear metaphor of mockery. It is also permissible that he likened the horsemen, for their coming at dawn, to the morning drink, by way of implicit mockery. "La-usbihanna" is an imaginative (takhyil) expression. "Seventy thousand" is the second object, and what is meant is abundance. "Al-a'qidin" is the plural of "aqid," and what is meant is: the forelocks of their horses, or the ends of their turbans behind them, or the hair of their heads. Tying the forelock is one of the signs of bravery and of disdain in battle. "Al-hiqab" is what a woman wraps around her waist, and it is also applied to the waist itself. "Al-huqayba" is a small bag behind the rider. "Al-halaq," with a kasra, is the plural of "halqa." "Al-dalas" is the smooth, shining coat of mail, used of both singular and plural. The meaning: they are wearing coats of mail, and nothing is in their saddlebags except them. "Al-qila§" are young female camels; that is, they combined both kinds, and he made them like lions of al-mahl, that is, drought, to indicate that they are hungry and thirsty for the flesh and blood of the enemies. The rule for the noun of "la" is that it be built on the fathah, so it is permissible that it was given a kasra for the sake of rhyme. The more apparent view is that the noun is in the sense of "ghayr," as in the Sihah, or "hina ghayr munas," or it was built on the kasra out of intention of idafah. He likened it to "nizal," or it is genitive by an implied "min" of totality, as passed in "wa-lat awan." It is also possible, though remote, that there is an omitted genitive in the speech, meaning "la hina la waqt munas," that is, a time of no retreat from war. It is also possible that "la" is extra between the two terms of the idafah, as in "bi-thara la hur sara," meaning the time of the horsemen's retreat and their flight.

If you say: how was it hidden from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who was the most eloquent of the Arabs and the most knowledgeable of their modes of speech, and of their figurative uses? [[He returned to his speech. He said: If you say, how was it hidden from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who was the most eloquent of those who uttered the Ḍād ... etc. Ahmad said: Al-Qadi, may Allah be pleased with him, denied the hadith of seeking forgiveness and did not authenticate it. Some people have been excessive in accepting it, to the point that they made it a foundation for the concept of contrary implication (mafhum al-mukhalafa), and built on it that the Prophet (peace be upon him) understood from the specification of the denial of forgiveness by seventy that forgiveness exists beyond it. That is the reason for al-Qadi's objection to them.]] It is hidden from no one that the mention of this number indicates abundance in seeking forgiveness. How, when He followed it with: "That is because they disbelieved..." (9:80), thus clarifying the obstacle that prevents their forgiveness, even so he said: "My Lord has given me a concession, so I will add to the seventy." I say: It was not hidden from him, but he imagined it by what he said, to show the utmost of his mercy and compassion toward those he was sent to. Like the words of Abraham, peace be upon him: "And whoever disobeys me, indeed You are Forgiving and Merciful" (14:36). In the Prophet's (ﷺ) showing of compassion and mercy there is kindness to his community and a call to them to show mercy to one another.

The ones left behind (al-mukhallafun) are those among the hypocrites who asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for permission, and he granted it and left them behind in Medina during the expedition of Tabuk. Alternatively, they are those whom their laziness, their hypocrisy, and Satan left behind, by their sitting out of the raid (bi-maq'adihim, "by their sitting"), "in opposition to the Messenger of God" (khilafa Rasul Allah), meaning behind him. It is said: "He stayed behind the tribe" (aqama khilafa al-hayy), meaning after them, when they departed and he did not depart with them. The variant reading (qira'ah) of Abu Haywah supports this: "behind (khalfa) the Messenger of God." It was also said that khilaf means opposition (mukhalafah), because they opposed him when they sat and he rose. Its grammatical position (intiṣab) is either as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu) or as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning they sat for the sake of opposing him, or while opposing him. "That they should strive with their wealth and their lives" is an allusion to the believers, who bore great hardships for the sake of God Most High, and to what they did of spending their wealth and their lives in the path of God Most High, preferring that to ease and comfort.

The hypocrites disliked this. How could they not dislike it, when they did not possess what the believers possessed of the impulse of faith and the call of certainty? ﴿Say: The Fire of Hell is more intense in heat﴾. This is a rebuke that shows them to be ignorant, because whoever protects himself from the hardship of an hour, and by that self-protection falls into the hardship of eternity, is more ignorant than any ignorant person. One of the poets said:

*A pleasure of ages, after which I met*
*the displeasure of a single day, whose honey is like the bitter aloe.*

So how much more so, when one meets the pleasure of an hour,
behind whose passing is the displeasure of ages.

[Al-Zamakhshari. "Al-ahqab" are many successive periods, the plural of huqb (with a damma), meaning an age. "Al-ara" is honey. "Al-shabah" is the like. "Al-sab" is a plant with a bitter taste. It was also said that it is the colocynth (al-handhal). The poet means that the joy of many ages, after which comes the distress of a single day, whose state resembles honey, is in reality like the colocynth; so what of the reverse?]

The meaning: "So let them laugh a little, and let them weep much," as a recompense. However, it was expressed in the form of a command, to indicate that it is a decreed and binding matter that cannot be otherwise. It is related that the hypocrites will weep in the Fire for the lifespan of the world; their tears will not dry up, and they will not be given the comfort of sleep.

Zamakhshari said: He said "to a group of them" because among them were those who repented of hypocrisy and regretted staying behind, or who offered a valid excuse. It was also said: not all of those who stayed behind were hypocrites, so by "the group" he meant the hypocrites among them. "They will ask your permission to go out" means: to a campaign after the campaign of Tabuk. "The first time" refers to going out to the campaign of Tabuk. Their removal from the register of those fighting was a punishment for them for their staying behind, which God knew was prompted only by hypocrisy, unlike the other stay-behinds, "with those who stay behind" (al-khalifin), whose interpretation has already been given. Malik ibn Dinar (may God have mercy on him) recited it as "maʿa al-khalifin" with the short form of al-khalifin (khalifin).

If you say: "marrah" is an indefinite noun placed in the position of the comparative for the plural of occurrences ("marrat"), so why is the comparative noun mentioned with the genitive noun attached to it, when it already indicates one of the occurrences? I say: the more common of the two usages is "Hind is the greatest of women," and she is the greatest of them. As for your saying "she is the greatest woman," it is hardly ever found. Rather, one says "she is the greatest woman," "the first time," and "the last time." It is related from Qatada: "It was related to us that they were twelve men, about whom what was said was said."

Narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to stand over the graves of the hypocrites and supplicate for them.[[I have not found it in this form. As for its beginning, "he used to stand," and so on to the end, and as for the story of Abdullah, it is in the acceptable reports of al-Mustadrak, by way of Ibn Ishaq: "al-Zuhri narrated to me, from Urwa, from Usama ibn Zayd, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon Abdullah ibn Ubayy to visit him during the illness from which he died. When he saw that death was upon him, he said to him: 'By Allah, I used to forbid you from loving the Jews.' He said: 'I have come to hate them.' As'ad ibn Zurara did not benefit him. When he died, his son came to him and said: 'He has died, so give me your shirt to shroud him in.' The Messenger (ﷺ) took off his shirt and gave it to him." As for his saying, "I sent to you only so that you would ask forgiveness for me, not to rebuke me," al-Tabarani added it by way of Ma'mar, from Qatada, who said: "Abdullah ibn Ubayy sent word to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was ill. When he entered upon him, the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'The love of the Jews has destroyed you.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I sent for you so that you would ask forgiveness for me, and I did not send for you to rebuke me.' He asked him for his shirt to shroud him in, and he gave it to him, and he asked forgiveness for him. He died, and he shrouded him in his shirt, spat upon his skin, and lowered him into his grave. Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And never pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾." Al-Bayhaqi, in al-Dala'il, by way of al-Waqidi with his chain in this story, said: "He said: 'This is not a time for reproach. It is death. If you die, attend my washing, and give me your shirt to shroud me in.' He gave it to him, then said: 'Pray over me and ask forgiveness for me.'" In another report, his son, who was called al-Hubab, said to him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named him Abdullah: "O Messenger of Allah, give him your shirt that is next to your skin." As for his saying, "al-Hubab is the name of a devil," Ibn Sa'd and al-Tabari narrated it by way of Urwa and others, who said: "When Abdullah ibn Ubayy became gravely ill, his son went to him and said: 'My father is near death, and I would like you to attend him and pray over him.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'What is your name?' He said: 'al-Hubab ibn Abdullah.' He said: 'No, you are Abdullah. Al-Hubab is the name of a devil.' He said: 'So he went with him until he attended him, and he dressed him in his shirt and prayed over him.' As for the saying of Umar, we have already mentioned that it is in the two Sahihs.]] So when the head of hypocrisy, Abdullah ibn Ubayy, fell ill, he sent for him to come to him. When he entered upon him, he said: "The love of the Jews has destroyed you."

He said: "O Messenger of Allah, I sent for you so that you would ask forgiveness for me, not to reproach me."[[His saying "not to reproach me" means to rebuke me with blame.]] He asked him to shroud him in his undergarment (shi'ar) that was next to his skin, and to pray over him. When he died, his son al-Hubab invited him to his funeral. He asked him his name, and he said: "You are Abdullah ibn Abdullah. Al-Hubab is the name of a devil." When he was about to pray over him, Umar said to him: "Will you pray over the enemy of Allah?" Then the verse was revealed. It is also said that he wanted to pray over him, and Jibril seized him by his garment, and [the verse] was revealed.[[Abu Ya'la narrated it by way of Yazid al-Raqashi, from Anas, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wanted to pray over Abdullah ibn Ubayy, but Jibril took hold of his garment and said: ﴿And never pray over any of them who has died, ever, nor stand over his grave﴾. Yazid is weak."]] If you ask: How was it permissible for him to show honor to a hypocrite and to shroud him in his shirt? I answer: That was a reward for a deed of his that preceded. When al-Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, the uncle of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), was taken prisoner at Badr, they could not find a shirt for him, and he was a tall man,[[His saying "he was a tall man": in al-Sihah, al-Tiwal, with a damma, means tall.]] so Abdullah clothed him in his shirt.[[Al-Bukhari narrated it by way of Amr ibn Dinar, who heard Jabir: "When the day of Badr came, the prisoners were brought, and al-Abbas was brought, and he had no garment. The Prophet (ﷺ) looked for a shirt, and they found the shirt of Abdullah ibn Ubayy that would fit him, so the Prophet (ﷺ) gave it to him to wear. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) took off his shirt that he had put on him." Ibn Utba said: "He had a favor with the Prophet (ﷺ), and he wanted to repay him." Al-Hakim narrated it in al-Mustadrak from the hadith of Jabir, and included the last statement in it.]] When the polytheists said to him on the day of Hudaybiya: "We will not permit Muhammad [to enter],[[His saying "we will not permit Muhammad" means to enter Makka. (ʿ)]] but we will permit you," he said:

"No. For me, in the Messenger of Allah, there is a good example."[[Al-Waqidi narrated in al-Maghazi: Jabir ibn Sulaym narrated to us, from Safwan ibn Uthman, who said: "On the day of Hudaybiya, Quraysh sent word to Abdullah ibn Ubayy: 'If you wish to enter and circumambulate, then do so.' His son was sitting with him, and he said to him: 'O father, remember Allah, [do not] circumambulate the House before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' Ibn Ubayy refused and said: 'I will not circumambulate until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) circumambulates.' The words reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he was pleased."]] The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) thanked him for that and granted his request, for he (ﷺ) would not turn away a petitioner, and he would attend to the motives of nobility and act by the customs of the generous. Out of honor for his son, a righteous man, it is reported that he said to him: "I ask you to shroud him in one of your shirts, and to stand over his grave so that the enemies do not gloat over him."[[I have not found it. The original of his son's request in the Sahih is as already mentioned.]] And [it was] knowing that shrouding him in his shirt would not benefit him in his disbelief, so there is no difference between it and any other shroud; and so that clothing him in it would be a kindness to others. It is reported that he was asked: "Why did you send to him your shirt while he was a disbeliever?" He said: "My shirt will not avail him anything from Allah, but I hope that through this means many will enter Islam." [[I have not seen it in this form. Its origin was narrated by al-Tabari by way of Ma'mar, from Qatada, who said: "It was mentioned to us that the Prophet (ﷺ) spoke to him about that, and he said: 'What good will my shirt do him before Allah? I truly hope that a thousand of his people will become Muslim through it.'"]] It is reported that a thousand of the Khazraj embraced Islam when they saw him seeking healing through a garment of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).[[I have not seen it in this form except in the mursal report of Qatada mentioned just before.]] Likewise, his (the Prophet's) showing mercy and asking forgiveness for him was for the purpose of calling to mercy and compassion, for when they see him showing mercy to one who displays faith while his inner state is otherwise, it calls the Muslim to show compassion to one whose heart conceals what his tongue says, and to regard it as a duty upon him. If you ask: Then how was praying over him permissible? I answer: No prohibition concerning praying over them had preceded, and they were treated as Muslims by virtue of their outward faith, because of the benefit in that. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "I do not know what this prayer was, except that I know the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) does not deceive."[[Sa'id ibn Dawud narrated it in his tafsir by his own chain. He said: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, who informed me: al-Hakam ibn Aban heard Ikrima, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When Abdullah ibn Ubayy fell ill with the illness from which he died, he said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Do me a favor: shroud me in your shirt and pray over me.' He said: So he shrouded him in his shirt and prayed over him. Ibn Abbas said: 'By Allah, I do not know what that prayer was. Allah knows best. No one ever deceived Muhammad.'"]] ﴿Who has died﴾ is a description of "anyone." The past tense "died," and "they died," are used with the meaning of the future, on the assumption of coming into being and existence, because it is inevitably something that will exist. ﴿Indeed they disbelieved﴾ is the reason for the prohibition. The phrase ﴿And do not let ... impress you﴾ has been repeated, because the recurrence of its revelation has significance in confirming what it was revealed for and in emphasizing it, and in intending that it be before the addressee, so that he does not forget it or neglect it, and so that he believes that acting upon it is important and requires special attention to it, especially when the interval between the two revelations is long, so it resembles a matter that is important to its owner, who returns to it in the course of his speech and turns to it. This meaning was repeated because of its strength concerning what must be guarded against.

Al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 90:

"The excusers" (al-mu'adhdhirun) are those who come from " 'adhdhara fi al-amr," meaning one who falls short in a matter and slackens and does not exert himself. Its real sense is that he gives the impression that he has an excuse in what he does, while he has no excuse. Alternatively, it is "al-mu'tadhirun" (those who make excuses), with the ta' assimilated into the dhal and its vowel moved onto the 'ayn. In Arabic it is permissible to vowel the 'ayn with a kasra because of the meeting of two sukun, or with a damma to follow the mim. But no recitation has been established with either, and they are those who make excuses falsely, as in His saying: ﴿They will make excuses to you when you return to them﴾. And it was recited as "al-mu'adhdhirun" with light pronunciation (takhfif):

This is the one who strives hard to make excuses and exerts himself in them. It was said: they were the tribes of Asad and Ghatafan. They said: "Indeed we have dependents, and indeed we are in hardship, so permit us to stay behind." It was also said: they were the kinsmen of 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl, who said: "If we join you in the campaign, the Arab tribe of Tayy will raid our families and our livestock." So the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God will suffice me without you." This is from Mujahid.

They were a group from Ghifar who made excuses, but God Most High did not accept their excuses. From Qatada: they made excuses with falsehood. And it was recited:

"al-Mu'adhdhirun" with the 'ayn and the dhal both shadda, from ta'adhdhara in the sense of i'tadhara (made an excuse). This is not sound, because the ta' is not assimilated into the 'ayn in the way it is assimilated into the ta', za' and sad, as in "al-mutawwi'in" (those who volunteer), and "azka" (purer) and "asdaq" (truer). It was also said: what is meant is "al-mu'tadhirun" in the sense of those who were sound (in their excuse), and by this was explained "al-mu'adhdhirun" and "al-mu'dhirun," according to the recitation of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him): those who did not fall short in the excuse. ﴿And those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back﴾: they are the hypocrites among the Bedouins who neither came nor made excuses, and thereby it became clear that they had lied to Allah and His Messenger in their claim of faith. Ubayy recited "kadhdhabu" with shadda. ﴿Those among them who disbelieved will be struck by a painful punishment﴾ from among the Bedouins: a punishment, painful, in this world by killing, and in the Hereafter by the Fire.

The weak, the aged and the chronically ill. Those who find nothing: the poor. It is said they were Muzayna, Juhayna and Banu Udhra.

Sincere counsel to Allah and His Messenger is: faith in them both, obedience to them in private and in public, loyalty to them, and love and hatred for their sake, as a loyal, sincere friend acts toward his companion. ﴿There is no blame on the doers of good﴾, meaning on the excused, sincere ones. The meaning of "there is no way against them" is: there is no blame upon them, and there is no path for the one who would reproach them.

﴿I find nothing﴾: "لا أجد" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the kāf in "أتوك" (atawka), with "qad" preceding it implied (muḍmara), as has been said regarding His words ﴿or they come to you, their hearts constrained﴾, meaning: when they come to you saying "لا أجد" (I find nothing), ﴿they turn away﴾.

Allah has indeed restricted the excused to staying behind: those who have no physical capacity, those who lacked the means of going out, and those who asked for assistance but did not find it. It is said the "seekers of mounts" were Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and his companions. It is said they were the weepers, six men from the Ansar.

﴿overflowing with tears﴾ is like your saying "تفيض دمعاً" (it overflows with tears), and it is more eloquent than "تفيض دمعها" (its tears overflow), because the eye is made as if it were entirely overflowing tears. "Min" here is for specification (bayān), as in your saying "أفديك من رجل" (I ransom you from a man).

The position of the prepositional phrase is accusative as a specification (tamyīz). "أَلَّا يَجِدُوا" means "so that they do not find." Its position is accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), and its governing word is the maf'ūl lahu which is ﴿grief﴾ (ḥazanan).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 93–94:

If you say: "What is the position of ﴿they are content﴾ (raḍū)?" I say: It is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf), as if it was said: "What is their state that they asked permission while they are wealthy?" So it was said: "They are content with baseness, lowliness, and being counted among the lingering-behind (al-khawālif)." ﴿And Allah has sealed their hearts﴾ means: the cause of their asking permission is their contentment with baseness and Allah's forsaking them.

If you say: "Is it permissible that His saying ﴿You have said, 'I do not find anything to mount you on'﴾ (qulta lā ajidu) be a similar resumptive clause, as if it was said: 'When they come to you to have you carry them, they turn away,' and so it was said: 'What is wrong with them that they turn away weeping?' Then it was said: 'You have said, "I do not find anything to carry you on."' But it is placed in the middle between the conditional and its response, like a parenthetical interjection (iʿtiraḍ)?" I say: Yes. And it is good that ﴿We will never believe you﴾ (lan nuʾmina lakum) is the reason for the prohibition of making excuses, because the aim of the one making an excuse is that he be believed regarding what he excuses himself with; so when it is known that he is a liar, it becomes necessary for him to abandon [[His saying "it becomes necessary for him to abandon" means: to leave off. It is said: "akhalla al-rajul bi-markazihi" when he leaves it. (ʿAyn)]]. And His saying ﴿Allah has informed us of your news﴾ (qad nabbaʾanā Allāh min akhbārikum) is the reason for the negation of their being believed, because when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, reveals to His Messenger the information about them and what is in their inner selves of evil and corruption, it is not consistent with that for their excuses to be believed. ﴿And Allah will see your deed﴾ (sa-yarā Allāh ʿamalakum): whether you repent or persist in your disbelief. ﴿Then you will be returned to Him﴾, and He knows every unseen and witnessed thing, secret and open, and will recompense you according to that.
