Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 95:

﴿So that you may turn away from them.﴾ So do not rebuke them, nor reproach them. ﴿So turn away from them.﴾ Give them what they ask for. ﴿Indeed, they are an abomination (rijs).﴾ This is the reason for leaving off reproaching them, meaning that reproach does not benefit them and does not reform them; rather, reproach is directed at the well-mannered person who has a sense of shame (dhu al-bashrah). The believer is rebuked for a slip that escapes from him, so that the rebuke may purify him by prompting him to repentance and seeking forgiveness.

As for these people, they are abominations for whom there is no way to purification. ﴿And their refuge is Hell.﴾ That is, the Fire suffices them as reproach and rebuke, so do not burden yourselves with reproaching them.

Your passage quotes Qur'an 9:96 as "لِتَرْضَوْا عَنْهُمْ" and "فَإِنْ تَرْضَوْا عَنْهُمْ" (the verse itself is not wrapped in ﴿ ﴾ markers here, so I render it as it stands).

"لِتَرْضَوْا عَنْهُمْ" means: their aim in swearing by Allah was to seek your approval, so that this would benefit them in their worldly life. "فَإِنْ تَرْضَوْا عَنْهُمْ" means: even if you are pleased with them, your approval alone will not benefit them, since Allah is angry with them, and they are liable to His immediate punishment and His deferred punishment. It has also been said that this was stated so that no one would suppose that the approval of the believers entails Allah's approval of them.

It is said: they were Jadd ibn Qays, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr and their companions, eighty men who were hypocrites. When the Prophet (ﷺ) arrived in Madinah, he said: "Do not sit with them, and do not speak with them." It has also been said: 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy came swearing that he would never stay behind from him.

The Bedouin Arabs (ahl al-badw) are more intense in disbelief and hypocrisy than the town dwellers (ahl al-hadar), because of their harshness, their roughness, and their wildness, and because they grow up far from witnessing the scholars and from knowing the Book and the Sunnah. They are more likely not to know, and more deserving of ignorance of the limits of the religion (al-din) and of what Allah has sent down of laws and rulings.

From this is his ﷺ saying: [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim), from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, within a hadith in which he said: "Indeed, the coarseness and the hardness of hearts are among the fadaddin, near the roots of the camels' tails." Thus al-Bukhari narrated it. Muslim has: "Indeed, the harshness and the hardness of hearts."]] "Indeed, the coarseness and the harshness are among the faddadin." [[His saying "and the harshness among the fadaddin": the fadaddin are those whose voices are raised over their crops and their livestock. A man is faddad: intensely loud, and al-fadid is the voice. Reported by al-Sihah. (ʿ)]]

And Allah is All-Knowing, knowing the state of every person among the dwellers of the hair (al-wabr) and the dwellers of the clay (al-madar), All-Wise in what He afflicts with it of the wrongdoer among them and the doer of good, the mistaken and the correct, of His punishment and His reward.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 98–99:**

﴿مَغْرَماً﴾ means a fine (*gharama*) and a loss (*khusran*). *Gharama* is what a man spends while it is not obligatory on him, because he spends only out of fear of the Muslims (*taqiyya*) and for show (*riyaʾ*), not for the sake of God, the Mighty and Majestic, seeking reward from Him. ﴿وَيَتَرَبَّصُ بِكُمُ الدَّوَائِرَ﴾ means the reversals of fortune (*dawāʾir al-zamān*): its changes and its outcomes. [[Mahmud said: "*Dawāʾir al-zamān* means its changes and its outcomes, so that your dominance over them may pass away..." etc. Ahmad said: In the verse of Bara'a there is an addition beyond the appropriateness of the supplication: the state of those invoked against and their saying. That is because what was attributed to them, waiting for reversals in an absolute sense, and what they were invoked with, the evil reversal, is restricted to the worst of reversals, not an absolute one. And God is the Granter of success.]] ﴿لِيَتَخَلَّصَ﴾ meaning, so that your dominance over them may pass away, so that he may be freed from giving charity. ﴿عَلَيْهِمْ دَائِرَةُ السَّوْءِ﴾ is an intervening supplication: He invoked against them with something like what they had invoked against the believers, as in the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَقَالَتِ الْيَهُودُ يَدُ اللَّهِ مَغْلُولَةٌ غُلَّتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ﴾ ("The Jews say: God's hand is shackled. Shackled are their hands"). It is also read *al-sūʾ* with a *ḍamma*, meaning punishment, just as it is said of it "*sayyiʾa*" (an evil deed). *Al-sūʾ* with a *fatḥa* is a condemnation of the reversal, as in your saying "*rajul sūʾ*" (a bad man), in contrast to your saying "*rajul ṣidq*" (a true man), because whoever is struck by it condemns it. ﴿وَاللَّهُ سَمِيعٌ لِمَا يَقُولُونَ﴾ when the charity is directed at them, ﴿عَلِيمٌ بِمَا يُضْمِرُونَ﴾ ("God is Hearing of what they say, Knowing of what they conceal"). It has been said that they were the Bedouin of Asad, Ghatafan and Tamim.

﴿قُرُبَاتٍ﴾ is the second object of *yattakhidh* (takes). The meaning: what he spends is a cause for obtaining nearness (*qurubāt*) with God, ﴿وَصَلَوَاتِ الرَّسُولِ﴾ and the prayers of the Messenger, because the Messenger would invoke good and blessing upon those who gave charity and would ask forgiveness for them, as in his saying: "O God, bless them" [or: "send blessings upon him"], and in his saying: "O God, bless the family of Abu Awfa." [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa, who said: "When people came to the Messenger of God ﷺ with their charity, he would say: 'O God, bless them.' Abu Awfa came with his charity, and he said: 'O God, bless the family of Abu Awfa.'"]] And the Exalted said: ﴿وَصَلِّ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ ("And pray for them"). So when what he spends was a cause of that, it was said: what he spends is made into nearnesses and prayers. ﴿أَلَا إِنَّهَا﴾ ("Indeed, it is...") is a testimony from God to the giver of charity regarding the soundness of what he believed, namely that his spending is nearness and prayers, and an affirmation of his hope, by way of a new statement, together with the two particles of alerting and confirmation (*alā* and *inna*), which indicate the firmness and establishment of the matter. Likewise ﴿سَيُدْخِلُهُمُ﴾ ("He will admit them"), and what the *sīn* contains of the confirmation of the promise. How strongly this speech indicates God's pleasure with those who give charity, and that charity has a high standing with Him when the intention is sincere from its owner. [[Mahmud said: "How strongly this speech indicates that charity has a high standing with God..." etc. Ahmad said: As you know, the Qadariyya hold the doctrine that the wrongdoer (*fāsiq*) is neither a believer nor an unbeliever, and that he is eternally in the Fire even if he is a monotheist. The aim of al-Zamakhshari is to make the wrongdoing with which the hypocrite is marked the same as that with which the monotheist is marked, so that the deserving of eternity for both is one. So beware of it, and God knows best.]]

﴿قُرْبَةٌ﴾ with a *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ* is also read. It has been said: they were ʿAbdullah, Dhu al-Bijadayn and his kinsmen.

The meaning: what he spends is a cause for obtaining nearness (*qurubāt*) with God, ﴿وَصَلَوَاتِ الرَّسُولِ﴾ and the prayers of the Messenger, because the Messenger would invoke good and blessing upon those who gave charity and would ask forgiveness for them, as in his saying: "O God, bless them" [or: "send blessings upon him"], and in his saying: "O God, bless the family of Abu Awfa." [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa, who said: "When people came to the Messenger of God ﷺ with their charity, he would say: 'O God, bless them.' Abu Awfa came with his charity, and he said: 'O God, bless the family of Abu Awfa.'"]] And the Exalted said: ﴿وَصَلِّ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ ("And pray for them"). So when what he spends was a cause of that, it was said: what he spends is made into nearnesses and prayers. ﴿أَلَا إِنَّهَا﴾ ("Indeed, it is...") is a testimony from God to the giver of charity regarding the soundness of what he believed, namely that his spending is nearness and prayers, and an affirmation of his hope, by way of a new statement, together with the two particles of alerting and confirmation (*alā* and *inna*), which indicate the firmness and establishment of the matter. Likewise ﴿سَيُدْخِلُهُمُ﴾ ("He will admit them"), and what the *sīn* contains of the confirmation of the promise. How strongly this speech indicates God's pleasure with those who give charity, and that charity has a high standing with Him when the intention is sincere from its owner. [[Mahmud said: "How strongly this speech indicates that charity has a high standing with God..." etc. Ahmad said: As you know, the Qadariyya hold the doctrine that the wrongdoer (*fāsiq*) is neither a believer nor an unbeliever, and that he is eternally in the Fire even if he is a monotheist. The aim of al-Zamakhshari is to make the wrongdoing with which the hypocrite is marked the same as that with which the monotheist is marked, so that the deserving of eternity for both is one. So beware of it, and God knows best.]]

﴿قُرْبَةٌ﴾ with a *ḍamma* on the *rāʾ* is also read. It has been said: they were ʿAbdullah, Dhu al-Bijadayn and his kinsmen.

The foremost, the first of the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun) and the Helpers (al-Ansar)... [Note: translating exactly.]

Let me give the faithful translation:

The foremost and first of the Emigrants (al-Muhajirin) are those who prayed toward both qiblahs. It is also said: those who witnessed Badr.

It is narrated from al-Sha'bi: those who pledged allegiance at al-Hudaybiyah, which was the Pledge of al-Ridwan, are between the two migrations. "And of the Helpers (al-Ansar)" refers to the People of the First Pledge at al-'Aqabah, who were seven men, and the People of the Second Pledge at al-'Aqabah, who were seventy, and those who believed when Abu Zurarah Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr came to them and taught them the Qur'an.

'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, read "wal-Ansaru" with a nominative ending (raf'), in coordination with "al-sabiqun." [[I have not seen it thus.]] It is also reported from 'Umar that he held that His words "wal-ladhina ittaba'uhum bi-ihsan" without a waw were an attribute of the Helpers, until Zayd said to him: "It is with a waw." He said: "Bring me Ubayy." He said: this is confirmed in the beginning of Surat al-Jumu'ah, "wa-akharina minhum," the middle of al-Hashr, "wal-ladhina ja'u min ba'dihim," and the end of al-Anfal, "wal-ladhina amanu min ba'du."

It is also narrated that he heard a man reading it with a waw, and said: "Who taught you this?" He said: "Ubayy." So he called him and said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught it to me, and you sell dried leaves of qarz in al-Baqi'." He said: "You have spoken truly. And if you wish, say: we witnessed and you were absent, we gave victory and you forsook, we sheltered and you drove away." [[I have not seen it thus. In al-Tabari, through Abu Ma'shar from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, who said: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab passed by a man reading 'wal-sabiqun al-awwalun min al-muhajirina wal-ansar,' so 'Umar took his hand and said: 'Who taught you this?' He said: 'Ubayy ibn Ka'b.' So he said:]]

From this 'Umar said: "I used to think we had attained a rank that no one after us would reach." The foremost is the subject of the sentence (mubtada'), and its predicate is "radiya Allahu 'anhum," meaning: He is pleased with them for their deeds, "wa-radu 'anhu," for what He poured upon them of His religious and worldly blessings.

In the codices of the people of Makkah it reads "tajri min tahtiha" (with min), which is the reading of Ibn Kathir, while in the rest of the codices it reads "tahtaha" without min.

And of those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites, (meaning) around your town, which is Madinah. They are Juhaynah, Aslam, Ashja', and Ghifar, who were camped around it. And of the people of Madinah (is a conjunction, *'atf*, on the predicate of the subject, which is "of those around you"). It is also permissible for it to be a sentence conjoined to the subject and predicate, if you estimate it as: "And among the people of Madinah are people who have become hardened in hypocrisy," with *maradu* being a descriptive attribute of an omitted noun, as in his saying:

*Ana ibnu Jala* (I am the son of Jala)
*wa-tala'i al-thana Yat* (and the scaler of difficult heights)
*mata adi'u al-'imamata ta'rifuni* (when I lay down the turban, you will know me)

*Wa-madha tabtaghi al-shu'ara'u minni* (And what do the poets seek from me)
*wa-qad jawaztu hadda al-arba'in* (when I have passed the limit of forty)

This is by Suhaym ibn Wathil al-Riyahi. He was an Abyssinian slave, and he was accused of (an affair with) his master's daughter, so he killed him. It is also said to be by al-Muthaqqib al-'Abdi, and the first verse is attributed to al-'Urajj. *Jala* is a descriptive attribute of an omitted noun, meaning "the son of a man whose (courage) became apparent and clear through bravery," so the verb is intransitive. Or (it means) "he removed the distress of war and uncovered its troubles," in which case it is transitive, and omitting the modified noun here is a poetic necessity, because it is only regular when the attribute can directly govern the operator, or when the modified noun is part of a noun governed by *min* or *fi*, as already mentioned. The annexation of *talla'* to what follows it is verbal, so it does not give it definiteness. The placement of the *waw* between the attributes emphasizes their connection to the modified noun. *Al-thana'ya* means difficult obstacles. He uses it metaphorically for great matters, as an explicit metaphor. *Al-tuluw* (scaling) is an intensifier (*tarshih*) for "when I lay down." The helmet of war on my head, "you will know me," is a metaphor for the descent of war, whereby his courage is established. It is also narrated as "tudri" instead of "tabtaghi," which is a reflexive form (*iftial*) from *al-diraya* (knowledge), meaning: "What do the poets seek to learn from me, while I have passed the limit of forty years?" The breaking of the nun of the plural is a dialectal form. It is also permissible that it is in the genitive by kasra, according to the dialect of those who inflect it like *al-hin* (the plural of the noun, inflected with the vowel of the oblique case).

On the first interpretation, it is either an independent statement or an attribute of "hypocrites." It is separated between them and it by a conjunction with its predicate: *maradu 'ala al-nifaq* (they became hardened in hypocrisy), meaning they became proficient in it, from *maran fulanun 'amalahu* (someone practiced his work), and *marada 'alayhi* means when one trained in it and became accustomed to it, until it became easy for him and he became skilled in it. The proficiency and skill in it is indicated by His saying: ﴿You do not know them﴾, meaning they conceal themselves from you despite your intelligence and perceptiveness. [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is that, despite your nobility, your intelligence, and the truthfulness of your insight, they conceal their condition from you..." Ahmad said: "It seems that His saying, the Exalted, *maradu 'ala al-nifaq* is a preparation for establishing that their state is hidden from him, peace be upon him, because of their expertise in hypocrisy and their persistence in it. And Allah knows best."]] and your nobility and the truthfulness of your insight, because of their extreme caution in avoiding anything that would cast doubt on their affair. Then He said: ﴿We know them﴾, meaning no one knows them except Allah, and no one is informed of their secret other than Him, because they conceal disbelief in the innermost depths of their hearts, and they display to you outwardly the appearance of sincere believers, so that you have no doubt about their faith. This is because they have become hardened in hypocrisy and accustomed to it, so they have the upper hand in it.

﴿We will punish them twice﴾. It is said: they are execution and the punishment of the grave. It is also said: disgrace and the punishment of the grave. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that they differed about these two times. He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood delivering a sermon on Friday and said: "Go out, O so-and-so, for you are a hypocrite. Go out, O so-and-so, for you are a hypocrite." So he expelled some people and disgraced them. This is the first punishment, and the second is the punishment of the grave. [[The statement "He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood..." apparently means that the speaker is Ibn 'Abbas.]] [[It was recorded by al-Tabari, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, through the chain of al-Suddi from Abu Malik from Ibn 'Abbas with this wording up to "and disgraced them," and he added: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab had not attended that Friday prayer due to a need he had. He met them and hid from them, then he entered the mosque, and a man said to him: 'O 'Umar, rejoice, for Allah has disgraced the hypocrites today.' This is the first punishment, and the second punishment is the punishment of the grave."]] And from al-Hasan: (it refers to) taking zakat from their wealth and wearing down their bodies. ﴿Then they will be returned to a great punishment﴾, meaning to the punishment of the Fire.

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 102:

They acknowledged their sins. That is, they did not offer false excuses for their staying behind, as others did, but acknowledged against themselves that they had done a wretched thing, being remorseful and regretful. They were three: Abu Lubaba Marwan ibn Abd al-Mundhir, Aws ibn Tha'laba, and Wadi'a ibn Hizam [[The statement "It is narrated that those who acknowledged their sins were three: Abu Lubaba Marwan ibn Abd al-Mundhir, Aws ibn Tha'laba, and Wadi'a ibn Hizam" — I have not found it.]]. It is also said that they were ten. Seven of them tied themselves up: when the news of what had been revealed concerning those who stayed behind reached them, they were certain of destruction, so they bound themselves to the pillars of the mosque. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived, entered the mosque and prayed two rak'as, as was his habit whenever he returned from a journey. He saw them bound and asked about them. He was told that they had sworn not to free themselves until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) himself freed them. He said: "And I swear that I will not free them until I am commanded concerning them." Then it was revealed, and he freed them and excused them. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, these are our wealth that kept us back from you; give it in charity on our behalf and purify us." He said: "I have not been commanded to take anything from your wealth." Then it was revealed: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [[Narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il and Ibn Mardawayh through the chain of Ali ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas regarding this verse, ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins﴾ — the verse. They were ten men who stayed behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the expedition of Tabuk. When the Prophet (ﷺ) was about to return, seven of them tied themselves to the pillars of the mosque — the hadith.]].

﴿A righteous deed﴾: going out to jihad. ﴿And another, wicked﴾: staying behind from it. From al-Hasan and from al-Kalbi: repentance and sin.

If you ask: each of them has been described as mixed, so what is the thing it is mixed with? I answer: each of them is both mixed and the thing mixed with, because the meaning is that each of the two was mixed with the other, as in your saying "I mixed the water and the milk." Thurayd: you mixed each of them with its companion. This carries a meaning that your saying "I mixed the water with the milk" does not, because in that you made the water the thing mixed and the milk the thing mixed with; but when you say it with the conjunction (wa), you make the water and the milk both mixed and mixed-with, as if you had said: "I mixed the water with the milk and the milk with the water." It may also be taken from their saying: "I sold the sheep, a sheep and a dirham," meaning a sheep for a dirham.

If you ask: how is it said ﴿that He may accept their repentance﴾ when their repentance has not been mentioned? I answer: when their acknowledgment of their sins has been mentioned, and that is evidence of repentance, then their repentance has been mentioned.

Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: The truth in this is that when you say "I mixed the water with the milk," what is expressly stated in this sentence is that the water that was mixed and the milk are the thing mixed with; what is implied by necessity, not by explicit statement, is that the water is mixed with it and the milk is mixed, and when you say "I mixed the water and the milk," what is expressly stated is that each of them was mixed. As for what each of them was mixed with, it is not expressly stated, but it is necessarily implied that each of them is mixed with the other. It may be a qualifier or something else. So Zamakhshari's statement, "your saying 'I mixed the water and the milk' conveys what it conveys with the particle 'bi' and more," is not so. The apparent meaning in the verse, and Allah knows best, is that the switch from "bi" was only to imply that "mixing" carries the sense of "doing": as if it were said, "they did a righteous deed and another wicked one," and then the sense of mixing was added to the deed, so both were expressed together with it. And Allah knows best.

Tuṭahhiruhum (تُطَهِّرُهُمْ) is an attributive description of ṣadaqah (charity). It is also read as tuṭahhiruhum, from aṭharahu, which has the same meaning as ṭahharahu. And it is read tuṭahhirhum with the jussive (jazm), as a response to the imperative. Wa-tuzakkīhim was read only with the affirmed yā' (ithbāt al-yā'). The tā' in tuṭahhiruhum is either addressed to the second person (lil-khiṭāb) or is the feminine third person (li-ghaybat al-mu'annath). Tazkiyah (purification) is an intensification of taṭhīr (purifying) and an addition to it. Or it means growth (al-inmā') and blessing (al-barakah) in wealth. Wa-ṣalli 'alayhim: bestow upon them (wa-'tuf 'alayhim) with supplication for them and mercy. The sunnah is that the one who collects the charity (al-muṣaddiq) prays for the owner of the charity when he takes it [[The phrase "the one who collects the charity (al-muṣaddiq)": al-muṣaddiq is the active participle of one who takes the charities, as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]]. From al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah have mercy on him: I like that the ruler say when taking the charity: "May Allah reward you for what you have given, make it a purification for you, and bless you in what you have kept." It was read: inna ṣalātaka (إنّ صلاتك), in the singular (al-tawḥīd), instead of ṣalawātika in the plural [[The phrase "read inna ṣalātaka in the singular" replaces the reading ṣalawātika in the plural. (ʿ)]]. Sakanun lahum (سَكَنٌ لَهُمْ): they find tranquility in it, and their hearts are reassured that Allah has accepted their repentance. Wallāhu samīʿun (وَاللَّهُ سَمِيعٌ): He hears their confession of their sins and their supplication. ʿAlīmun (عَلِيمٌ): He knows what is in their hearts, and the distress (al-ghamm) arising from the regret (al-nadam) for what they had committed.

Recited with both the ya' and the ta' (as ﴿أَلَمْ يَعْلَمُوا﴾ and ﴿أَلَمْ تَعْلَمُوا﴾). There are two interpretations of this. The first is that it refers to those who have repented, meaning: Did they not know, before they were forgiven and their charities were accepted, that ﴿Allah is He who accepts repentance﴾ when it is sincere, and accepts charities when they are given with pure intention. The word "He" (هو) here is for specification and emphasis, and (it indicates) that it is among the nature of Allah the Exalted to accept the repentance of those who repent. It has also been said that the meaning of specification in "He" is that this does not rest with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); rather, Allah, glorified is He, is the One who accepts repentance and rejects it, so direct your repentance to Him and turn toward Him with it.

Say to them, "Those who have repented, carry on with your deeds; your deeds will not remain hidden from Allah and His servants, whether they are good or evil, just as you have seen and it has become clear to you." The second [interpretation] is that what is meant is those who have not repented, as an encouragement to them to repent. It is related that when they [the earlier group] were forgiven, those who had not repented said, "These who have repented were with us yesterday; they were not spoken to and not sat with, so what [has happened] to them?" Then this was revealed.

If you ask, "What is the meaning of His words, 'and takes the charities'?" I answer: it is a metaphor for His accepting them. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that charity falls into the hand of Allah the Exalted before it falls into the hand of the one who asks. [Narrated by 'Abd al-Razzaq and al-Tabarani through the chain of 'Abdullah ibn Qatadah al-Muharibi from him. In the two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayrah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "No one gives a charity of good [earnings] — and Allah accepts only the good — except that the Merciful takes it with His right hand..." the hadith.]

The meaning is that He accepts it and multiplies its reward. And His words, "then Allah will see," are a warning to them and a caution against the consequence of persistence and of neglecting repentance.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 106:

It is recited as murjawn and murja'un, from arjaytuhu. And ar-jata'tuhu: when I delayed it. From it comes al-Murji'a (the Murji'ah, a theological school that deferred judgment on the status of sinning believers), meaning:

"And others [are] held in suspense regarding their affair: either He will punish them, if they remain persistent [in sin] and do not repent, or He will turn to them in forgiveness, if they repent." They were three: Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayya, and Murara ibn al-Rabi'.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded his Companions not to greet them or speak to them. They did not do as Abu Lubaba and his companions did, who bound themselves to the pillars and displayed distress and grief. When they knew that no one was looking at them, they entrusted their affair to Allah the Exalted, sincerely purified their intentions, and their repentance was sincere, so Allah had mercy on them [[I have not found this in this wording. The story is in the Two Sahihs from the hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik, and it is the hadith of Ibn Abbas that precedes it, in abridged form.]] "And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise." In the recitation of Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud]: "Forgiving, Merciful." As for "wa-imma lil-'ibad" (and in another sense, for the servants): that is, fear for them the punishment, and hope for them mercy.

[[The phrase "wa-imma lil-'ibad, i.e. fear for them the punishment, and hope for them mercy" — the wording of al-Nasafi: "wa-imma" here is the expression of doubt, and it refers back to the servants. (Ghayn/editor's note)]]

The Companions of Medina and Syria read it without the conjunction waw: *alladhīna ittakhadhū* (﴿Those who took﴾). This is because it begins a separate narrative (*qiṣṣa*) in its own right. In the other codices it is read with waw, *wa-alladhīna ittakhadhū*, as a conjunction linking it to the story of the mosque of harm (*masjid al-ḍirār*) which the hypocrites established, and to their other narratives.

It is related that when the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf built the Mosque of Quba, they sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asking him to come to them. He came and prayed in it. Their brothers, the Banu Ghanm ibn 'Awf, envied them. [[I have not found this context except in al-Tha'labi, without an isnad, and its opening is not sound. The Mosque of Quba had been founded when the Prophet (ﷺ) first arrived at Quba after his migration, whereas the Mosque of Harm was built at the time of the expedition to Tabuk, and there are nine years between the two. However, Ibn Mardawayh related through Muhammad ibn Sa'd al-'Awfi, from his father, from his paternal uncle, from his father, from his grandfather 'Atiyya ibn Sa'd, from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) built the Mosque of Quba, men from among them went out: 'Arraj, the grandfather of 'Abdullah ibn Hunayf, Wadi'a ibn Hizam, and Mujama' ibn Harithah, and they built a mosque..." — the hadith — from his saying "they built a mosque beside the Mosque of Quba," to the end. Ibn Ishaq mentioned it in the Maghazi, and al-Tabari from his chain, from al-Zuhri, Yazid ibn Ruman and others, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came and halted at Dhu Awan, an hour's distance from Medina. The people of the Mosque of Harm had come to him while he was preparing for the expedition to Tabuk..." — the hadith. He did not mention among those sent to demolish it except Malik ibn al-Dukhshum and Ma'n ibn 'Adi; he did not mention Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah, nor 'Amir ibn al-Sakan. Ibn Mardawayh related it through Ibn Ishaq, who said: al-Zuhri mentioned from Ibn Ukaymah al-Laythi, from a nephew of Wahm, that he heard Abu Rahm al-Ghifari and related something similar. As for their having built it because of Abu 'Amir, Ibn Mardawayh related it through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both).]] They said: "We will build a mosque, and send to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to pray in it, and Abu 'Amir the monk will pray in it when he comes from Syria," so that they might establish for themselves superiority and advantage over their brothers. This Abu 'Amir was the one whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named "the Wicked" (*al-Fasiq*). He said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud: "I do not find a people fighting you without my fighting you with them." He continued to fight him until the day of Hunayn. When Hawazin was defeated, he fled to Syria and sent to the hypocrites:

"Prepare whatever strength and weapons you can, for I am going to Caesar and will bring troops and expel Muhammad and his Companions from Medina."

So they built a mosque beside the Mosque of Quba and said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We have built a mosque for the sick, the needy, and the night of rain and cold. We would love for you to pray in it and to invoke blessing upon us." He (ﷺ) said: "I am on a journey and preoccupied. When we return, if Allah wills, we will pray in it." When he returned from the expedition to Tabuk, they asked him to come to the mosque, and then the verse was revealed to him. He summoned Malik ibn al-Dukhshum, Ma'n ibn 'Adi, 'Amir ibn al-Sakan, and Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah, and said to them: "Go to this mosque whose people are wrongdoers, demolish it and burn it." They did so, and he ordered that its place be made a rubbish heap where carrion and refuse would be thrown. Abu 'Amir died in Syria, at Qinnasrin.

*Dirar*: harming, causing injury, to the brothers, the people of the Mosque of Quba and Ma'aza. *Kufr*: disbelief, and strengthening of hypocrisy. *Tafriq*: dividing the believers, because they used to pray together in the Mosque of Quba, which would become full of them, so they wanted to separate from it and have their word divided. *Irṣad*: preparing, making ready, *li*, for the sake of, *man ḥārab Allāh wa-rasūlahu*: whoever wars against Allah and His Messenger, and this was the monk: they prepared it for him so that he might pray in it and gain ascendancy over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). [[The phrase "fayaghtaṣṣ" means it becomes filled. (ʿ)]]

It has been said: every mosque built for vainglory, show, or reputation, or for any purpose other than seeking the face of Allah, or with unlawful wealth, is akin to the mosque of harm. It is related from Shaqiq that he did not witness prayer in the mosque of the Banu 'Amir. It was said to him: "The mosque of such-and-such people, they have not yet prayed in it." He said: "I do not love to pray in it, for it was built on harm, and every mosque built on harm, or show, or reputation, its origin leads back to the mosque that was built for harm."

It is related from 'Ata': when Allah, exalted is He, opened the cities through the hand of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), he ordered the Muslims to build mosques, and not to have two mosques in one city that harm one another.

If you ask: what is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of *alladhīna ittakhadhū*? I say: its position is in the accusative by way of specification (*ikhtiṣāṣ*), like His saying ﴿the establishers of prayer﴾. It has also been said: it is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "and among those we have described are those who took..." like His saying ﴿the male thief and the female thief﴾.

If you ask: with what does *min qablu* (﴿before﴾) connect? I say: with *ittakhadhū*, that is, they took a mosque before these people became hypocrites by staying behind.

﴿We intended only good﴾: that is, what we intended by building this mosque was only the good end, or the good intention, which is prayer, the remembrance of Allah, and the expansion of accommodation for those who pray.

﴿A mosque founded upon piety from the first day﴾: it has been said this is the Mosque of Quba, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) founded and prayed in during his stay at Quba; and that was Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, and he went out on Friday. This view is preferable, because the comparison between the two mosques of Quba and Medina is more fitting. It has also been said it is the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Medina. It is related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the mosque founded upon piety, and he took a pebble, struck it on the ground, and said: 'It is this mosque of yours, the mosque of Medina.'" [[Narrated by Muslim in its wording.]]

﴿from the first day﴾: from the first day of its existence. ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾: it has been said that when this was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) walked with the emigrants until he stood at the door of the Mosque of Quba, where the Ansar were sitting. He said: "Are you believers?" The people were silent. He repeated it, and 'Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah, they are indeed believers, and I am with them." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Are you content with the decree?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Will you be patient in affliction?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Will you be thankful in ease?" They said: "Yes." He (ﷺ) said: "Believers, by the Lord of the Ka'bah." Then he sat down and said: "O assembly of the Ansar, Allah, mighty and majestic, has praised you. What do you do at ablution and at relieving yourselves?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we follow excrement with three stones, then we follow the stones with water." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾. [[I have not found it in this form; it seems to be a composite of two hadiths. The first, whose source al-Tabarani gives in al-Awsat, says: "Al-Haytham ibn Khalaf al-Duri related to us with his chain to Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon 'Umar, with some people, and said: "Are you believers?" They were silent, three times. 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, we believe in what you have brought us, we praise Allah in ease, we are patient in affliction, and we are content with the decree." He said: "Believers, by the Lord of the Ka'bah."' End. In this there is a difference between the two versions that is not hidden. As for the second, Ibn Mardawayh related through Ibn 'Abbas something similar.]]

It is read *an yaṭahharū* with assimilation (*idghām*). It has been said: this is general to purification from all impurities. It has been said: they did not sleep at night in a state of major impurity (*janabah*), and they followed water with the traces of urine. It is related from al-Hasan: it is purification from sins by repentance. It has been said: they love to purify themselves by the fever that expiates their sins, so they were all struck by fever.

If you ask: what is the meaning of the two loves? I say: their love of purification is that they prefer it and are eager for it, like the eagerness of one who loves a thing he desires to prefer it. The love of Allah, exalted is He, for them is that He is pleased with them and does good to them, as the lover does to his beloved.

The Companions of Medina and Syria read it without the conjunction waw: *alladhīna ittakhadhū* (﴿Those who took﴾). This is because it begins a separate narrative (*qiṣṣa*) in its own right. In the other codices it is read with waw, *wa-alladhīna ittakhadhū*, as a conjunction linking it to the story of the mosque of harm (*masjid al-ḍirār*) which the hypocrites established, and to their other narratives.

It is related that when the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf built the Mosque of Quba, they sent to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asking him to come to them. He came and prayed in it. Their brothers, the Banu Ghanm ibn 'Awf, envied them. [[I have not found this context except in al-Tha'labi, without an isnad, and its opening is not sound. The Mosque of Quba had been founded when the Prophet (ﷺ) first arrived at Quba after his migration, whereas the Mosque of Harm was built at the time of the expedition to Tabuk, and there are nine years between the two. However, Ibn Mardawayh related through Muhammad ibn Sa'd al-'Awfi, from his father, from his paternal uncle, from his father, from his grandfather 'Atiyya ibn Sa'd, from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) built the Mosque of Quba, men from among them went out: 'Arraj, the grandfather of 'Abdullah ibn Hunayf, Wadi'a ibn Hizam, and Mujama' ibn Harithah, and they built a mosque..." — the hadith — from his saying "they built a mosque beside the Mosque of Quba," to the end. Ibn Ishaq mentioned it in the Maghazi, and al-Tabari from his chain, from al-Zuhri, Yazid ibn Ruman and others, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came and halted at Dhu Awan, an hour's distance from Medina. The people of the Mosque of Harm had come to him while he was preparing for the expedition to Tabuk..." — the hadith. He did not mention among those sent to demolish it except Malik ibn al-Dukhshum and Ma'n ibn 'Adi; he did not mention Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah, nor 'Amir ibn al-Sakan. Ibn Mardawayh related it through Ibn Ishaq, who said: al-Zuhri mentioned from Ibn Ukaymah al-Laythi, from a nephew of Wahm, that he heard Abu Rahm al-Ghifari and related something similar. As for their having built it because of Abu 'Amir, Ibn Mardawayh related it through 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both).]] They said: "We will build a mosque, and send to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to pray in it, and Abu 'Amir the monk will pray in it when he comes from Syria," so that they might establish for themselves superiority and advantage over their brothers. This Abu 'Amir was the one whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named "the Wicked" (*al-Fasiq*). He said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of Uhud: "I do not find a people fighting you without my fighting you with them." He continued to fight him until the day of Hunayn. When Hawazin was defeated, he fled to Syria and sent to the hypocrites:

"Prepare whatever strength and weapons you can, for I am going to Caesar and will bring troops and expel Muhammad and his Companions from Medina."

So they built a mosque beside the Mosque of Quba and said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We have built a mosque for the sick, the needy, and the night of rain and cold. We would love for you to pray in it and to invoke blessing upon us." He (ﷺ) said: "I am on a journey and preoccupied. When we return, if Allah wills, we will pray in it." When he returned from the expedition to Tabuk, they asked him to come to the mosque, and then the verse was revealed to him. He summoned Malik ibn al-Dukhshum, Ma'n ibn 'Adi, 'Amir ibn al-Sakan, and Wahshi, the slayer of Hamzah, and said to them: "Go to this mosque whose people are wrongdoers, demolish it and burn it." They did so, and he ordered that its place be made a rubbish heap where carrion and refuse would be thrown. Abu 'Amir died in Syria, at Qinnasrin.

*Dirar*: harming, causing injury, to the brothers, the people of the Mosque of Quba and Ma'aza. *Kufr*: disbelief, and strengthening of hypocrisy. *Tafriq*: dividing the believers, because they used to pray together in the Mosque of Quba, which would become full of them, so they wanted to separate from it and have their word divided. *Irṣad*: preparing, making ready, *li*, for the sake of, *man ḥārab Allāh wa-rasūlahu*: whoever wars against Allah and His Messenger, and this was the monk: they prepared it for him so that he might pray in it and gain ascendancy over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). [[The phrase "fayaghtaṣṣ" means it becomes filled. (ʿ)]]

It has been said: every mosque built for vainglory, show, or reputation, or for any purpose other than seeking the face of Allah, or with unlawful wealth, is akin to the mosque of harm. It is related from Shaqiq that he did not witness prayer in the mosque of the Banu 'Amir. It was said to him: "The mosque of such-and-such people, they have not yet prayed in it." He said: "I do not love to pray in it, for it was built on harm, and every mosque built on harm, or show, or reputation, its origin leads back to the mosque that was built for harm."

It is related from 'Ata': when Allah, exalted is He, opened the cities through the hand of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), he ordered the Muslims to build mosques, and not to have two mosques in one city that harm one another.

If you ask: what is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of *alladhīna ittakhadhū*? I say: its position is in the accusative by way of specification (*ikhtiṣāṣ*), like His saying ﴿the establishers of prayer﴾. It has also been said: it is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "and among those we have described are those who took..." like His saying ﴿the male thief and the female thief﴾.

If you ask: with what does *min qablu* (﴿before﴾) connect? I say: with *ittakhadhū*, that is, they took a mosque before these people became hypocrites by staying behind.

﴿We intended only good﴾: that is, what we intended by building this mosque was only the good end, or the good intention, which is prayer, the remembrance of Allah, and the expansion of accommodation for those who pray.

﴿A mosque founded upon piety from the first day﴾: it has been said this is the Mosque of Quba, which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) founded and prayed in during his stay at Quba; and that was Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, and he went out on Friday. This view is preferable, because the comparison between the two mosques of Quba and Medina is more fitting. It has also been said it is the mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in Medina. It is related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the mosque founded upon piety, and he took a pebble, struck it on the ground, and said: 'It is this mosque of yours, the mosque of Medina.'" [[Narrated by Muslim in its wording.]]

﴿from the first day﴾: from the first day of its existence. ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾: it has been said that when this was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) walked with the emigrants until he stood at the door of the Mosque of Quba, where the Ansar were sitting. He said: "Are you believers?" The people were silent. He repeated it, and 'Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah, they are indeed believers, and I am with them." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Are you content with the decree?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Will you be patient in affliction?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Will you be thankful in ease?" They said: "Yes." He (ﷺ) said: "Believers, by the Lord of the Ka'bah." Then he sat down and said: "O assembly of the Ansar, Allah, mighty and majestic, has praised you. What do you do at ablution and at relieving yourselves?" They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we follow excrement with three stones, then we follow the stones with water." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾. [[I have not found it in this form; it seems to be a composite of two hadiths. The first, whose source al-Tabarani gives in al-Awsat, says: "Al-Haytham ibn Khalaf al-Duri related to us with his chain to Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered upon 'Umar, with some people, and said: "Are you believers?" They were silent, three times. 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, we believe in what you have brought us, we praise Allah in ease, we are patient in affliction, and we are content with the decree." He said: "Believers, by the Lord of the Ka'bah."' End. In this there is a difference between the two versions that is not hidden. As for the second, Ibn Mardawayh related through Ibn 'Abbas something similar.]]

It is read *an yaṭahharū* with assimilation (*idghām*). It has been said: this is general to purification from all impurities. It has been said: they did not sleep at night in a state of major impurity (*janabah*), and they followed water with the traces of urine. It is related from al-Hasan: it is purification from sins by repentance. It has been said: they love to purify themselves by the fever that expiates their sins, so they were all struck by fever.

If you ask: what is the meaning of the two loves? I say: their love of purification is that they prefer it and are eager for it, like the eagerness of one who loves a thing he desires to prefer it. The love of Allah, exalted is He, for them is that He is pleased with them and does good to them, as the lover does to his beloved.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 109:

It is read as ﴿أَسَّسَ بُنْيَانَهُ﴾ and ﴿أُسِّسَ بُنْيَانُهُ﴾, with the verb in the active and in the passive. And ﴿أَسَاسَ بُنْيَانِهِ﴾ is the plural of asas (foundation).

Read in the construct (idafah) form, ﴿أَسَاسَ بُنْيَانِهِ﴾, with fatha and with kasra, is the plural of ass (base). ﴿آسَاسَ بُنْيَانِهِ﴾ is on the pattern af'al, also the plural of ass. And ﴿أُسُّ بُنْيَانِهِ﴾. The meaning is: ﴿أَفَمَنْ أَسَّسَ بُنْيَانَهُ﴾ [[His saying "the one who founded the structure of his religion" is like the hadith "Islam is built upon five." (Ibn Ghalib? marginal note: ʿ)]] on a strong, firm foundation, which is the truth that is the fear of God and His good pleasure, ﴿خَيْرٌ أَمْ مَنْ أَسَّسَهُ عَلَىٰ شَفَا جُرُفٍ هَارٍ﴾ ... rather, the one who founded it on a foundation that is the weakest of foundations, the most unstable, and the least lasting, which is falsehood and hypocrisy, whose likeness is ﴿شَفَا جُرُفٍ هَارٍ﴾ in its lack of stability and holding. The edge of the precipice is placed in opposition to piety, because it is made a metaphor for what contradicts piety. If you say: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿فَانْهَارَ بِهِ فِي نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ﴾? I say: since the crumbling precipice was made a metaphor for falsehood, it was said ﴿فَانْهَارَ بِهِ فِي نَارِ جَهَنَّمَ﴾, meaning: falsehood brought him down into the fire of Hell. Except that he drew out the metaphor, so he used the word "collapse", which belongs to the precipice, to depict that the one who pursues falsehood is as if he had founded a structure on the edge of a precipice over the valleys of Hell, so that the precipice collapsed with him and he fell into its depths. Al-shafa is the edge and the lip. The jurf of a valley is its side whose base is undermined by water and eroded by torrents, so it remains weak. Al-har is the crumbling, that which is split and on the verge of ruin and falling. Its pattern is fa'il shortened from fa'il, like khalf from khalif, and its counterpart is shak and sat, from sha'ik and sa'it. Its alif is not the alif of the doer; it is its middle radical. Its root is h-w-r, shuk and sawt. You will find no more eloquent speech than this, nor one more indicative of the reality of falsehood and the nature of its matter. It is also read ﴿جُرُفٍ﴾ with the ra sukun.

If you say: what is the explanation of what Sibawayh narrated from Isa ibn Umar: ﴿عَلَىٰ تَقْوَىٰ مِنَ اللَّهِ﴾ with tanwin? I say: he made the alif for extension (ilhaq), not for feminine marking, like tatara in the reading of those who apply tanwin; he attached it to ja'far.

In the codex of Ubayy: ﴿فَانْهَارَتْ بِهِ قَوَاعِدُهُ﴾.

It is said: a spot of the Mosque of Harm was dug, and smoke was seen rising from it. It is narrated that Majma' ibn Harithah was their imam in the Mosque of Harm. The Banu Amr ibn Awf asked the companions of the Mosque of Quba, during the caliphate of Umar ibn al-Khattab, to permit Majma' to lead them in prayer in their mosque. He said: "No, and not a delight to the eye. Is he not the imam of the Mosque of Harm?" He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, do not hasten against me. By God, I prayed with them while God knows that I did not know what they concealed in it. Had I known, I would not have prayed with them in it. I was a young man who recited the Qur'an, and they were elders who recited nothing of the Qur'an." So he excused him, believed him, and ordered him to lead his people in prayer.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 110:

Doubt about the religion, and hypocrisy, and the people were hypocrites. What led them to build that mosque was their disbelief and hypocrisy, as He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿harm and disbelief﴾. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) demolished it, they increased, because of what angered them and weighed heavily on them, in their determination upon hypocrisy and their hatred of Islam. So the meaning of His words ﴿Their building which they built will not cease to be a cause of doubt in their hearts﴾ is: its demolition will remain a cause of doubt and hypocrisy, in addition to their existing doubt and hypocrisy, whose mark will not leave their hearts and whose effect will not vanish, ﴿unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾, cut into fragments and scattered parts. Then they will forget it. As long as they remain whole and intact, the doubt remains firmly lodged in them. It is possible that the mention of cutting [[His words "it is possible that the mention of cutting" are according to the reading taqatta'a with doubled tā' in the passive voice. (ʿ)]] is a depiction of the removal of doubt from them. It is also possible that the literal cutting of their hearts is intended, and what will happen to them of it, through their being killed, or in the graves, or in the Fire. It has also been read as yaqta'a with a yā', and as taqatta'a with a single tā', and as taqta'a with an open tā', meaning tataqatta'a.

And ﴿their hearts are cut﴾, with the address directed to the Messenger, meaning: unless you cut their hearts by killing them. Al-Hasan read ﴿ilā an﴾ (until). In the recitation of Abdullah: ﴿even if their hearts were cut﴾. And from Talhah: ﴿even if their hearts were cut﴾ with the address directed to the Messenger or to every addressee. It was also said: its meaning is ﴿unless they repent with a repentance by which their hearts are cut with remorse and grief over their negligence﴾.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 9, verse 111:

God has likened His granting them Paradise in return for their giving up their lives and their wealth in His cause to a bargain (bi-l-shirwa) [[His words "bi-l-shirwa" are like al-jidwa (benefit, return). In al-Sihah and al-Wishah it is said to mean "the like" (al-mithl). The opinion here is that it is a noun meaning "purchase" (al-ishtira'). (Ta'}]]. It is also narrated: "He made Him a merchant who made the price dear for them." And from ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him: "He gave them both transactions together." And from al-Hasan: "anfusan" is His creating them, and "amwalan" is His provision to them. It is narrated that when the Ansar pledged allegiance to him at al-ʿAqaba, ʿAbdullah ibn Rawaha said: "Stipulate for your Lord and for yourselves whatever you wish." [[Al-Tabari transmitted it through Abu Maʿshar from Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi and others, who said: "When the Ansar pledged allegiance on the night of al-ʿAqaba," and he mentioned it.]] He said: "I stipulate for my Lord that you worship Him and associate nothing with Him, and I stipulate for myself that you protect me from what you protect yourselves from." They said: "If we do that, what do we get?" He said: "For you is Paradise."

They said: "The sale has been profitable; we will neither cancel it nor seek its cancellation." A Bedouin passed by the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was reciting it, and said: "Whose speech is this?" He said: "The speech of God." He said: "By God, it is a profitable sale; we will neither cancel it nor seek its cancellation." Then he went out to fight and was martyred. [[Al-Tha'labi mentioned it in this form without a chain, from al-Basri as a mursal report, but its chain to al-Hasan al-Basri is at the beginning of his book. I say: Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted it through Abu Shayba from ʿAta' al-Khurasani from Jabir: "This verse, 'Indeed, God has purchased...', was revealed to the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was in the mosque, and the people in the mosque exclaimed Allahu akbar. A man from the Ansar came and said: 'Was this verse revealed?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'A profitable sale. We will neither cancel it nor seek its cancellation.'" ʿAbd ibn Humayd also transmitted it: Ibrahim—that is Ibn ʿAbd al-Hakam ibn Aban—narrated to us from his father from ʿIkrima: "When this verse, 'Indeed, God has purchased...' was revealed, a man from the Ansar said: 'O what a sale, how profitable it is! By God, we will neither cancel it nor seek its cancellation.'" Al-Tabari also transmitted it through Muhammad ibn Kaʿb and others, who said: ʿAbdullah ibn Rawaha said to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Stipulate for your Lord and for yourselves whatever you wish." He said: "I stipulate for my Lord that you worship Him and associate nothing with Him. And I stipulate for myself that you protect me from what you protect yourselves and your wealth from." They said: "If we do that, what do we get?" He said: "Paradise." They said: "The sale has been profitable; we will neither cancel it nor seek its cancellation."]]. "Fighting" (yuqatiluna) here carries the sense of a command, like His words: ﴿You strive in the way of God with your wealth and your lives﴾. It is also read as "fa-yaqtulun wa-yuqtalun," with the first verb active and the second passive, and vice versa. "Waʿdan" is an emphasizing verbal noun (masdar muʾakkid). He informs that this promise which He made to those who strive in His way is a firm promise, which He has affirmed in the Torah and the Gospel as He affirmed it in the Qur'an. Then He said: ﴿And who is more faithful to his covenant than God?﴾, because breaking a promise is ugly, and noble people among creatures do not commit it, though it is possible for them because of their need; how much more so for the Self-Sufficient, to whom ugliness never applies. You will not find an encouragement to jihad more excellent or more eloquent than this.

"At-tā'ibūna" (al-tā'ibūna, the repentant) is in the nominative (marfū'), by way of praise (ʿalā al-madḥ). That is: "they are the repentant ones", meaning the believers mentioned. Evidence for this is the reading of ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿūd) and Ubayy (Ibn Kaʿb), may Allah be pleased with them both, "al-tā'ibīna" with a yāʾ, down to "wa-al-ḥāfiẓīna" (and the guardians), in the accusative by way of praise. It is also permissible for it to be in the genitive (jarr) as an adjective (ṣifah) of "the believers". Al-Zajjāj permitted that it be a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate (khabar) is omitted, meaning: "the repentant, the worshippers, [and] also the people of Paradise, even if they did not fight", like His words ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾. It was also said that it is in the nominative as a substitution (badal) from the pronoun in "yuqātilūna" (they fight). It is also permissible that it be a subject with "al-ʿābidūna" (the worshippers) as its predicate, and what follows it a predicate after a predicate, meaning: those who repent from unbelief in the true sense, combining these qualities. From al-Ḥasan (al-Baṣrī): they are those who repented from polytheism and disavowed hypocrisy. "Al-ʿābidūna": those who worshipped Allah alone, sincerely devoted worship to Him, and were eager for it. "Al-sāʾiḥūna" (the wanderers): the fasting ones, likened to people of wandering in the earth in their restraint from their desires. It was also said: they are seekers of knowledge who travel the earth seeking it in its sources.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 113:

It is said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said to his uncle Abu Talib: "You are the greatest of people in your claim upon me, and the best of them in his kindness to me. So say a word by which I may intercede for you." He refused, and so he (ﷺ) said: "I will not cease to seek forgiveness for you unless I am forbidden from it." [It is agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib from his father, in a narration; al-Hakim overlooked it and so added it to his al-Mustadrak.] Then this was revealed.

It is also said: When he conquered Makkah, he asked which of his two parents he had most recent remembrance of. It was said: "Your mother Aminah." So he visited her grave at al-Abwa', then stood weeping and said: "I asked my Lord for permission to visit the grave of my mother, and He permitted me. I asked Him for permission to seek forgiveness for her, but He did not permit me." Then this was revealed. This view is more sound, because the death of Abu Talib occurred before the Hijrah, whereas this is the last thing revealed at Madinah. It is also said: he sought forgiveness for his father. It is also said: the Muslims said, "What prevents us from seeking forgiveness for our fathers and our close relatives, when Ibrahim sought forgiveness for his father, and here is Muhammad seeking forgiveness for his uncle?" So Allah revealed: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to seek forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they were close relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire﴾, meaning: it was not valid for him to seek forgiveness, according to the judgment and wisdom of Allah, after it had become clear to them that they are companions of Hellfire, because they died in shirk.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 114:

Talha recited, "wa-ma istaghfara Ibrahimu li-abihi" (and Ibrahim did not ask forgiveness for his father). It is also reported from him: "wa-ma yastaghfiru Ibrahimu" (and Ibrahim did not ask forgiveness), in the sense of relating a past situation. ﴿Except for a promise he had made to him﴾: that is, Ibrahim promised his father, and this is his saying, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you" (﴿la-astaghfiranna laka﴾). What supports this is the reading of al-Hasan and Hammad, in the transmission: "wa'adaha abahu" (he promised his father).

If you ask: how was it hidden from Ibrahim that asking forgiveness for an unbeliever is not permitted, so that he had to be promised (before he realized)? I answer: it is possible that he thought that as long as there was hope of his faith, it was permissible to ask forgiveness for him. Moreover, the impermissibility of asking forgiveness for an unbeliever is known only through revelation, since reason permits that God might forgive an unbeliever. Do you not see the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to his uncle: "I will surely ask forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden"? It is reported from al-Hasan that it was said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "So-and-so asks forgiveness for his polytheist parents," and he said: "We too ask forgiveness for them," and then it was revealed. [[I have not found it.]] It is reported from Ali, may God be pleased with him: "I saw a man asking forgiveness for his two parents while they were polytheists, so I said to him, and he said: Did not Ibrahim ask forgiveness for his father?" [[Narrated by al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shayba, Abu Ya'la and al-Bazzar, through Abu al-Khalil from Ali, who said: "I heard a man asking forgiveness for his parents..." — the hadith.]]

If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying, ﴿So when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of God, he disowned him﴾? I answer: its meaning is that when it became clear to him, through revelation, that he would not believe and would die an unbeliever, and his hope in him was cut off, he ceased asking forgiveness for him. It is like His saying, ﴿after it had become clear to them that they are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾. ﴿Awwah﴾ is an intensive form (fa'\"al), from "awwah," like "kal'al" from "lu'lu'" (pearl), and it means one who frequently utters "uff" (sighs in sorrow). Its meaning is that, because of his great compassion, tenderness and forbearance, he was inclined toward his unbelieving father and asked forgiveness for him, despite the father's harshness toward him. [[His saying "despite his harshness toward him" means his difficulty of disposition. In al-Sihah: "a man shaks" (with sukun) means one difficult in temperament. (Ghayn)]] And His saying, ﴿and that I stone you﴾.

This means: what Allah commanded them to guard against and avoid, such as seeking forgiveness for the polytheists and other things He forbade. He made clear that it is prohibited, and He does not hold His servants whom He guided to Islam accountable for it, nor does He call them misguided or forsake them, unless they commit it after the prohibition has been made clear to them and they know that it must be guarded against and avoided. Before knowledge and clarification, there is no blame upon them, just as they are not held accountable for drinking wine or for exchanging a saa' for two saa's before its prohibition. This is an explanation of the excuse of one who feared being held accountable for seeking forgiveness for the polytheists before the prohibition of it was revealed. In this verse there is a severe warning that should not be overlooked: whoever is guided to Islam and then commits some of Allah's prohibited acts falls under the ruling of leading astray.

What is meant by "that which they guard against" is what must be guarded against because of a prohibition. As for what is known to be forbidden by reason [[Mahmud said: "As for what its prohibition is perceived by reason... etc." Ahmad said: This is a branch of the principle of "goodness and ugliness" (tahsin wa-taqbih, the doctrine that acts are good or bad by their nature as judged by reason), and that reason is the judge, while the revealed law uncovers what reason finds obscure and follows its requirement. This principle has already been shown to be invalid in more than one place, and God is the one who grants success.]], such as truthfulness in reporting and returning a deposit, it does not depend on revelatory prescription (tawqif, the principle that rulings are known only through revelation).

[[The statement "As for what is known by reason, such as truthfulness" is based on the view of the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) that a ruling may be known by reason, whereas according to Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni scholars) there is no ruling before the revealed law. (Gh.)]]

This means: what Allah commanded them to guard against and avoid, such as seeking forgiveness for the polytheists and other things He forbade. He made clear that it is prohibited, and He does not hold His servants whom He guided to Islam accountable for it, nor does He call them misguided or forsake them, unless they commit it after the prohibition has been made clear to them and they know that it must be guarded against and avoided.
