The Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 9, verse 117:

﴿Allah turned in forgiveness to the Prophet﴾, like His saying ﴿that Allah may forgive you your earlier and later sins﴾, and His saying ﴿and seek forgiveness for your sin﴾. This is an exhortation to the believers to repentance, and an indication that no believer is free of need for repentance and seeking forgiveness, not even the Prophet, the Emigrants and the Helpers. It also shows the excellence of repentance and its high standing with Allah, and that the attribute of those who repent and turn often (al-tawwabin al-awwabin) is the attribute of the prophets, just as He described them as the righteous (al-salihin), to make manifest the excellence of righteousness.

It has been said: its meaning is that Allah turned in forgiveness to him concerning his granting permission to the hypocrites to remain behind from him, like His saying ﴿Allah pardon you﴾.

﴿In the hour of hardship﴾: in its time. The word "hour" (sa'a) is used in the sense of unrestricted time, just as the morning (ghadah), the evening (ashiyyah) and the day (yawm) are used. The poet says:

*"In the morning when the scholars of Bakr ibn Wa'il rose up, and the horses' chests swayed toward the side of Tamim"*

The "morning" here means unrestricted time, to suit the praise. *Tafat* (with the letter fa') means: rose and became high. It is also transmitted with the letter ghayn, and the meaning is likewise "rose high." *ʿUlamaʾ* originally is *ʿalā al-māʾ* (upon the water), and the meaning is that their status rose in honour and glory while that of others sank, just as an object rises upon the surface of water while another sinks. Or the meaning is that they overflowed (taghaw), with the ghayn, like the most overflowing thing, water: water overflows over people, and they overflow over it. In this is an indication of courage. Bakr ibn Wa'il is the name of the father of a tribe, and the tribe was named after him. *Al-wa'il* originally means the one who hastens and seeks refuge.

*Wa-ʿaajat*: that is, they inclined the chests of their horses. The striking of waves upon the chests is used because motion and turning from one direction to another are manifested by them.

*Shatr*: that is, the direction of the tribe of Tamim.

*"And when we reckoned every fair one to be fat, on the evening when we clashed with Judham and Himyar"*

*"So when we clashed spear with spear, some of them, their staves refused to break."*

These verses are by Zufar ibn al-Harith al-Kilabi, one of the Successors, who witnessed the Battle of Siffin and others. It is said as a proverb: "Not every fair one is fat, nor every black one a date," so what is here is an allusion to it. The "evening" here means unrestricted time, not only the end of the day, as the context indicates. *Al-muqarʿah* means striking with spears and swords. It is also transmitted as "nights when we met." Judham is the name of a tribe, named after it, and it is from Yemen; they used to dwell in the mountains of Hasma, and it is said they were the first place from which the flood receded because of their elevation. Himyar is also the name of an ancestor of a tribe, named after him. It is also transmitted as *Judaman*, with tanwin, out of poetic necessity.

*Al-nabʿ* is a tree from which spears are made. He says: we had thought them weak, that we would defeat them as we had others. His saying "every fair one is fat" is a metaphorical image (istiʿarah tamthiliyyah) for this. *ʿAshiyyah* is in the accusative, governed by *ḥasibnā*. When the spears met between us, they refused to break. He likened them to something that can truly refuse, by way of metonymy (kinayah). "Refused" is a takhyil (imaginative figure), and beyond that it is a metonymy for the strength of the two tribes and their not being defeated. It is also said that he describes them with generosity and good hospitality, so the whole speech, with its metaphor and metonymy, is transferred from the state of the meeting of lines in war to the state of the meeting of guests with the host and his not being unable to provide for them, by way of simile. But the evening remains in its literal sense. Even with this interpretation, his saying "we had reckoned every fair one to be fat" tells against it, and this is the saying of one who did not read the rest of the poem, for it explicitly states that the meaning is their fighting against them and their repaying them.

*"When my heir comes one day seeking wealth, he will find a handful gathered, neither full nor empty."*

*"He will find a horse like the bridle, and a sword which, when shaken, does not accept the chopping."*

*"And a spear of Khatt, whose joints are like the stones of the qaseb date, exceeding by a cubit the ten cubits."*

These are by Hatim al-Ta'i. The "day" here means unrestricted time, unlike "daytime" (nahar), which is restricted to a bounded span, and this is the general usage of the Arabs. The "wealth" means the estate, since it is its cause. *Jam'u kaff* (with a damma): the clenched hand, so it is an idafah of attribute to what it qualifies. *Mal'a* means full. *Ṣafara* (with kasra) and *aṣfara* mean: he became poor, and *ṣafr* (with damma, and also with kasra) means empty. *Al-ṣārim*: the cutting sword. *Ḥasama al-shay'*: he cut it with a very sharp sword, and it is also applied to the sharpness of iron. *Al-habr*: cutting off a large piece of flesh. *Al-sumrah*: a colour between whiteness and dark brown. *Al-khatt*: a place to which fine spears are attributed. *Al-kaʿb*: what lies between two joints. *Al-qasb*: a kind of date with a hard stone. *Rawaʾa al-shay'* and *arba*: increased. Its *bā'* is sometimes changed to *mīm*, as transmitted: *qad armā*. *Dhirāʿan* is a specification (tamyiz), meaning it exceeds the ten cubits by one cubit, so its measure is eleven cubits, and the clause is a description of the spear. It is possible that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the joints: that is, the joints exceed, in the state where it is a cubit beyond ten of the joints, so *dhirāʿan* is a circumstance within a circumstance, and when its joints resemble the stones in this state, each cubit of it exceeds ten joints. It is also permissible that *dhirāʿan* is a specification transferred from the subject, that is: each cubit of this spear exceeds ten joints. He says:

When my heir seeks my estate, he will find things truly worth grasping in the hand out of eagerness for them, so his saying "a gathered handful" is a metonymy for that. It is "neither full" in the case of one who loves wealth, and "neither empty" for one who meets heroes. The second clause replaces the first. He likened his horse to the bridle in slenderness and firmness; "when shaken," that is, moved, is a metonymy for striking with it. He likened it to one who can be pleased, by way of metonymy, and "did not accept" is a takhyil: that is, he finds a lean horse, a cutting sword, and a long or firm spear. The present verb is put in the jussive after *idhā*, and this is rare.

And *al-ʿusrah*: their condition in the expedition of Tabuk, when they were in hardship of mounts: ten would take turns riding a single camel. And in hardship of provision: they ate spoiled dates, rotten barley, and rancid fat. [Note by the editor: his saying "and rancid fat" means the stinking oil. *Ḥamarrat al-qayẓ*, with the rāʾ doubled, means the intensity of its heat, from *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*. (ʿ)] The hardship reached such a point that two people would share a single date, and sometimes a group would suck on it to drink water after it. And in hardship of water, until they slaughtered the camels and squeezed out their dung. And in a hard time, from the scorching of summer and from drought, famine and severe straitness, ﴿the hearts of a group of them nearly swerved﴾ from steadfastness in faith, or from following the Messenger in that expedition and going out with him. In ﴿nearly﴾ there is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), and Sibawayh likened it to their saying: "There is no creation like Him." It was also read as *yazīgh* with the letter yāʾ. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud): ﴿after the hearts of a group of them had swerved﴾, meaning the believers who stayed behind, like Abu Lubabah and others. ﴿Then He turned to them in forgiveness﴾ is a repetition for emphasis. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the group: He turned to them in forgiveness for their having been on the verge of it.

﴿And [He also turned in forgiveness] to the three who were left behind,﴾ [i.e.] Ka'b ibn Malik, Murarah ibn al-Rabi', and Hilal ibn Umayyah. The meaning of *khullifu* is that they were left behind from the expedition (ghazw). It is also said: [it refers to] Abu Lubabah and his companions, when they were forgiven after them. It was also read as *khallafu*, meaning they left behind those who fought, who stayed in Medina, or [it means] they became corrupt, from *al-khalifah* (one who has no good in him) and *khulufu al-fam* (the change of the mouth's odor). [[Note of the editor on "al-khalifah" and "khulufu al-fam": *al-khalifah* is that which has no good in it, and *khulufu al-fam* is its change; from *al-Sihah*. (ʿ)]] Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, read it as *khalafu*. Al-A'mash read: ﴿and upon the three who were left behind﴾ (al-mukhallafin). [The phrase] ﴿with all its vastness﴾ means: despite its expanse. It is a metaphor for their bewilderment in their affair, as though they found no place in it in which to settle, from their anxiety and distress over what they were in. ﴿and their souls constricted for them﴾ means their hearts, which could hold neither comfort nor joy, because they were torn apart by extreme loneliness and grief. ﴿And they thought﴾ and knew ﴿that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him﴾, that is, in seeking His forgiveness. ﴿Then He turned to them so that they might repent﴾: then He returned to them with acceptance and mercy again and again, so that they would remain steadfast in their repentance and be firm, and so that they would repent also in what is to come, should any fault again escape them, knowing that Allah is Ever-Relenting toward whoever repents, even if he returns a hundred times in a day.

It is reported that some of the believers stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Among them were some who then regretted it, hated their position, and caught up with him. From al-Hasan: "It reached me that one of them had an orchard that was better than a hundred thousand dirhams, and he said: 'O my orchard, only your shade and waiting for your fruit kept me back. Go, for you are in the way of Allah.' Another had nothing but his family, and he said: 'O my family, only my attachment to you held me back and kept me from going. By Allah, I will surely endure the deserts until I catch up with the Messenger of Allah.' He mounted and caught up with him. Another had nothing but himself, neither family nor property, and he said: 'O self, only love of life for you held me back. By Allah, I will surely endure hardships until I catch up with the Messenger of Allah,' so he slung his provisions and caught up with him." Al-Hasan said: "That is how, by Allah, the believer repents of his sins and does not persist in them."

From Abu Dharr al-Ghifari: his camel was slow with him, so he carried his belongings on his back and followed the trail of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on foot. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw his figure, he said: "Be Abu Dharr!" The people said: "It is he." He said: "May Allah have mercy on Abu Dharr: he walks alone, dies alone, and will be raised alone." [[Narrated by Ibn Ishaq in *al-Maghazi*, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il*. He said: "Buraydah ibn Sufyan told me, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: 'When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out for Tabuk, a man kept lagging behind' — and he mentioned it at length.]] And from Abu Khaythamah [[Narrated by Ibn Sa'd in this form without a chain. Al-Waqidi mentioned it in *al-Maghazi*: "Muhammad ibn Rifa'ah ibn Tha'labah ibn Abi Malik told us, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: 'I asked Zayd ibn Thabit about the expedition of Tabuk,' and he related the long story. In it: 'Abu Khaythamah, whose name was Abdullah ibn Khaythamah al-Salimi, returned after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had traveled ten days, until he entered upon his two wives on a hot day' — and he mentioned it. Ibn Ishaq narrated it in *al-Maghazi*, and al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi by his route, saying: 'Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Amr ibn Hazm told me that Abu Khaythamah Salim...' and he mentioned it. It has another route with al-Tabarani, from the route of Ibrahim ibn Sa'd ibn Khaythamah: 'My father told us, from his father, who said: I stayed behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the expedition of Tabuk, until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went on, and I entered an orchard' — and he mentioned the report, similar to it." In the two *Sahihs*, in the long hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik: "When he reached Tabuk, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'What has happened to Ka'b ibn Malik?'" — and he mentioned the report. In it: "While they were like that, they saw a man approaching through the mirage. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Be Abu Khaythamah!' and it was Abu Khaythamah."]] that he reached his orchard, where he had a beautiful wife. She had spread out the shade for him, laid down the mat, and brought him ripe dates and cold water. He looked and said:

"A dense shade, ripe dates, cold water, and a beautiful woman, while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is in the sun and the wind. This is not good!" So he stood up, saddled his she-camel, took his sword and spear, and went off like the wind. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cast his gaze toward the road, and behold, a rider was lifted up by the mirage. He said: "Be Abu Khaythamah," and it was he. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rejoiced at him and asked forgiveness for him.

Among them were some who remained and did not catch up with him, namely the three. Ka'b said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) returned, I greeted him, and he answered me as one who was angry. After he had mentioned me, he said: 'I wish I knew what kept Ka'b back.' It was said to him: 'What held him back was the fineness of his two cloaks and his looking at his own sides.' He said: 'Far be it! By Allah, I know of him only virtue and Islam.'" [[Agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Ka'b ibn Malik, from Ka'b ibn Malik, in long form. In it: "A man from the Banu Salamah said: 'His two cloaks held him back,' and Mu'adh ibn Jabal said: 'What a bad thing you have said' — the hadith." The compiler (al-mukhrij) remarked: the error in it is from the author. Ahmad also narrated it, and in it: "A man from my people said: 'O Messenger of Allah, his two cloaks held him back and his looking at his own sides.'" Al-Waqidi in *al-Maghazi* reported that the one who said this was Abdullah ibn Qays.]] The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade people from speaking to us, the three of us, so people became strange toward us, and no one spoke to us, near or far. When forty nights had passed, we were commanded to keep away from our wives and not to approach them. When fifty nights were complete, behold, I heard a call from the summit of Sal': "Good news, O Ka'b ibn Malik!" I fell down in prostration. I was as my Lord described me: ﴿the earth constricted for them despite its vastness, and their souls constricted for them﴾. Good tidings followed one another. I put on my garment and went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and behold, he was sitting in the mosque with the Muslims around him. Talhah ibn Ubaydullah got up to me, hurrying until he shook my hand and said: "May Allah's forgiveness of you be a happy thing for you." I will never forget that for Talhah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whose face was shining like the moon, said: "Good news, O Ka'b ibn Malik, of the best day that has passed over you since your mother bore you." Then he recited the verse to us. [[Note on "Sal'": *Sal'* is a mountain in Medina, from *al-Sihah*. (ʿ)]]

From Abu Bakr al-Warraq: he was asked about sincere repentance (al-tawbah al-nasuh), and he said:

"If the earth constricts for the penitent despite its vastness, and his own soul constricts for him, that is the repentance of Ka'b ibn Malik and his two companions."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verse 119–121:

﴿with the truthful﴾. It is also read: ﴿from the truthful﴾. They are those who were truthful in the religion of God in intention, speech and action; or those who were truthful in their faith and in their covenant with God and His Messenger to obey, from His saying: ﴿Among the believers are men who have been true to what they covenanted with God﴾. It is said: they are the three (who stayed behind). That is, be like these in their truthfulness and steadfastness. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him, that the address is to those among the People of the Book who believed: that is, be with the Muhajirun and the Ansar, agree with them, join their ranks, and be truthful as they are truthful. It is also said that it is addressed to those of the Tulaqa' who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk. It is narrated from Ibn Masʿud, may God be pleased with him [[Al-Tha'labi narrated it through the transmission of Wahb ibn Jarir from Shuʿbah from ʿAmr ibn Murrah from Abu ʿUbaydah from his father, as a statement of Ibn Masʿud (mawquf); Ishaq also narrated it in his Musnad from Wahb, and al-Bayhaqi related it in abridged form in al-Shuʿab. al-Hakim related it as a marfuʿ report, through the transmission of Abu al-Ahwas from ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud, raising it: "Lying is not fitting in earnest or in jest, nor that a man promise his son and then not fulfil it."]]: Lying is not fitting in earnest or in jest, nor that any of you promise his child and then not fulfil it. Recite, if you wish: ﴿and be with the truthful﴾. Is there then any concession in it?

﴿and that they should not prefer themselves over his self﴾. They were commanded to accompany him in hardship and adversity, to endure together with him the terrors with willingness, eagerness and gladness, and to cast themselves into the hardships that he himself encounters, knowing that his self is the most honoured soul with God and the most dear to Him. So when that soul, with its nobility and dignity, is exposed to plunging into hardship and terror, it is incumbent upon all other souls to rush headlong [[His saying "tatahafat" means "tatasaqat" (fall down). (ʿ)]] into what it is exposed to, and its owners should not care for it or give it any weight, and it should be the lightest and least valued thing to them. Much more so, they should not hold themselves too high [[His saying "yarbaʾu" means "yartafiʿu" (rise up). From al-Sihah. (ʿ)]] to follow and accompany it, and should not grudge themselves for what he has freely given himself for. This is a forceful prohibition, together with a condemnation of their conduct, a rebuke to them for it, and an incitement to follow him with pride and zeal. ﴿That﴾ refers to what is indicated by His saying: ﴿it was not for the people of Medina and the Bedouins around them to stay behind﴾, namely the obligation to accompany him, as if it were said: that obligation is because ﴿they will not suffer thirst, nor fatigue, nor hunger in the way of God﴾, and they do not tread on any place of the unbelievers with the hooves of their horses, the hooves of their mounts, or their feet, nor do they act in a way that enrages them and constricts their chests, ﴿and they inflict no harm upon an enemy﴾, neither by killing, capturing, plunder, defeat, nor otherwise, ﴿but a righteous deed is recorded for them thereby﴾, and they deserve reward and nearness with God, and that is what necessitates accompanying him. It is possible that by treading (wat') is meant striking and annihilation, not treading with feet and hooves, as in his saying, peace be upon him: "The last trampling that God trampled at Wajj" [[His saying "Wajj" is a town in al-Taʾif. From al-Sihah. (ʿ)]]. The "mawti'" is either a verbal noun like "al-mawrid," or a place. If it is a place, then the meaning of ﴿that enrages the unbelievers﴾ is: their being trodden upon enrages them. "Al-nayl" may also be an emphatic verbal noun, or may mean "al-manil." It is said: "nala minhu" when he harmed him and diminished him; and it is general to everything that grieves them, distresses them, and inflicts harm upon them. This indicates that whoever intends good, his striving therein is appreciated, whether standing, sitting, walking, speaking, or otherwise; and likewise for evil. By this verse the companions of Abu Hanifa have argued that reinforcements arriving after the end of the war share in the spoils with us, since treading upon their abodes is something that enrages them and afflicts them. Indeed the Prophet, peace be upon him, gave a share to the Banu ʿAmir who arrived after the war had ended [[I have not seen it in this form. al-Tibi attributed it to Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi. In the Sahihayn, from Abu Musa: "We heard of the emigration of the Prophet while we were in Yemen, so I and some brothers of mine set out emigrating to him—I was the youngest of them—" the hadith; he said: "So he gave us a share, and he gave no share to anyone who was absent from the conquest of Khaybar except the companions of our ship."]]. And Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, sent al-Muhajir ibn Abi Umayya and Ziyad ibn Abi Labid as reinforcements with ʿIkrimah ibn Abi Jahl with five hundred men; they joined after the conquest, and he gave them a share [[Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it: Abdullah ibn Idris narrated to us from Muhammad ibn Ishaq from Yazid ibn Abi Habib: "Abu Bakr sent ʿIkrimah ibn Abi Jahl as reinforcement for al-Muhajir ibn Abi Umayya and Ziyad ibn Asad. They reached the people after it had been conquered for them." He said: "So he made them partners in the spoils." al-Waqidi related it in his Maghazi: Ismail ibn Ibrahim narrated to us from ʿUqbah from al-Harith ibn Fudayl, who said: When the letter of Ziyad ibn Labid came—and he mentioned something similar.]]. According to al-Shafiʿi: reinforcements do not share in the spoils with those who gained them. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read: "ẓamaʾ" with a long vowel. It is said: "ẓamiʾa ẓamaʾah" and "ẓamaʾ." ﴿And they spend no expenditure, small or large﴾, ﴿even a date, or even the lash of a whip﴾, ﴿nor a large amount, like what ʿUthman, may God be pleased with him, spent for the army of hardship﴾. ﴿And they cross no valley﴾: that is, no land, in their going and coming. The "wadi" is every opening between mountains and hills that serves as a channel for floods; in origin it is a form of "fāʿil" from "wadā," meaning it flowed. From it comes "al-wadi" (a kind of seminal fluid). It has become common in the usage of the Arabs in the sense of land. They say: "Do not pray in the valley of someone other than you." ﴿except that a record is made for them of that﴾, namely of the expenditure and the crossing of the valley. It is possible that the pronoun in it refers to "righteous deed." His saying ﴿that He may recompense them﴾ is connected to "was written" (kutiba), meaning: it was recorded in their scrolls for the purpose of recompense.

﴿with the truthful﴾. It is also read: ﴿from the truthful﴾. Recite, if you wish: ﴿and be with the truthful﴾. Is there then any concession in it?

﴿and that they should not prefer themselves over his self﴾. They were commanded to accompany him in hardship and adversity, to endure together with him the terrors with willingness, eagerness and gladness, and to cast themselves into the hardships that he himself encounters, knowing that his self is the most honoured soul with God and the most dear to Him. So when that soul, with its nobility and dignity, is exposed to plunging into hardship and terror, it is incumbent upon all other souls to rush headlong [[His saying "tatahafat" means "tatasaqat" (fall down). (ʿ)]] into what it is exposed to, and its owners should not care for it or give it any weight, and it should be the lightest and least valued thing to them. Much more so, they should not hold themselves too high [[His saying "yarbaʾu" means "yartafiʿu" (rise up). From al-Sihah. (ʿ)]] to follow and accompany it, and should not grudge themselves for what he has freely given himself for. This is a forceful prohibition, together with a condemnation of their conduct, a rebuke to them for it, and an incitement to follow him with pride and zeal. ﴿That﴾ refers to what is indicated by His saying: ﴿it was not for the people of Medina and the Bedouins around them to stay behind﴾, namely the obligation to accompany him, as if it were said: that obligation is because ﴿they will not suffer thirst, nor fatigue, nor hunger in the way of God﴾, and they do not tread on any place of the unbelievers with the hooves of their horses, the hooves of their mounts, or their feet, nor do they act in a way that enrages them and constricts their chests, ﴿and they inflict no harm upon an enemy﴾, neither by killing, capturing, plunder, defeat, nor otherwise, ﴿but a righteous deed is recorded for them thereby﴾, and they deserve reward and nearness with God, and that is what necessitates accompanying him. It is possible that by treading (wat') is meant striking and annihilation, not treading with feet and hooves, as in his saying, peace be upon him: "The last trampling that God trampled at Wajj" [[His saying "Wajj" is a town in al-Taʾif. From al-Sihah. (ʿ)]]. The "mawti'" is either a verbal noun like "al-mawrid," or a place. If it is a place, then the meaning of ﴿that enrages the unbelievers﴾ is: their being trodden upon enrages them. "Al-nayl" may also be an emphatic verbal noun, or may mean "al-manil." It is said: "nala minhu" when he harmed him and diminished him; and it is general to everything that grieves them, distresses them, and inflicts harm upon them. This indicates that whoever intends good, his striving therein is appreciated, whether standing, sitting, walking, speaking, or otherwise; and likewise for evil. By this verse the companions of Abu Hanifa have argued that reinforcements arriving after the end of the war share in the spoils with us, since treading upon their abodes is something that enrages them and afflicts them. Indeed the Prophet, peace be upon him, gave a share to the Banu ʿAmir who arrived after the war had ended [[I have not seen it in this form. al-Tibi attributed it to Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi. In the Sahihayn, from Abu Musa: "We heard of the emigration of the Prophet while we were in Yemen, so I and some brothers of mine set out emigrating to him—I was the youngest of them—" the hadith; he said: "So he gave us a share, and he gave no share to anyone who was absent from the conquest of Khaybar except the companions of our ship."]]. And Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him, sent al-Muhajir ibn Abi Umayya and Ziyad ibn Abi Labid as reinforcements with ʿIkrimah ibn Abi Jahl with five hundred men; they joined after the conquest, and he gave them a share [[Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated it: Abdullah ibn Idris narrated to us from Muhammad ibn Ishaq from Yazid ibn Abi Habib: "Abu Bakr sent ʿIkrimah ibn Abi Jahl as reinforcement for al-Muhajir ibn Abi Umayya and Ziyad ibn Asad. They reached the people after it had been conquered for them." He said: "So he made them partners in the spoils." al-Waqidi related it in his Maghazi: Ismail ibn Ibrahim narrated to us from ʿUqbah from al-Harith ibn Fudayl, who said: When the letter of Ziyad ibn Labid came—and he mentioned something similar.]]. According to al-Shafiʿi: reinforcements do not share in the spoils with those who gained them. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read: "ẓamaʾ" with a long vowel. It is said: "ẓamiʾa ẓamaʾah" and "ẓamaʾ." ﴿And they spend no expenditure, small or large﴾, ﴿even a date, or even the lash of a whip﴾, ﴿nor a large amount, like what ʿUthman, may God be pleased with him, spent for the army of hardship﴾. ﴿And they cross no valley﴾: that is, no land, in their going and coming. The "wadi" is every opening between mountains and hills that serves as a channel for floods; in origin it is a form of "fāʿil" from "wadā," meaning it flowed. From it comes "al-wadi" (a kind of seminal fluid). It has become common in the usage of the Arabs in the sense of land. They say: "Do not pray in the valley of someone other than you." ﴿except that a record is made for them of that﴾, namely of the expenditure and the crossing of the valley. It is possible that the pronoun in it refers to "righteous deed." His saying ﴿that He may recompense them﴾ is connected to "was written" (kutiba), meaning: it was recorded in their scrolls for the purpose of recompense.

The lam here reinforces the negation. Its meaning is that it is neither correct nor possible for the whole body of believers to leave their homelands in order to seek knowledge.

[[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is that a general mobilisation of all of them to seek knowledge is not possible... etc." Ahmad said: His words, ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾, on the first interpretation, are an command, not a prohibition. On the second, they are a report whose intended meaning is a prohibition. On the first, the reference is to sending groups from the desert tribes to Madina to acquire fiqh (understanding of religion). Had it been possible for all of them to do this, it would have been permissible or obligatory. If it was not possible, it became obligatory on some of them to stand in for the rest, in the manner of the collective obligation (fard kifaya). Ahmad said: I find no excuse for my absence from attending the campaigns except that my aspiration was diverted to warning against this author. Despite that, I hope from God for a good orientation. May God grant us good, make us successful in what pleases Him, and make our deeds sincere for His noble countenance.]]

It is also said: if it were correct and possible, and did not lead to corruption, it would be obligatory, because the understanding of religion is obligatory on the whole community, and because seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim man and woman. ﴿Why then did not a group from every party of them go forth﴾: since it was not possible for the whole body to go forth, and it was not beneficial, why did not a group from every party of them go forth? That is, from every large congregation, a small group of them, who would suffice for them in going forth, ﴿in order that they might gain understanding in religion﴾, that is, that they might undertake the pursuit of fiqh in it and bear its hardships in acquiring and attaining it; ﴿and that they might warn their people﴾, and that they make their aim and the target of their aspiration in seeking fiqh the warning and guidance of their people and giving them sincere counsel, not the base aims and vile purposes that some jurists pursue, such as seeking prominence, leadership, spreading themselves through the lands, imitating the oppressors in their clothing and mounts, competing with one another, the spread of envy among them, the turning of one's eyes, upon seeing another's school, to glare with jealousy, or the bowing of people before one who is evil, and his zeal to have his heel trodden on, to be followed rather than all other people. How far these are from the words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿They do not desire haughtiness in the land, nor corruption﴾ (28:83). ﴿So that they may beware﴾: intending that they beware of God, so that they act righteously.

Another interpretation: when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) dispatched an expedition, after the Battle of Tabuk and after the severe verses had been revealed concerning those who stayed behind, all the believers would hasten to go forth and all of them cut themselves off from listening to revelation and from understanding religion. So they were commanded that from every party of them a group should go forth to jihad, while the rest remained behind to pursue understanding of religion, so that they would not be cut off from fiqh, which is the greater jihad, because argument by proof has a greater effect than striking with the sword. As for His words ﴿that they may gain understanding﴾, the pronoun in it refers to the groups remaining after the detachment that went forth from among them, ﴿and that they may warn their people﴾, meaning that the remaining groups warn their people who went forth, when they return to them, with what they acquired of knowledge during the days of their absence. According to the first interpretation, the pronoun refers to the group that went forth to Madina for fiqh.

يَلُونَكُمْ: ﴿those who are near to you﴾, أي يقربون منكم، والقتال واجب مع كافة الكفرة قريبهم وبعيدهم [[قال محمود: «القتال واجب مع كافة الكفرة قريبهم وبعيدهم ... الخ» قال أحمد: يتعين القتال على أحد فريقين: إما من نزل بهم عدو وفيهم قوة عليه، ثم على من قرب منهم حتى يكتفوا. وإما من عينهم الامام لذلك وإن بعدت بهم الدار. وإذا أوجب الله على هذه الأمة القتال وإزعاج العدو من دياره وإخراجه من قراره، فوجوبه وقد نزل العدو بدار الإسلام أجدر.]]، ولكن الأقرب فالأقرب أوجب. ونظيره ﴿وَأَنْذِرْ عَشِيرَتَكَ الْأَقْرَبِينَ﴾ [And warn your closest kinsfolk]. وقد حارب رسول الله (ﷺ) قومه، ثم غيرهم من عرب الحجاز، ثم غزا الشأم. وقيل: هم قريظة والنضير وفدك وخيبر. وقيل: الروم، لأنهم كانوا يسكنون الشأم والشأم أقرب إلى المدينة من العراق وغيره، وهكذا المفروض على أهل كل ناحية أن يقاتلوا من وليهم، ما لم يضطر إليهم أهل ناحية أخرى.

وعن ابن عمر رضي الله عنه أنه سئل عن قتال الديلم؟ فقال: عليك بالروم. وقرئ غِلْظَةً بالحركات الثلاث (harakat, the vowel signs), فالغلظة كالشدّة، والغلظة كالضغطه، والغاظة كالسخطة ونحوه ﴿وَاغْلُظْ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ [be harsh with them] ﴿وَلا تَهِنُوا﴾ [and do not weaken], وهو يجمع الجرأة والصبر على القتال وشدّة العداوة والعنف في القتل والأسر، ومنه ﴿وَلا تَأْخُذْكُمْ بِهِما رَأْفَةٌ فِي دِينِ اللَّهِ﴾ [and let not compassion for them take hold of you in the religion of Allah]. ﴿مَعَ الْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ [with the God-fearing]: ينصر من اتقاه فلم يترأف على عدوّه.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 124–125:

﴿Among them are those who say﴾ — that is, among the hypocrites, some say to one another: "Which of you has had his faith increased by this surah?" — by way of denial and mockery of the believers, who hold that faith increases with the increase of knowledge gained through revelation and with acting upon it.

"Which of you" (ayyukum) is in the nominative case, as the subject (mubtada') of the sentence. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read it as ayyakum, in the accusative, with a verb understood that is explained by the following zādathu. The sense is: "Which of you has had this surah increase his faith?" ﴿As for those who believe, it has increased them in faith﴾, because it adds to certainty and steadfastness and brings coolness to the heart. Or, it increased them in action, since the increase of action is an increase in faith, as faith applies both to belief and to action. ﴿But as for those in whose hearts is a disease, it has added defilement to their defilement﴾, that is, disbelief added to their disbelief, because every time revelation is renewed by God they increase in disbelief and hypocrisy; their disbelief grows firm, and their punishment is multiplied.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 9, verses 126–127:**

It was read: ﴿وَلَا يَرَوْنَ﴾ with the ya' and with the ta' (as ﴿وَلَا يَرَوْنَ﴾ and ﴿وَلَا تَرَوْنَ﴾). ﴿يُفْتَنُونَ﴾ means they are tested with sickness, famine and other trials from God, ﴿ثُمَّ لَا يَنْتَهُونَ﴾ (then they do not desist) and ﴿وَلَا يَتُوبُونَ﴾ (nor do they repent) of their hypocrisy, ﴿وَلَا يَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾ (nor do they remember), ﴿وَلَا يَعْتَبِرُونَ﴾ (nor do they take heed), and ﴿وَلَا يَنْظُرُونَ﴾ (nor do they reflect) on their own affairs. Or they are tested in jihad alongside the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they witness his affair and what God sends down to him of His aid and support. Or Satan tempts them, so they lie and break their covenants with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he kills them and punishes them, yet ﴿ثُمَّ لَا يَنْزَجِرُونَ﴾ (then they do not withdraw). ﴿نَظَرَ بَعْضُهُمْ إِلَى بَعْضٍ﴾ (they glance at one another) means they signal to each other with their eyes, denying the revelation [[Mahmud said: "its meaning is that they signal with their eyes, denying the revelation... etc." Ahmad said: it may be a supplication, as he explained. It may also be a statement that God has turned their hearts, that is, prevented them from receiving the truth with acceptance. But al-Zamakhshari shies away from taking it as a statement, because turning hearts away from the truth is not permissible for God, in his view, based on the principle of al-salah wal-aslah (the doctrine that God must do what is best for His servants). He keeps interpreting the apparent meaning whenever this requires it, as he did before in His words ﴿خَتَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَى قُلُوبِهِمْ﴾ (God has sealed their hearts). Since this verse equally allows the supplicatory and the declaratory reading, he is bound, in his view, to take it as a supplication. Then in this supplication there is a fitting correspondence with the act they committed, namely turning away, like His words ﴿وَقَالَتِ الْيَهُودُ يَدُ اللَّهِ مَغْلُولَةٌ غُلَّتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ﴾ (the Jews say, "God's hand is chained." Their hands are chained), and like His words ﴿وَيَتَرَبَّصُ بِكُمُ الدَّوَائِرَ عَلَيْهِمْ دَائِرَةُ السَّوْءِ﴾ (and who wait for misfortune to befall you; upon them be the circle of misfortune).]] and mockery of it, saying ﴿هَلْ يَرَاكُمْ مِنْ أَحَدٍ﴾ (Does anyone see you?) from among the Muslims, ﴿لِنَنْصَرِفَ﴾ (so that we may slip away), for we cannot bear to listen to it, and laughter overcomes us, and we fear exposure among them. Or they exchange glances, consulting on how to plan the departure and slipping away, when they say: ﴿هَلْ يَرَاكُمْ مِنْ أَحَدٍ﴾ (Does anyone see you?). It was also said: its meaning is that when a surah is revealed denouncing the hypocrites, ﴿صَرَفَ اللَّهُ قُلُوبَهُمْ﴾ (God has turned their hearts away), as a supplication against them, with abandonment and with turning their hearts away from the expansion of heart that is in the hearts of the people of faith. ﴿بِأَنَّهُمْ قَوْمٌ لَا يَفْقَهُونَ﴾ (because they are a people who do not understand) means because they do not reflect, so that they would come to understand.

It may also be a statement that God has turned their hearts, that is, prevented them from receiving the truth with acceptance. But al-Zamakhshari shies away from taking it as a statement, because turning hearts away from the truth is not permissible for God, in his view, based on the principle of al-salah wal-aslah (the doctrine that God must do what is best for His servants). He keeps interpreting the apparent meaning whenever this requires it, as he did before in His words ﴿خَتَمَ اللَّهُ عَلَى قُلُوبِهِمْ﴾ (God has sealed their hearts). Since this verse equally allows the supplicatory and the declaratory reading, he is bound, in his view, to take it as a supplication. Then in this supplication there is a fitting correspondence with the act they committed, namely turning away, like His words ﴿وَقَالَتِ الْيَهُودُ يَدُ اللَّهِ مَغْلُولَةٌ غُلَّتْ أَيْدِيهِمْ﴾ (the Jews say, "God's hand is chained." Their hands are chained), and like His words ﴿وَيَتَرَبَّصُ بِكُمُ الدَّوَائِرَ عَلَيْهِمْ دَائِرَةُ السَّوْءِ﴾ (and who wait for misfortune to befall you; upon them be the circle of misfortune).]] and mockery of it, saying ﴿هَلْ يَرَاكُمْ مِنْ أَحَدٍ﴾ (Does anyone see you?) from among the Muslims, ﴿لِنَنْصَرِفَ﴾ (so that we may slip away), for we cannot bear to listen to it, and laughter overcomes us, and we fear exposure among them. Or they exchange glances, consulting on how to plan the departure and slipping away, when they say: ﴿هَلْ يَرَاكُمْ مِنْ أَحَدٍ﴾ (Does anyone see you?). It was also said: its meaning is that when a surah is revealed denouncing the hypocrites, ﴿صَرَفَ اللَّهُ قُلُوبَهُمْ﴾ (God has turned their hearts away), as a supplication against them, with abandonment and with turning their hearts away from the expansion of heart that is in the hearts of the people of faith. ﴿بِأَنَّهُمْ قَوْمٌ لَا يَفْقَهُونَ﴾ (because they are a people who do not understand) means because they do not reflect, so that they would come to understand.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 9, verses 128–129:**

"From yourselves" (min anfusikum): from your own kind and your own lineage, an Arab, a Qurashi, like you. Then he mentions the consequences that follow from kinship and closeness, in His words: "It grieves him that you suffer hardship" (ʿazīzun ʿalayhi mā ʿanittum), meaning: it is difficult for him and burdensome, because he is a part of you, that you should suffer hardship and encounter what you dislike. He fears for you an evil outcome and falling into punishment. "He is eager for you" (ḥarīṣun ʿalaykum), so that no one among you departs from following him and from the happiness of the religion of truth that he brought. "Toward the believers" (bil-muʾminīn), whether among you or among others, "compassionate and merciful" (raʾūfun raḥīm).

It is also recited "min anfusikum," meaning from the most noble and most excellent of you. It is said that this is the reading of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Fatimah and ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with them. It is also said that Allah did not combine two of His names for anyone other than the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), in His saying "compassionate and merciful."

"But if they turn away" (fa-in tawallaw): if they turn away from believing in you and oppose you, then seek help and entrust the matter to Him. He is sufficient for you against their harm, and they cannot harm you, and He is your helper against them.

"The Mighty" (al-ʿaẓīm) is also recited in the nominative case (bil-rafʿ). It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him: "No one can measure the Throne's true extent." It is reported from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "The last verse revealed was: 'There has certainly come to you a Messenger from yourselves.'"

It is reported from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "The Qur'an was not revealed to me except verse by verse and letter by letter, except for Sūrat Barāʾah and Qul huwa Allāhu aḥad, for they were revealed to me along with seventy thousand rows of angels."
